## 2.3 Hashes

### 2.3.1 Concept and encoding

A Hash maps **field -> value** (both strings) under one key. It is the natural representation of an object or record when you need to read or write individual fields.

| Encoding | Condition (defaults) | Property |
|---|---|---|
| `listpack` [7.0+; `ziplist` before] | <= `hash-max-listpack-entries` (128) fields AND every field/value <= `hash-max-listpack-value` (64 bytes) | compact, O(N) lookup over small N |
| `hashtable` | otherwise | O(1) lookup, ~ several times more memory per field |
| `listpackex` [7.4+] | internal variant used when fields have TTLs and the hash is small | you may see it in `OBJECT ENCODING` |

### 2.3.2 Syntax

```
HSET key field value [field value ...]        # multi-field; returns number of NEW fields
HGET key field         HMGET key f1 f2 ...    HGETALL key
HSETNX key field value
HDEL key f1 [f2 ...]   HEXISTS key field      HLEN key     HSTRLEN key field
HINCRBY key field n    HINCRBYFLOAT key field x
HKEYS key   HVALS key  HRANDFIELD key [count [WITHVALUES]]   [6.2+]
HSCAN key cursor [MATCH pat] [COUNT n] [NOVALUES]            [NOVALUES: 7.4+]
```

`HMSET` is **deprecated since 4.0**: `HSET` accepts multiple field/value pairs and should be used instead. (`HMSET` still returns `OK`; `HSET` returns the count of newly created fields.)

**Hash field expiration [7.4+]**, per-field TTL:

```
HEXPIRE key seconds [NX|XX|GT|LT] FIELDS numfields field [field ...]
HPEXPIRE / HEXPIREAT / HPEXPIREAT    (ms, absolute s, absolute ms variants)
HTTL key FIELDS numfields field ...  HPTTL  HEXPIRETIME  HPEXPIRETIME
HPERSIST key FIELDS numfields field ...
```

Each returns an array, one integer per field: `1` TTL set, `0` condition (NX/XX/GT/LT) not met, `-2` field or key does not exist, `2` field deleted (TTL of 0 / time in the past). `HTTL` returns `-1` for a field without TTL and `-2` for a missing field.

**New in 8.0** (atomic combined operations with field TTL):

```
HGETEX key [EX s | PX ms | EXAT ts | PXAT ts | PERSIST] FIELDS numfields field ...   [8.0+]
HSETEX key [FNX | FXX] [EX s | PX ms | EXAT ts | PXAT ts | KEEPTTL] FIELDS numfields field value ...   [8.0+]
HGETDEL key FIELDS numfields field ...                                                [8.0+]
```

`FNX`/`FXX` mean "only if none/all of the fields exist". These give you atomic "read and refresh TTL" and "write with TTL" without a Lua script. Valkey 9 also implements hash field expiration (including `HGETEX`/`HSETEX`); verify exact command availability for your Valkey version.

### 2.3.3 Practical examples

```
127.0.0.1:6379> HSET user:1 name "Tareq" email "t@example.com" plan "pro" logins 0
(integer) 4
127.0.0.1:6379> HGET user:1 name
"Tareq"
127.0.0.1:6379> HMGET user:1 name plan nope
1) "Tareq"
2) "pro"
3) (nil)
127.0.0.1:6379> HINCRBY user:1 logins 1
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> HEXISTS user:1 email
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> HDEL user:1 plan
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> HGETALL user:1
1) "name"
2) "Tareq"
3) "email"
4) "t@example.com"
5) "logins"
6) "1"
127.0.0.1:6379> HSCAN user:1 0 MATCH "e*"
1) "0"
2) 1) "email"
   2) "t@example.com"
127.0.0.1:6379> OBJECT ENCODING user:1
"listpack"

# Field TTL [7.4+]
127.0.0.1:6379> HSET session:s1 userId 42 csrf abc123
(integer) 2
127.0.0.1:6379> HEXPIRE session:s1 300 FIELDS 1 csrf
1) (integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> HTTL session:s1 FIELDS 2 csrf userId
1) (integer) 298
2) (integer) -1
127.0.0.1:6379> HEXPIRE session:s1 600 GT FIELDS 1 csrf     # GT: only extend
1) (integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> HEXPIRE session:s1 100 GT FIELDS 1 csrf     # not greater -> 0
1) (integer) 0

# 8.0
127.0.0.1:6379> HSETEX cart:u7 EX 3600 FIELDS 2 sku:1 2 sku:9 1
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> HGETEX cart:u7 EX 3600 FIELDS 1 sku:1       # read + refresh TTL
1) "2"
127.0.0.1:6379> HGETDEL cart:u7 FIELDS 1 sku:9               # atomic read + remove
1) "1"
```

(Exact reply values such as remaining seconds will differ on your machine.)

### 2.3.4 Hashes vs JSON strings

| Concern | Hash | JSON string (`SET`/`GET`) | RedisJSON (2.12) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Update one field | `HSET` O(1), atomic | read-modify-write or Lua | `JSON.SET key $.a.b v` atomic |
| Read whole object | `HGETALL` (flat strings, you parse types) | `GET` + `JSON.parse` | `JSON.GET key` |
| Nested data | no | yes | yes |
| Types | strings only | any | JSON types, numeric ops |
| Per-field TTL | [7.4+] | no | no |
| Memory (small objects) | very low in listpack | low | higher (tree nodes) |
| Whole-object atomic replace | multiple fields, use `MULTI`/Lua | single `SET` | `JSON.SET $` |
| Cross-language readability | good | good | good |

Measure it yourself:

```
127.0.0.1:6379> HSET h:1 id 1 name "Alice Johnson" email "alice@example.com" age 31 plan "pro"
(integer) 5
127.0.0.1:6379> SET j:1 "{\"id\":1,\"name\":\"Alice Johnson\",\"email\":\"alice@example.com\",\"age\":31,\"plan\":\"pro\"}"
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> MEMORY USAGE h:1
(integer) 152
127.0.0.1:6379> MEMORY USAGE j:1
(integer) 136
```

The numbers above are illustrative; run it on your build. Typical finding: for a *single small object* the JSON string and listpack hash are the same order of magnitude (the hash pays for field names inside the listpack on every object, just like JSON does). The hash advantage is **field-level access and updates**, not necessarily smaller size. Hash wins clearly when you read/update 1 or 2 fields of a 30-field object often; a JSON string wins when you always read the whole object and values are nested or typed.

A TypeScript service for typed objects stored as a hash:

```ts
import { redis } from './redis';

export interface UserProfile {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  email: string;
  logins: number;
  plan: 'free' | 'pro';
}

const key = (id: string) => `user:${id}`;

export async function saveUser(u: UserProfile): Promise<void> {
  await redis.hset(key(u.id), {
    id: u.id, name: u.name, email: u.email, logins: String(u.logins), plan: u.plan,
  });
}

export async function getUser(id: string): Promise<UserProfile | null> {
  const raw = await redis.hgetall(key(id)); // {} when the key is missing
  if (Object.keys(raw).length === 0) return null;
  return {
    id: raw.id, name: raw.name, email: raw.email,
    logins: Number(raw.logins), plan: raw.plan as UserProfile['plan'],
  };
}

export const recordLogin = (id: string) => redis.hincrby(key(id), 'logins', 1);

// Field TTL [7.4+]: ioredis has no typed wrapper for all versions, use call()
export async function setCsrf(sessionId: string, token: string): Promise<void> {
  await redis.hset(`session:${sessionId}`, 'csrf', token);
  await redis.call('HEXPIRE', `session:${sessionId}`, 300, 'FIELDS', 1, 'csrf');
}
```

### 2.3.5 Time complexity

| Command | Complexity |
|---|---|
| `HGET`, `HSET` (per field), `HDEL` (per field), `HEXISTS`, `HINCRBY`, `HLEN`, `HSTRLEN` | O(1) (O(N) on listpack lookup where N <= 128 by default) |
| `HMGET` | O(N) fields requested |
| `HGETALL`, `HKEYS`, `HVALS` | O(N) all fields. Dangerous on big hashes |
| `HSCAN` | O(1) per call, O(N) for full iteration |
| `HRANDFIELD` | O(N) with count, O(1) without |
| `HEXPIRE` family | O(N) fields specified |

### 2.3.6 Memory considerations

- **Listpack vs hashtable**: a hashtable-encoded hash uses several times the memory of a listpack for the same data. Keep objects small and under the thresholds if you have millions of them. Raising `hash-max-listpack-entries` above ~512-1000 trades memory for CPU on every access.
- **Bucketing trick**: instead of 100M keys `img:<id> -> small`, use `img:<id/1000>` as the Hash key and `<id%1000>` as the field. This is the classic Instagram-style memory optimization; it makes each hash <= 1000 fields (raise the listpack limit to match, and note you lose per-entry TTL unless using 7.4+ field TTL).
- Field-TTL metadata adds a per-field overhead; only use it when you need independent expiry.
- Field names are repeated in every hash. Short field names (`n`, `e`) save memory at scale, at the cost of readability. Decide deliberately.

### 2.3.7 Use cases

User/profile/object storage, shopping carts (field = SKU, value = quantity, `HINCRBY`), sessions with per-field expiry, feature flags per tenant, aggregated counters per entity (`HINCRBY stats:2026-11-19 api_calls 1`), small config maps, bucketed key-compaction.

### 2.3.8 Limitations

- Values are strings: no nesting, no native numeric/bool types.
- No per-field TTL before 7.4 (so older versions need workaround keys or Sorted Sets).
- `HGETALL` on huge hashes blocks the server; prefer `HSCAN` or maintain a bounded structure.
- Cannot index by value (no "find users where plan=pro"); you maintain Sets or use the Query Engine in Redis 8.
- In Cluster, a Hash lives on one shard, so one giant "global" hash is a hot key / big key.

### 2.3.9 Interview questions

**Q1. Hash or JSON string for a user object?**
- *Short:* Hash if you update/read fields individually; JSON string if you always read/write the whole thing or the data is nested.
- *Detail:* Hash gives atomic per-field ops (`HINCRBY`) and avoids read-modify-write races. A JSON string is a single GET and handles nesting. RedisJSON gives both.
- *Senior follow-up:* How do you do a partial update on a JSON string safely? `WATCH`/`MULTI` optimistic locking or a Lua script; or move to RedisJSON where `JSON.SET $.path` is atomic.
- *Common wrong answer:* "Hashes are always more memory efficient." Only in some shapes; measure with `MEMORY USAGE`.

**Q2. Why is `HGETALL` a production risk, and what are the alternatives?**
- *Short:* O(N) with N unbounded; blocks the event loop and creates huge replies.
- *Detail:* A 500k-field hash makes `HGETALL` take tens of ms and many MB of output. Use `HMGET` with known fields, or `HSCAN` with `COUNT`, and keep hashes bounded (bucket them).
- *Senior follow-up:* Is `HSCAN` a consistent snapshot? No. It guarantees every element present for the whole scan is returned at least once; elements added/removed during the scan may or may not appear, and duplicates are possible.
- *Common wrong answer:* "Use `KEYS` on the hash." `KEYS` is for the keyspace, not a hash's fields.

---

## 2.4 Lists

### 2.4.1 Concept and encoding

A List is an **ordered sequence of strings** with fast push/pop at both ends. Think of it as a deque, not an array: access by index is O(N).

| Encoding | Condition | Property |
|---|---|---|
| `listpack` [7.2+; `ziplist` before] | small lists (within `list-max-listpack-size`) | one contiguous block |
| `quicklist` | otherwise | doubly linked list of listpack nodes; each node capped by `list-max-listpack-size` (default `-2` = 8 KB per node) |

Optional `list-compress-depth` compresses interior nodes (LZF), keeping the ends uncompressed; useful for long lists that are mostly accessed at the ends.

### 2.4.2 Syntax

```
LPUSH key e1 [e2 ...]   RPUSH key e1 [e2 ...]      LPUSHX / RPUSHX (only if list exists)
LPOP key [count]        RPOP key [count]           # count: [6.2+]
LLEN key
LRANGE key start stop   LINDEX key i   LSET key i v   LTRIM key start stop
LINSERT key BEFORE|AFTER pivot element   LREM key count element   LPOS key element [RANK r] [COUNT c] [MAXLEN m]
LMOVE src dst LEFT|RIGHT LEFT|RIGHT                       # [6.2+]
BLPOP k1 [k2 ...] timeout     BRPOP k1 [k2 ...] timeout
BLMOVE src dst LEFT|RIGHT LEFT|RIGHT timeout              # [6.2+]
LMPOP numkeys k1 [k2 ...] LEFT|RIGHT [COUNT n]            # [7.0+]
BLMPOP timeout numkeys k1 [k2 ...] LEFT|RIGHT [COUNT n]   # [7.0+]
```

`RPOPLPUSH` and `BRPOPLPUSH` are **deprecated since 6.2**; use `LMOVE`/`BLMOVE`. Timeouts for blocking commands are in seconds (6.0+ accepts decimals); `0` means block forever.

### 2.4.3 Practical examples

```
127.0.0.1:6379> RPUSH q:emails "a" "b" "c"
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> LPUSH q:emails "z"
(integer) 4
127.0.0.1:6379> LRANGE q:emails 0 -1
1) "z"
2) "a"
3) "b"
4) "c"
127.0.0.1:6379> LPOP q:emails 2
1) "z"
2) "a"
127.0.0.1:6379> LLEN q:emails
(integer) 2
127.0.0.1:6379> LTRIM q:emails 0 99          # keep only newest 100 when used with LPUSH
OK

127.0.0.1:6379> LMOVE q:emails q:processing LEFT RIGHT
"b"
127.0.0.1:6379> BLPOP q:empty 2             # blocks 2 seconds, then:
(nil)
(2.01s)
127.0.0.1:6379> BLPOP q:emails 0            # returns key+value
1) "q:emails"
2) "c"
```

### 2.4.4 Reliable queue pattern

`RPOP`/`BRPOP` removes the item *before* the worker processes it. If the worker crashes, the job is lost. The **reliable queue** pattern moves it atomically to a processing list:

```
 producer             pending list                 processing list
 LPUSH ───────────▶ [ job3 job2 job1 ] ──BLMOVE──▶ [ job1 ]     worker
                       (RIGHT end)       RIGHT→LEFT              │
                                                                 ├─ success: LREM processing 1 job1
                                                                 └─ crash:   a reaper moves stale items back
```

```ts
import Redis from 'ioredis';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';

const PENDING = 'jobs:pending';
const PROCESSING = 'jobs:processing';
const LEASES = 'jobs:leases'; // sorted set: member = raw job payload, score = lease expiry (ms)

export async function enqueue(redis: Redis, payload: object): Promise<string> {
  const id = randomUUID();
  await redis.lpush(PENDING, JSON.stringify({ id, payload }));
  return id;
}

export class ListWorker {
  private running = false;
  // Blocking commands need their own connection
  private readonly blocking: Redis;

  constructor(private readonly redis: Redis, private readonly handler: (p: unknown) => Promise<void>,
              private readonly leaseMs = 30_000) {
    this.blocking = redis.duplicate();
  }

  async start(): Promise<void> {
    this.running = true;
    while (this.running) {
      // Atomically pop from PENDING (right) and push to PROCESSING (left)
      const raw = await this.blocking.blmove(PENDING, PROCESSING, 'RIGHT', 'LEFT', 5);
      if (raw === null) continue;
      await this.redis.zadd(LEASES, Date.now() + this.leaseMs, raw);
      try {
        const { payload } = JSON.parse(raw) as { id: string; payload: unknown };
        await this.handler(payload);
        await this.redis.multi().lrem(PROCESSING, 1, raw).zrem(LEASES, raw).exec();
      } catch (err) {
        // leave it in PROCESSING; the reaper requeues after the lease expires
        console.error('job failed', err);
      }
    }
  }

  async stop(): Promise<void> {
    this.running = false;
    this.blocking.disconnect();
  }
}

/** Run every few seconds from one instance (use a lock) to recover crashed work. */
export async function reapExpired(redis: Redis): Promise<number> {
  const expired = await redis.zrangebyscore(LEASES, '-inf', Date.now());
  let n = 0;
  for (const raw of expired) {
    const tx = await redis
      .multi()
      .lrem(PROCESSING, 1, raw)
      .zrem(LEASES, raw)
      .lpush(PENDING, raw)
      .exec();
    if (tx && (tx[0][1] as number) > 0) n++;
  }
  return n;
}
```

Notes on this design: it gives at-least-once delivery, so handlers must be idempotent. Identical payloads are distinguished because each carries a UUID. There is no retry limit, delay, priority, dead-letter queue or visibility into progress. That list is the reason queue libraries exist.

### 2.4.5 Limitations as a production queue

| Gap | Consequence |
|---|---|
| No acknowledgment concept | You hand-roll processing lists and reapers (above) |
| No delayed/scheduled jobs | Need a Sorted Set as well |
| No per-job state, retries, backoff, DLQ | You build all of it |
| No consumer groups / fan-out | One consumer receives each item; multiple readers do not each get a copy |
| Visibility / inspection | `LRANGE` only; no "jobs by state" |
| Big payloads | Whole payload copied between lists |
| Ordering under failure | Requeued jobs lose their original position |

Alternatives: **BullMQ** (built on Lists + Sorted Sets + Hashes + Lua, giving retries, delays, rate limits, flows), **Streams** with consumer groups (2.6) for log-like durable messaging, or a broker (RabbitMQ/SQS/Kafka) for cross-system guarantees. Lists remain excellent for lightweight, loss-tolerant or simple work queues, capped "recent items" feeds (`LPUSH` + `LTRIM`), and BLMOVE-based round-robin.

### 2.4.6 Time complexity

| Command | Complexity |
|---|---|
| `LPUSH`, `RPUSH`, `LPOP`, `RPOP` (no count), `LLEN`, `LMOVE`, `BLMOVE` | O(1) |
| `LPOP/RPOP key count` | O(N) in count |
| `LRANGE` | O(S + N): S = offset from nearest end, N = elements returned |
| `LINDEX`, `LSET` | O(N) distance to the nearest end (O(1) at ends) |
| `LINSERT`, `LREM`, `LPOS` | O(N) |
| `LTRIM` | O(N) elements removed |

### 2.4.7 Memory considerations

- Listpack nodes make small elements cheap (a few bytes overhead each) compared with pointer-based linked lists.
- Uncapped lists grow forever. Use `LTRIM` after `LPUSH`, or in a pipeline, to bound them.
- Very long lists with `LRANGE 0 -1` return the whole thing: bound the range.
- Blocking clients waiting on empty lists cost almost nothing, but thousands of them with a short timeout reconnect-storm easily. Use timeouts of 1-5 seconds and loop.

### 2.4.8 Use cases

Simple job queue, activity feed / "latest N" (`LPUSH` + `LTRIM`), undo history, round-robin scheduling (`LMOVE key key LEFT RIGHT` rotates a list), producer/consumer hand-off, capped logs.

### 2.4.9 Interview questions

**Q1. How would you make a Redis List queue not lose jobs when a worker crashes?**
- *Short:* Use `BLMOVE` (previously `BRPOPLPUSH`) to move jobs to a processing list, delete on success, requeue stale entries.
- *Detail:* Pop + process is two steps; moving is one atomic step on the server, so the job is always in exactly one list.
- *Senior follow-up:* Why still not production-ready? No visibility timeout, retries, backoff, DLQ, or consumer groups; at-least-once semantics need idempotent handlers. Use BullMQ or Streams.
- *Common wrong answer:* "Use `BRPOP`, it is atomic." Atomic pop does not protect against failure after the pop.

**Q2. `BLPOP` blocks. How does that interact with Node.js and ioredis?**
- *Short:* It occupies the connection, so use a dedicated connection.
- *Detail:* Redis responds in order per connection. A blocked connection cannot serve `GET`s; sharing one in your app stalls everything queued behind it. `redis.duplicate()` creates a sibling with the same options.
- *Senior follow-up:* What happens on graceful shutdown? Disconnect or send a small non-zero timeout loop so the worker can observe a stop flag; `BLPOP 0` can hang a deployment.
- *Common wrong answer:* "Node is async so it doesn't matter." The blocking is on the Redis connection protocol level, not the JS thread.


---

## 2.5 Sets

### 2.5.1 Concept and encoding

A Set is an **unordered collection of unique strings**. Membership tests and add/remove are O(1), and the server can compute intersections, unions and differences for you.

| Encoding | Condition (defaults) | Property |
|---|---|---|
| `intset` | all members are integers that fit in 64 bits and count <= `set-max-intset-entries` (512) | sorted array of ints, very compact, binary search |
| `listpack` [7.2+] | small, non-integer members: <= `set-max-listpack-entries` (128) and values <= `set-max-listpack-value` (64 bytes) | compact, O(N) lookup on small N |
| `hashtable` | otherwise | O(1) lookup, highest memory |

### 2.5.2 Syntax

```
SADD key m1 [m2 ...]       SREM key m1 [m2 ...]     SCARD key
SISMEMBER key m            SMISMEMBER key m1 m2 ...  # [6.2+]
SMEMBERS key               SSCAN key cursor [MATCH p] [COUNT n]
SPOP key [count]           SRANDMEMBER key [count]   # negative count allows repeats
SMOVE src dst member
SINTER k1 k2 ...    SUNION k1 k2 ...    SDIFF k1 k2 ...
SINTERSTORE dst k1 k2 ...   SUNIONSTORE dst ...   SDIFFSTORE dst ...
SINTERCARD numkeys k1 k2 ... [LIMIT limit]        # [7.0+]
```

`SINTERCARD` returns only the **cardinality** of the intersection (optionally capped by `LIMIT`, so it can stop early), avoiding materializing a huge result.

### 2.5.3 Practical examples

```
127.0.0.1:6379> SADD tags:post:1 redis nodejs cache
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> SADD tags:post:2 redis streams
(integer) 2
127.0.0.1:6379> SISMEMBER tags:post:1 redis
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> SMISMEMBER tags:post:1 redis kafka
1) (integer) 1
2) (integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> SINTER tags:post:1 tags:post:2
1) "redis"
127.0.0.1:6379> SUNION tags:post:1 tags:post:2
1) "redis"
2) "nodejs"
3) "cache"
4) "streams"
127.0.0.1:6379> SDIFF tags:post:1 tags:post:2
1) "nodejs"
2) "cache"
127.0.0.1:6379> SINTERCARD 2 tags:post:1 tags:post:2 LIMIT 10
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> SCARD tags:post:1
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> SSCAN tags:post:1 0 COUNT 100
1) "0"
2) 1) "redis"
   2) "nodejs"
   3) "cache"
```

(Member order from `SMEMBERS`/`SINTER` is not guaranteed.)

### 2.5.4 TypeScript: tags and social relationships

```ts
import { redis } from './redis';

// --- Tags: two directions maintained together ---
export async function tagPost(postId: string, tags: string[]): Promise<void> {
  const p = redis.multi();
  p.sadd(`post:${postId}:tags`, ...tags);
  for (const t of tags) p.sadd(`tag:${t}:posts`, postId);
  await p.exec();
}
export const postsWithAllTags = (tags: string[]) =>
  redis.sinter(...tags.map((t) => `tag:${t}:posts`));

// --- Follow graph ---
export const follow = (a: string, b: string) =>
  redis.multi().sadd(`following:${a}`, b).sadd(`followers:${b}`, a).exec();

export const mutualFollows = (a: string, b: string) =>
  redis.sinter(`following:${a}`, `following:${b}`);

/** People I follow who follow user X ("friends who follow X") */
export const friendsWhoFollow = (me: string, x: string) =>
  redis.sinter(`following:${me}`, `followers:${x}`);

/** Suggestions: followed-by-my-follows minus already followed (bounded to avoid huge unions) */
export async function suggestions(me: string, limit = 20): Promise<string[]> {
  const myFollows = await redis.srandmember(`following:${me}`, 50); // sample
  if (myFollows.length === 0) return [];
  const tmp = `tmp:sugg:${me}:${Date.now()}`;
  await redis
    .multi()
    .sunionstore(tmp, ...myFollows.map((f) => `following:${f}`))
    .sdiffstore(tmp, tmp, `following:${me}`)
    .srem(tmp, me)
    .expire(tmp, 30)
    .exec();
  return redis.srandmember(tmp, limit);
}
```

Unique visitors: `SADD visitors:2026-11-19 <userId>` and `SCARD`. Exact, but memory grows linearly; see 2.8/2.9 for cheaper options.

### 2.5.5 Time complexity

| Command | Complexity |
|---|---|
| `SADD`, `SREM`, `SISMEMBER`, `SCARD`, `SPOP` (no count), `SMOVE` | O(1) per member |
| `SMISMEMBER` | O(N) members checked |
| `SMEMBERS`, `SUNION`, `SDIFF` | O(N) total size |
| `SINTER` | O(N*M), N = smallest set, M = number of sets |
| `SINTERCARD` | same as `SINTER`, but can stop at `LIMIT` |
| `*STORE` variants | same plus the write of the result |
| `SSCAN` | O(1) per call, O(N) for full iteration |

### 2.5.6 Memory considerations

- `intset` is superb for numeric IDs (about 2/4/8 bytes per entry depending on range). If your IDs are numeric strings, keep them numeric; adding one non-integer member converts the whole set to `listpack`/`hashtable`.
- Hashtable sets cost ~50-80 bytes per member. A 100M-user set is multi-GB; consider Bitmaps (dense numeric IDs) or HyperLogLog (approximate count only).
- Big `SUNIONSTORE`/`SINTERSTORE` create big temporary keys; give them a TTL.

### 2.5.7 Use cases

Unique visitors (exact), tags and category membership, followers/following graphs, access-control membership (user-in-role), "who has seen this" dedup, random sampling (`SRANDMEMBER`), lottery draws (`SPOP`), deduplicating job IDs.

### 2.5.8 Limitations

- Unordered: no pagination other than `SSCAN`, which gives no ordering guarantee and may return duplicates.
- `SMEMBERS` on large sets is O(N) and blocking.
- Set algebra across keys requires all keys in the same hash slot on Cluster (use hash tags `{user:1}:following`), which constrains sharding.
- Not suitable for ranking or time-ordering; use Sorted Sets.

### 2.5.9 Interview questions

**Q1. How do you find mutual friends at scale?**
- *Short:* `SINTER following:a following:b` or `SINTERCARD` for just the count.
- *Detail:* Cost is O(N*M) with N the smaller set, so it is fast when one side is small. For celebrities with millions of followers, the intersection is expensive; cap with `SINTERCARD ... LIMIT`, precompute asynchronously, or sample.
- *Senior follow-up:* In Cluster? Keys must be in one slot. Hash tag them (`{a}`) only when you can afford co-location; otherwise intersect in the application or in a graph database.
- *Common wrong answer:* "Fetch both with `SMEMBERS` and intersect in Node." That moves megabytes over the wire and blocks on O(N) reads.

**Q2. Set vs HyperLogLog for unique counts?**
- *Short:* Set is exact and lets you list/test members; HLL is approximate (~0.81% error), fixed at 12 KB, count only.
- *Detail:* Use a Set when you need "has user X visited?" or the list. Use HLL for huge cardinalities where the count suffices.
- *Senior follow-up:* How do you do unique counts per week from daily data? `PFMERGE` for HLL; `SUNIONSTORE` for Sets (memory heavy).
- *Common wrong answer:* "HLL stores hashes of every element." It stores small registers, not elements.

---

## 2.6 Sorted Sets (ZSETs)

### 2.6.1 Concept and encoding

A Sorted Set holds **unique members, each with a floating-point score**, kept ordered by (score, then member lexicographically). It is the structure behind leaderboards, priority queues, time-ordered indexes and rate-limiters.

| Encoding | Condition (defaults) | Property |
|---|---|---|
| `listpack` [7.0+; `ziplist` before] | <= `zset-max-listpack-entries` (128) and member <= `zset-max-listpack-value` (64 bytes) | compact, linear scans |
| `skiplist` + `hashtable` | otherwise | the skiplist gives ordered traversal and rank in O(log N); the hash table gives O(1) `ZSCORE` |

Scores are IEEE-754 doubles: integers are exact up to 2^53; beyond that you lose precision (do not pack 64-bit IDs into a score). `+inf`/`-inf` are accepted.

### 2.6.2 Syntax

```
ZADD key [NX | XX] [GT | LT] [CH] [INCR] score member [score member ...]
ZINCRBY key increment member
ZSCORE key member     ZMSCORE key m1 m2 ...   [6.2+]
ZRANK key member [WITHSCORE]   ZREVRANK key member [WITHSCORE]     # WITHSCORE: [7.2+]
ZCARD key   ZCOUNT key min max   ZLEXCOUNT key min max
ZREM key m1 [m2 ...]   ZREMRANGEBYRANK key start stop   ZREMRANGEBYSCORE key min max
ZPOPMIN key [count]    ZPOPMAX key [count]    BZPOPMIN k1 [k2 ...] timeout    BZPOPMAX ...
ZMPOP numkeys k1 [k2 ...] MIN|MAX [COUNT n]   BZMPOP timeout numkeys ...        # [7.0+]
ZRANGE key start stop [BYSCORE | BYLEX] [REV] [LIMIT offset count] [WITHSCORES]  # [6.2+]
ZRANGESTORE dst src start stop [BYSCORE|BYLEX] [REV] [LIMIT off cnt]            # [6.2+]
ZUNIONSTORE / ZINTERSTORE dst numkeys k1 ... [WEIGHTS w...] [AGGREGATE SUM|MIN|MAX]
ZUNION / ZINTER / ZDIFF ... [WITHSCORES]       # [6.2+]
ZINTERCARD numkeys k1 ... [LIMIT n]            # [7.0+]
ZRANDMEMBER key [count [WITHSCORES]]           # [6.2+]
```

**ZADD flags:**

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `NX` | only add new members; never update existing |
| `XX` | only update existing; never add |
| `GT` [6.2+] | update only if the new score is **greater** than current (new members are still added unless `XX`) |
| `LT` [6.2+] | update only if new score is **less** than current |
| `CH` | return the number of members **changed** (added + updated) rather than only added |
| `INCR` | act like `ZINCRBY`; takes exactly one score/member and returns the new score (or nil if a condition blocked it) |

`NX` cannot be combined with `GT`/`LT`/`XX`.

**Deprecated (since 6.2) in favor of `ZRANGE` with options:** `ZREVRANGE`, `ZRANGEBYSCORE`, `ZREVRANGEBYSCORE`, `ZRANGEBYLEX`, `ZREVRANGEBYLEX`. They still work and are still widely used in libraries and tutorials; BullMQ itself uses some internally. Prefer the unified `ZRANGE` in new code when your minimum server is >= 6.2. Valkey keeps both.

`ZRANGE` argument order matters when using `BYSCORE`/`BYLEX`: with `REV` the first bound is the **max**, the second is the **min**:

```
ZRANGE lb 0 9 REV WITHSCORES                       # top 10 by rank
ZRANGE lb 100 200 BYSCORE WITHSCORES               # score in [100, 200], ascending
ZRANGE lb 200 100 BYSCORE REV LIMIT 0 5            # score in [100,200], descending, first 5
ZRANGE lb "(100" "+inf" BYSCORE                    # exclusive lower bound
ZRANGE names "[a" "(c" BYLEX                       # lexicographic (all scores must be equal)
```

### 2.6.3 Practical examples

```
127.0.0.1:6379> ZADD lb 1500 alice 1200 bob 1800 carol
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> ZADD lb GT CH 1700 bob            # 1700 > 1200: updated
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> ZADD lb GT CH 1000 bob            # lower: ignored
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> ZINCRBY lb 50 alice
"1550"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZRANGE lb 0 -1 REV WITHSCORES
1) "carol"
2) "1800"
3) "bob"
4) "1700"
5) "alice"
6) "1550"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZREVRANK lb alice                  # 0-based rank, highest first
(integer) 2
127.0.0.1:6379> ZRANK lb alice WITHSCORE           # [7.2+]
1) (integer) 0
2) "1550"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZSCORE lb carol
"1800"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZRANGE lb 1600 +inf BYSCORE WITHSCORES
1) "bob"
2) "1700"
3) "carol"
4) "1800"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZPOPMIN lb
1) "alice"
2) "1550"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZCOUNT lb 1000 1750
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> ZREM lb bob
(integer) 1
```

### 2.6.4 TypeScript: leaderboard service

Requirements: update score only if higher (best score), show top N, show a player's rank with neighbours, and handle ties deterministically.

```ts
import Redis from 'ioredis';

export interface Entry { member: string; score: number; rank: number }

export class LeaderboardService {
  constructor(private readonly redis: Redis, private readonly board: string) {}

  private key(season = 'current') { return `lb:${this.board}:${season}`; }

  /** Keep each player's BEST score. GT only updates when higher; returns true if changed. */
  async submitBest(playerId: string, score: number, season?: string): Promise<boolean> {
    const changed = await this.redis.zadd(this.key(season), 'GT', 'CH', score, playerId);
    return changed > 0;
  }

  /** Cumulative points (e.g. XP). */
  addPoints(playerId: string, points: number, season?: string): Promise<string> {
    return this.redis.zincrby(this.key(season), points, playerId);
  }

  async top(n = 10, season?: string): Promise<Entry[]> {
    const flat = await this.redis.zrange(this.key(season), 0, n - 1, 'REV', 'WITHSCORES');
    const out: Entry[] = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < flat.length; i += 2) {
      out.push({ member: flat[i], score: Number(flat[i + 1]), rank: i / 2 + 1 });
    }
    return out;
  }

  /** Player's rank (1-based) and score in a single round trip. */
  async rankOf(playerId: string, season?: string): Promise<{ rank: number; score: number } | null> {
    const k = this.key(season);
    const [[, rank], [, score]] = (await this.redis
      .multi()
      .zrevrank(k, playerId)
      .zscore(k, playerId)
      .exec()) as [[Error | null, number | null], [Error | null, string | null]];
    if (rank === null || score === null) return null;
    return { rank: rank + 1, score: Number(score) };
  }

  /** Players around me: rank window [rank-radius, rank+radius]. */
  async around(playerId: string, radius = 3, season?: string): Promise<Entry[]> {
    const k = this.key(season);
    const r = await this.redis.zrevrank(k, playerId);
    if (r === null) return [];
    const start = Math.max(0, r - radius);
    const flat = await this.redis.zrange(k, start, r + radius, 'REV', 'WITHSCORES');
    const out: Entry[] = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < flat.length; i += 2) {
      out.push({ member: flat[i], score: Number(flat[i + 1]), rank: start + i / 2 + 1 });
    }
    return out;
  }

  /** Trim to the top K to cap memory (e.g. keep 100k players). */
  trimTo(k: number, season?: string): Promise<number> {
    return this.redis.zremrangebyrank(this.key(season), 0, -(k + 1));
  }
}
```

**Tie-breaking.** Equal scores sort by member lexicographically (byte order), which is deterministic but arbitrary. For "earliest to reach the score wins", encode time into the fractional part of the score: `score = points + (1 - ts / MAX_TS)`, where `ts` is epoch seconds and `MAX_TS` is a constant larger than any timestamp (for example 4e9). Doubles carry about 15-16 significant decimal digits, so check that `points` plus the fraction still fits; if it does not, keep the real score in a Hash and use the ZSET only for ordering.

**Scaling a leaderboard.** One ZSET holds tens of millions of members comfortably (about 100 bytes each in skiplist encoding). Beyond that, or for hot-key reasons, shard by region/season, and merge top-K with `ZUNION` on a smaller candidate set.

### 2.6.5 Time-based scheduling and delayed work

Score = Unix ms when the item is due. A poller fetches due items:

```
ZADD delayed 1768000005000 "job:42"
ZRANGE delayed -inf 1768000000000 BYSCORE LIMIT 0 100
```

Claiming safely when many pollers run: use `ZPOPMIN` (then re-add if not yet due), or a Lua script that atomically does `ZRANGE ... BYSCORE LIMIT` + `ZREM`:

```ts
import { redis } from './redis';

const CLAIM_DUE = `
local items = redis.call('ZRANGE', KEYS[1], '-inf', ARGV[1], 'BYSCORE', 'LIMIT', 0, ARGV[2])
if #items > 0 then redis.call('ZREM', KEYS[1], unpack(items)) end
return items
`;

export async function claimDue(limit = 100): Promise<string[]> {
  return (await redis.eval(CLAIM_DUE, 1, 'delayed', Date.now(), limit)) as string[];
}
```

BullMQ's delayed jobs use exactly this idea internally (a Sorted Set scored by due time), but that is a BullMQ implementation detail, not a Redis feature.

### 2.6.6 Pagination

| Strategy | How | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rank/offset | `ZRANGE k (page*size) (page*size+size-1) REV` | simple | O(log N + page); items shift when scores change |
| `LIMIT offset count` with `BYSCORE` | `ZRANGE k max min BYSCORE REV LIMIT off cnt` | works on score ranges | offset cost O(offset) |
| **Score cursor** | remember `(lastScore, lastMember)` and ask for strictly after it | stable, O(log N + page) regardless of depth | needs care with duplicate scores |

Score-cursor pagination (newest-first feed, scores = timestamps, ties broken by member):

```ts
import { redis } from './redis';

export interface Cursor { score: number; member: string }

export async function pageFeed(key: string, size: number, cursor?: Cursor) {
  // First page: everything. Next pages: score <= cursor.score, skip entries already seen.
  const max = cursor ? String(cursor.score) : '+inf';
  // Over-fetch to cover duplicates of the cursor score, then drop up to the cursor member.
  const flat = await redis.zrange(key, max, '-inf', 'BYSCORE', 'REV', 'LIMIT', 0, size + 50, 'WITHSCORES');
  let items: { member: string; score: number }[] = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < flat.length; i += 2) items.push({ member: flat[i], score: Number(flat[i + 1]) });

  if (cursor) {
    // With REV and equal scores, members come in reverse lexicographic order.
    const idx = items.findIndex((it) => it.score === cursor.score && it.member === cursor.member);
    items = idx >= 0 ? items.slice(idx + 1) : items.filter((it) => it.score < cursor.score);
  }
  const page = items.slice(0, size);
  const last = page[page.length - 1];
  return { page, next: page.length === size ? ({ score: last.score, member: last.member } as Cursor) : null };
}
```

The `+50` over-fetch assumes fewer than 50 items share one score; for timestamp scores with potentially many collisions, make scores unique (add a sequence fraction) or loop until you pass the cursor. For deep, stable pagination this beats offset: offset-based `LIMIT 100000 20` is O(100000) per request.

### 2.6.7 Time complexity

| Command | Complexity |
|---|---|
| `ZADD`, `ZREM`, `ZINCRBY`, `ZPOPMIN/MAX` (per element) | O(log N) |
| `ZSCORE`, `ZMSCORE` | O(1) |
| `ZRANK`, `ZREVRANK` | O(log N) |
| `ZCARD` | O(1) |
| `ZCOUNT` | O(log N) |
| `ZRANGE` (index/score/lex) | O(log N + M), M = returned elements |
| `ZREMRANGEBYRANK/SCORE` | O(log N + M) |
| `ZUNIONSTORE`, `ZINTERSTORE` | O(N) + O(M log M) / O(N*K) + O(M log M) (see docs) |

### 2.6.8 Memory considerations

- Skiplist + hashtable stores each member twice (once in the dict, once in the skiplist): roughly 70-120 bytes per entry plus the member string. Small listpack ZSETs are far leaner.
- Members are strings; storing a JSON blob as the member makes updating it a delete + insert. Prefer an ID as the member and store details in a Hash.
- Unbounded growth is a common leak (time-series indexes, rate-limit logs). Trim with `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE`/`ZREMRANGEBYRANK` on a schedule or inline.

### 2.6.9 Use cases

Leaderboards, priority queues (`ZPOPMIN`/`BZPOPMIN`), delayed/scheduled jobs, sliding-window rate limiters (timestamps as scores), time-ordered indexes ("recent N events per user"), autocomplete via `BYLEX`, top-K trending with decay, secondary indexes into Hashes.

### 2.6.10 Limitations

- One score per member; multi-criteria sorting needs composite scores (precision limits) or the Query Engine.
- Rank is O(log N), but "rank of everyone" is still O(N).
- Scores are doubles: no exact big integers, no decimals-as-money.
- Deleting by member requires knowing the exact member string.
- Cluster: multi-key ops (`ZUNIONSTORE`) need the same slot.

### 2.6.11 Interview questions

**Q1. Design a real-time leaderboard for 10M players.**
- *Short:* One Sorted Set, `ZADD GT`/`ZINCRBY` to update, `ZRANGE ... REV` for top N, `ZREVRANK` for a player's position.
- *Detail:* All of these are O(log N), well under a millisecond at 10M members (memory ~1 GB). Keep display data in a Hash. Handle seasons by key name and `EXPIRE`. Cap with `ZREMRANGEBYRANK`.
- *Senior follow-up:* What if one ZSET becomes a hot key or is too large? Shard by region/league and keep a small global ZSET of regional champions, or partition by score bucket; accept that exact global rank then needs aggregation.
- *Common wrong answer:* "Use SQL `ORDER BY score LIMIT 10` and cache it." It works for top-N but gives no cheap per-player rank.

**Q2. Why prefer `ZRANGE ... REV` over `ZREVRANGE`?**
- *Short:* `ZREVRANGE` is deprecated since 6.2; unified `ZRANGE` covers index, score and lex ranges, reverse, limit, and `ZRANGESTORE`.
- *Detail:* Deprecated commands are not removed in the 7.x/8.x lines, so old code keeps working. One syntax lowers cognitive load. Note that with `BYSCORE REV` the bounds swap (max first).
- *Senior follow-up:* Compatibility? `ZRANGE` options require >= 6.2; managed services on older versions will reject them.
- *Common wrong answer:* "`ZREVRANGE` was removed in Redis 7." It was not.

## 2.7 Streams

### 2.7.1 Concept and encoding

A Stream is an **append-only log** of entries. Each entry has an ID (`<ms-timestamp>-<sequence>`, e.g. `1768000000000-0`) and a set of field-value pairs. Streams support:

- reading ranges by ID (time-travel through history),
- blocking tail-reads (`XREAD BLOCK`),
- **consumer groups**, where entries are distributed among consumers with per-entry acknowledgment, a pending list and redelivery.

Internally a Stream is a **radix tree** keyed by entry IDs whose leaves are **listpacks** holding many entries (field names are stored once per listpack via delta encoding, which makes entries with identical field sets very compact). Consumer groups keep a *last-delivered-id* and a **PEL** (Pending Entries List: delivered, not yet acknowledged) per group, plus per-consumer PELs.

### 2.7.2 Syntax

```
XADD key [NOMKSTREAM] [MAXLEN | MINID [= | ~] threshold [LIMIT count]] <* | id> field value [field value ...]
XLEN key     XDEL key id [id ...]     XTRIM key MAXLEN|MINID [= | ~] threshold [LIMIT count]
XRANGE key start end [COUNT n]        XREVRANGE key end start [COUNT n]       # "-" and "+" are min/max
XREAD [COUNT n] [BLOCK ms] STREAMS key [key ...] id [id ...]                  # "$" = only new entries
XGROUP CREATE key group <id | $> [MKSTREAM] [ENTRIESREAD n]
XGROUP CREATECONSUMER key group consumer      XGROUP DESTROY key group     XGROUP DELCONSUMER ...
XGROUP SETID key group <id | $>
XREADGROUP GROUP group consumer [COUNT n] [BLOCK ms] [NOACK] STREAMS key [key ...] <id | >>
XACK key group id [id ...]
XPENDING key group [[IDLE min-idle-ms] start end count [consumer]]
XCLAIM key group consumer min-idle-ms id [id ...] [IDLE ms] [RETRYCOUNT n] [FORCE] [JUSTID]
XAUTOCLAIM key group consumer min-idle-ms start [COUNT n] [JUSTID]            # [6.2+]
XINFO STREAM key [FULL [COUNT n]]   XINFO GROUPS key   XINFO CONSUMERS key group
```

Version notes: `NOMKSTREAM`, `MINID` and `LIMIT` on trimming arrived in 6.2; `XAUTOCLAIM` and `XGROUP CREATECONSUMER` in 6.2; `ENTRIESREAD`, lag and `entries-added` info in 7.0. Redis 8.2 added `XDELEX` and `XACKDEL` with reference-handling options (`KEEPREF`, `DELREF`, `ACKED`) for cleaning entries that several consumer groups still reference [8.2+]. Check your server version before relying on them.

**Trimming operators:** `MAXLEN 1000` is exact (can be expensive if it must remove many entries). `MAXLEN ~ 1000` is **approximate**: Redis trims only whole listpack nodes, so the stream may be slightly longer than 1000. It is much cheaper and is what you almost always want in production. `MINID ~ <id>` trims by age (use a timestamp ID, e.g. `Date.now() - retentionMs` followed by `-0`). `LIMIT count` caps work per call when using `~`.

### 2.7.3 Practical examples

```
127.0.0.1:6379> XADD orders MAXLEN ~ 100000 * orderId 1001 total 49.90
"1768000000000-0"
127.0.0.1:6379> XADD orders * orderId 1002 total 12.00
"1768000000001-0"
127.0.0.1:6379> XLEN orders
(integer) 2
127.0.0.1:6379> XRANGE orders - + COUNT 10
1) 1) "1768000000000-0"
   2) 1) "orderId"
      2) "1001"
      3) "total"
      4) "49.90"
2) 1) "1768000000001-0"
   2) 1) "orderId"
      2) "1002"
      3) "total"
      4) "12.00"
127.0.0.1:6379> XREAD COUNT 10 STREAMS orders 0            # from the beginning
127.0.0.1:6379> XREAD BLOCK 5000 STREAMS orders $          # wait up to 5 s for NEW entries

# Consumer group
127.0.0.1:6379> XGROUP CREATE orders billing 0 MKSTREAM
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> XREADGROUP GROUP billing worker-1 COUNT 1 STREAMS orders >
1) 1) "orders"
   2) 1) 1) "1768000000000-0"
         2) 1) "orderId"
            2) "1001"
            3) "total"
            4) "49.90"
127.0.0.1:6379> XPENDING orders billing
1) (integer) 1
2) "1768000000000-0"
3) "1768000000000-0"
4) 1) 1) "worker-1"
      2) "1"
127.0.0.1:6379> XACK orders billing 1768000000000-0
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> XAUTOCLAIM orders billing worker-2 60000 0 COUNT 10
1) "0-0"
2) (empty array)
3) (empty array)
```

`XREADGROUP ... >` means "entries never delivered to any consumer in this group". Using a concrete ID (like `0`) instead reads **this consumer's own pending entries** (its PEL), which is how a restarted consumer recovers.

### 2.7.4 Diagram

```
                      ┌──────────────── stream "orders" ────────────────┐
 producers ─XADD────▶ │ e1 | e2 | e3 | e4 | e5 | e6 | e7 ...             │
                      └─────┬─────────────────────────────┬─────────────┘
                            │ group "billing"             │ group "email"   (each group sees ALL entries)
                            │ last-delivered-id=e5        │ last-delivered-id=e7
                            ▼                             ▼
                   ┌─────── PEL ───────┐           ┌─────── PEL ───────┐
                   │ e3 -> worker-1    │           │ (empty)           │
                   │ e4 -> worker-2    │           └───────────────────┘
                   └───────────────────┘
   inside a group, entries are SPLIT across consumers (competing consumers);
   XACK removes from PEL;  XAUTOCLAIM transfers entries idle > N ms to a live consumer
```

### 2.7.5 TypeScript: stream consumer group with recovery

```ts
import Redis from 'ioredis';

type Fields = Record<string, string>;
type RawEntry = [id: string, fields: string[]];
type ReadReply = [stream: string, entries: RawEntry[]][] | null;

const toObj = (arr: string[]): Fields => {
  const o: Fields = {};
  for (let i = 0; i < arr.length; i += 2) o[arr[i]] = arr[i + 1];
  return o;
};

export class StreamConsumer {
  private running = false;
  private readonly blocking: Redis;

  constructor(
    private readonly redis: Redis,
    private readonly stream: string,
    private readonly group: string,
    private readonly consumer: string,
    private readonly handler: (id: string, data: Fields) => Promise<void>,
    private readonly opts = { batch: 20, blockMs: 5000, minIdleMs: 60_000, maxDeliveries: 5 },
  ) {
    this.blocking = redis.duplicate();
  }

  async init(): Promise<void> {
    try {
      await this.redis.xgroup('CREATE', this.stream, this.group, '$', 'MKSTREAM');
    } catch (e) {
      if (!String(e).includes('BUSYGROUP')) throw e; // group already exists
    }
  }

  async run(): Promise<void> {
    this.running = true;
    await this.drainOwnPending();                 // 1) recover what this consumer had before a crash
    let lastReclaim = 0;
    while (this.running) {
      if (Date.now() - lastReclaim > this.opts.minIdleMs) {
        await this.reclaimStale();                // 2) steal entries abandoned by dead consumers
        lastReclaim = Date.now();
      }
      const res = (await this.blocking.xreadgroup(
        'GROUP', this.group, this.consumer,
        'COUNT', this.opts.batch, 'BLOCK', this.opts.blockMs,
        'STREAMS', this.stream, '>',
      )) as ReadReply;
      if (!res) continue;
      for (const [, entries] of res) for (const [id, f] of entries) await this.process(id, toObj(f));
    }
  }

  private async process(id: string, data: Fields): Promise<void> {
    try {
      await this.handler(id, data);
      await this.redis.xack(this.stream, this.group, id);
    } catch (err) {
      console.error(`failed ${id}`, err); // stays in PEL, will be retried via reclaim
    }
  }

  private async drainOwnPending(): Promise<void> {
    let start = '0';
    for (;;) {
      const res = (await this.redis.xreadgroup(
        'GROUP', this.group, this.consumer, 'COUNT', this.opts.batch, 'STREAMS', this.stream, start,
      )) as ReadReply;
      const entries = res?.[0]?.[1] ?? [];
      if (entries.length === 0) return;
      for (const [id, f] of entries) await this.process(id, toObj(f));
      start = entries[entries.length - 1][0];
    }
  }

  private async reclaimStale(): Promise<void> {
    let cursor = '0-0';
    do {
      // returns [nextCursor, entries, deletedIds]
      const [next, entries] = (await this.redis.xautoclaim(
        this.stream, this.group, this.consumer, this.opts.minIdleMs, cursor, 'COUNT', this.opts.batch,
      )) as [string, RawEntry[], string[]?];
      for (const [id, f] of entries) {
        const [[, , , deliveries]] = (await this.redis.xpending(
          this.stream, this.group, id, id, 1,
        )) as [string, string, number, number][];
        if (deliveries > this.opts.maxDeliveries) {
          // poison message: park it in a dead-letter stream and ack
          await this.redis.multi()
            .xadd(`${this.stream}:dlq`, '*', 'origId', id, ...f)
            .xack(this.stream, this.group, id)
            .exec();
        } else {
          await this.process(id, toObj(f));
        }
      }
      cursor = next;
    } while (cursor !== '0-0');
  }

  async stop(): Promise<void> {
    this.running = false;
    this.blocking.disconnect();
  }
}
```

Operational notes: use one `consumer` name per process (e.g. hostname + PM2 instance id) so the PEL stays attributable; delete dead consumers with `XGROUP DELCONSUMER` after reclaiming their entries. Consumer groups give **at-least-once** delivery: handlers must be idempotent.

### 2.7.6 Retention and trimming

Streams never expire entries by themselves. Unbounded streams eat memory. Options:

- On every write: `XADD ... MAXLEN ~ N` (bounded size) or `MINID ~ <cutoff>` (bounded age).
- Periodically: `XTRIM key MINID ~ <cutoff> LIMIT 1000` from a cron job.
- Be careful: trimming does not check whether consumer groups have processed an entry. If a group lags more than your retention, **it silently loses entries** (they vanish from the PEL reads; `XINFO` `lag` may become null). Monitor `XINFO GROUPS` lag and pending counts.
- `XDEL` marks entries deleted (space is reclaimed lazily); mass `XDEL` is not a retention policy.

### 2.7.7 Streams vs Kafka vs RabbitMQ

| Aspect | Redis Streams | Kafka | RabbitMQ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Model | single in-memory log + consumer groups | partitioned, replicated commit log on disk | broker with exchanges/queues |
| Retention | memory-bound; trim policy | days/weeks/forever on disk | until consumed (queues); streams plugin exists |
| Throughput | very high per node, bounded by RAM | very high, horizontally partitioned | high, lower than Kafka for huge fan-in |
| Ordering | total order within a stream | per partition | per queue |
| Replay | yes (within retention) | yes (excellent) | no for classic queues |
| Delivery | at-least-once with ack/PEL | at-least-once/exactly-once (transactions) | at-least-once with acks, DLX |
| Routing | none (one stream = one topic) | topics/partitions, keys | rich (topic, fanout, headers) |
| Durability | AOF/replication, async replicas can lose acknowledged writes | strong (ISR, acks=all) | durable queues, quorum queues |
| Ops cost | tiny if you already run Redis | high | moderate |
| Best fit | event streams/task fan-out within a service boundary, moderate retention | event backbone, analytics, long retention | complex routing, per-message TTL/priority |

Choose Streams when Redis is already in your stack, volume fits memory, and losing a few seconds of data in a failover is acceptable. Choose Kafka for long retention, replay at scale, and strong durability. Choose RabbitMQ for sophisticated routing. For job processing in Node.js, BullMQ (built on Redis Lists/ZSETs/Hashes, not Streams) often beats raw Streams on ergonomics: retries, delays and rate limiting are built in.

### 2.7.8 Time complexity

| Command | Complexity |
|---|---|
| `XADD` | O(1) (plus trimming cost with `MAXLEN`/`MINID`; `~` makes it amortized O(1)) |
| `XLEN` | O(1) |
| `XRANGE`, `XREVRANGE` | O(log N + M) |
| `XREAD` | O(N) with N = entries returned (per stream, plus seek O(log N)) |
| `XREADGROUP` | O(M) for new entries; O(M) for pending-history reads (M = returned) |
| `XACK` | O(1) per ID |
| `XPENDING` (summary) | O(N) with N = number of consumers; extended form O(N) with N = returned |
| `XCLAIM`, `XAUTOCLAIM` | O(log N) per entry claimed |
| `XTRIM` | O(N), N = entries evicted |
| `XDEL` | O(1) per ID |

### 2.7.9 Memory considerations

- Entries with the same field set compress well in listpacks; repeating different long field names across entries wastes memory.
- Each group's PEL stores one record per unacknowledged entry. A stuck consumer makes the PEL (and memory) grow; monitor it.
- Each entry is kept until trimmed, regardless of acknowledgment; ACK only removes from the PEL.
- `stream-node-max-bytes` (4096) and `stream-node-max-entries` (100) control listpack node size, which in turn sets `~` trimming granularity.

### 2.7.10 Use cases

Event sourcing/audit trails with bounded retention, task fan-out to worker groups, change-data feeds (publish DB changes), IoT/metrics ingestion buffers, notification pipelines, lightweight inter-service events.

### 2.7.11 Limitations

- Memory-bound, no tiered storage; capacity is RAM.
- No partitions: one stream is one key on one shard. To scale, shard manually (`events:{0..N}`) and route by key; ordering then holds only per shard.
- Replication is asynchronous: acknowledged `XADD`s can be lost on failover (`WAIT` reduces, not eliminates, this).
- No built-in retry counter limits or DLQ: you implement them (see code above) using delivery counts from `XPENDING`.
- No per-message delay or priority.

### 2.7.12 Interview questions

**Q1. How do Redis Streams consumer groups handle a consumer that crashes mid-processing?**
- *Short:* The entry stays in the group's PEL; another consumer reclaims it with `XAUTOCLAIM` (or `XCLAIM`) after it has been idle long enough.
- *Detail:* Delivery marks the entry pending with the consumer name, idle time and delivery count. `XACK` clears it. After `min-idle-time`, `XAUTOCLAIM` transfers ownership and increments the delivery counter, enabling poison-message detection.
- *Senior follow-up:* How do you avoid double-processing after a slow (not dead) consumer is reclaimed? Handlers must be idempotent (dedupe on entry ID or a business key), and `min-idle-time` should exceed p99 processing time.
- *Common wrong answer:* "Redis re-delivers automatically after a timeout." Redis never redelivers on its own; consumers must claim.

**Q2. Streams or Pub/Sub?**
- *Short:* Streams persist and support replay and acks; Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget.
- *Detail:* A Pub/Sub message is lost if no subscriber is connected at that instant. Streams keep entries until trimmed and let consumers resume from an ID.
- *Senior follow-up:* When is Pub/Sub the right choice anyway? Ephemeral signals (cache invalidation hints, presence, websocket fan-out) where loss is tolerable and latency matters.
- *Common wrong answer:* "Streams are just Pub/Sub with history." The consumer-group/PEL semantics are the real difference.

**Q3. Why `MAXLEN ~`?**
- *Short:* Approximate trimming removes whole nodes, so it is much cheaper than exact trimming.
- *Detail:* Exact trimming can split a listpack and rewrite it on every `XADD`. Approximate allows slight overshoot for O(1)-ish cost.
- *Senior follow-up:* Does trimming respect unprocessed entries? No; size your retention for your slowest consumer group.
- *Common wrong answer:* "`~` trims to *at most* N." It trims to *roughly at least* N, so the stream may hold more than N.
