```ts
import { REDIS_CLIENT } from '../redis/redis.constants';

const RELEASE = `if redis.call('get',KEYS[1])==ARGV[1] then return redis.call('del',KEYS[1]) else return 0 end`;

@Injectable()
export class LockService {
  constructor(@Inject(REDIS_CLIENT) private readonly redis: Redis) {}

  /** Runs `fn` if the lock is acquired; returns undefined if someone else holds it. */
  async runExclusive<T>(name: string, ttlMs: number, fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T | undefined> {
    const key = `shop:lock:${name}`;
    const token = randomUUID();
    const ok = await this.redis.set(key, token, 'PX', ttlMs, 'NX');
    if (ok !== 'OK') return undefined;
    try {
      return await fn();
    } finally {
      await this.redis.eval(RELEASE, 1, key, token).catch(() => undefined); // best effort; TTL is the backstop
    }
  }
}
```

If `fn` can take longer than `ttlMs`, you need renewal (section 4.9 shows the renewal loop) or you accept that overlap can occur.

## 4.8 Rate limiting overview

> Algorithms, Lua scripts and benchmarking are covered in a dedicated rate-limiting module. Overview here.

Rate limiting needs **shared** counters, otherwise the effective limit multiplies with the instance count (4.1.2).

| Algorithm | Redis structure | Characteristics |
|---|---|---|
| Fixed window | `INCR` + TTL per window | Simplest, cheapest; allows 2x bursts across a window boundary |
| Sliding window log | Sorted Set of timestamps | Exact, memory proportional to requests in window |
| Sliding window counter | Two fixed-window counters, weighted | Good approximation, cheap |
| Token bucket | Hash (tokens, last refill) + Lua | Allows controlled bursts; smooth average |
| Leaky bucket | Queue or Lua | Smooths output rate |

Fixed window using the helper from 4.5.3:

```ts
// src/rate-limit/rate-limit.guard.ts
import { CanActivate, ExecutionContext, HttpException, HttpStatus, Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { CounterService } from '../counters/window-counter.service';

@Injectable()
export class RateLimitGuard implements CanActivate {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(RateLimitGuard.name);
  constructor(private readonly counters: CounterService) {}

  async canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext): Promise<boolean> {
    const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest();
    const windowMs = 60_000;
    const limit = 100;
    const bucket = Math.floor(Date.now() / windowMs);
    const key = `shop:rl:${req.ip}:${bucket}`; // window id in the key; TTL cleans up

    try {
      const n = await this.counters.hit(key, windowMs * 2);
      if (n > limit) {
        throw new HttpException('Too Many Requests', HttpStatus.TOO_MANY_REQUESTS);
      }
      return true;
    } catch (e) {
      if (e instanceof HttpException) throw e;
      this.logger.error(`rate limiter unavailable, failing open: ${(e as Error).message}`);
      return true; // fail OPEN for general APIs; fail CLOSED for abuse-sensitive endpoints (login, OTP)
    }
  }
}
```

Layering: Nginx `limit_req` (cheap, per-instance-of-Nginx, before Node) for crude protection, application-level limits (per user, per API key, per endpoint) in Redis for fairness. `@nestjs/throttler` supports Redis storage through a community storage adapter; treat it as a library convenience over the same counters.

## 4.9 Leader election

### 4.9.1 Concept

Leader election makes **exactly one** instance (the leader) perform a task: cron jobs, cleanup, polling an external system, owning a singleton consumer. If the leader dies, another instance takes over.

```
 Instances:   A        B        C
              │        │        │
 t0           SET leader:cron A NX PX 15000  -> OK        (A is leader, lease 15 s)
              B, C: SET ... NX -> nil                     (followers retry periodically)
 t5, t10      A renews: if get==A then PEXPIRE 15000      (heartbeat every 5 s)
 t12          A crashes (or is paused for 20 s)
 t27          lease expires
 t28          B: SET leader:cron B NX PX 15000 -> OK      (B is leader)
 t30          A wakes from the pause, believes it is still leader ◄── the dangerous case
              A's next renewal: get == B != A -> renewal fails -> A steps down
```

The gap between "A's lease expired in Redis" and "A learns it" is the unavoidable hazard. Two leaders can overlap briefly.

### 4.9.2 Caveats and how to handle them

| Caveat | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Overlap during pause or partition | Make the leader's work **idempotent**; check lease validity before each unit of work |
| Leader must stop when it cannot renew | Track `lastRenewedAt`; consider yourself leader only while `now - lastRenewedAt < ttl - safetyMargin` (local clock for elapsed time, using a monotonic source, such as `process.hrtime`/`performance.now`, avoids wall-clock jumps) |
| Failover may lose the lease key | Same as locks; idempotency again |
| Redis is a single point of failure for election | If Redis is down, nobody can renew: the leader steps down and the task pauses (safe, but the task does not run). Decide whether the task can stop |
| Thundering election | Add jitter to follower retry interval |
| Strong correctness required | Use a consensus-based system (etcd, ZooKeeper, Kubernetes Lease objects) or fencing tokens |
| Simplest alternative | Run cron in **one dedicated worker process** (a PM2 app with `instances: 1`, or a separate container) and no election at all. Cheap and often best; trade-off is a single point of failure for the schedule |
| Alternative using a queue library | BullMQ repeatable jobs/job schedulers create the scheduled job once (keyed by repeat key) and a single worker processes each job. That is a BullMQ feature, not a Redis feature; evaluate it before building election by hand |

### 4.9.3 NestJS: leader election service

```ts
// src/leader/leader-election.service.ts
import {
  Inject, Injectable, Logger, OnApplicationBootstrap, OnApplicationShutdown,
} from '@nestjs/common';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';
import { Redis } from 'ioredis';
import { REDIS_CLIENT } from '../redis/redis.constants';

const RENEW_LUA = `
if redis.call('get', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call('pexpire', KEYS[1], ARGV[2])
end
return 0`;
const RELEASE_LUA = `
if redis.call('get', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call('del', KEYS[1])
end
return 0`;

@Injectable()
export class LeaderElectionService implements OnApplicationBootstrap, OnApplicationShutdown {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(LeaderElectionService.name);
  private readonly key = 'shop:leader:scheduler';
  private readonly instanceId = `${process.pid}-${randomUUID()}`; // unique per process
  private readonly ttlMs = 15_000;
  private readonly tickMs = 5_000;
  private readonly safetyMarginMs = 3_000;

  private timer?: NodeJS.Timeout;
  private leaderSince: number | null = null;     // monotonic ms (performance.now) of last successful acquire/renew
  private stopped = false;

  constructor(@Inject(REDIS_CLIENT) private readonly redis: Redis) {}

  onApplicationBootstrap(): void {
    void this.tick();
  }

  /** True only while the lease is provably still ours, by our own clock. */
  isLeader(): boolean {
    if (this.leaderSince === null) return false;
    return performance.now() - this.leaderSince < this.ttlMs - this.safetyMarginMs;
  }

  private async tick(): Promise<void> {
    if (this.stopped) return;
    const started = performance.now();
    try {
      if (this.leaderSince !== null) {
        const renewed = await this.redis.eval(RENEW_LUA, 1, this.key, this.instanceId, this.ttlMs);
        if (renewed === 1) {
          this.leaderSince = started; // lease measured from when we SENT the request: conservative
        } else {
          this.stepDown('lease lost (key owned by someone else or expired)');
        }
      } else {
        const ok = await this.redis.set(this.key, this.instanceId, 'PX', this.ttlMs, 'NX');
        if (ok === 'OK') {
          this.leaderSince = started;
          this.logger.log(`Became leader (${this.instanceId})`);
        }
      }
    } catch (e) {
      // Cannot talk to Redis: isLeader() will turn false by itself when the margin passes.
      this.logger.warn(`leader tick failed: ${(e as Error).message}`);
    } finally {
      if (!this.stopped) {
        const jitter = Math.random() * 500;
        this.timer = setTimeout(() => void this.tick(), this.tickMs + jitter);
      }
    }
  }

  private stepDown(reason: string): void {
    if (this.leaderSince !== null) this.logger.warn(`Stepping down: ${reason}`);
    this.leaderSince = null;
  }

  async onApplicationShutdown(): Promise<void> {
    this.stopped = true;
    if (this.timer) clearTimeout(this.timer);
    if (this.leaderSince !== null) {
      this.leaderSince = null;
      // Release promptly so a follower takes over in seconds instead of waiting for TTL expiry.
      await this.redis.eval(RELEASE_LUA, 1, this.key, this.instanceId).catch(() => undefined);
    }
  }
}
```

Timing reasoning: lease TTL 15 s, renew every ~5 s, so two consecutive renewal failures still leave the lease valid; `isLeader()` becomes false 3 s before the Redis key can expire, so the old leader stops before a new one can start (assuming no process pause longer than the margin). A long stop-the-world pause bypasses this guarantee, hence idempotent work.

### 4.9.4 NestJS: cron that runs on one instance only

```ts
// src/jobs/nightly-report.job.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Cron } from '@nestjs/schedule';
import { LeaderElectionService } from '../leader/leader-election.service';

@Injectable()
export class NightlyReportJob {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(NightlyReportJob.name);
  constructor(private readonly leader: LeaderElectionService) {}

  @Cron('0 2 * * *') // fires on EVERY instance at 02:00; only the leader proceeds
  async run(): Promise<void> {
    if (!this.leader.isLeader()) {
      this.logger.debug('Not leader, skipping');
      return;
    }
    await this.generateReport(new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10));
  }

  /** Idempotent: re-running for the same day must not duplicate emails or rows. */
  private async generateReport(day: string): Promise<void> {
    // e.g. INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (report_day) DO NOTHING, or a Redis SET NX "done:report:<day>" marker
  }
}
```

Edge case: leadership may change between 01:59:58 and 02:00:00, and the new leader's ticks may not have acquired yet at exactly 02:00: a fire could be missed entirely if no instance is leader at that second. If missing a run is unacceptable, either run the check on a catch-up schedule ("if today's report is not marked done, do it") or move the scheduling into a queue with persisted delayed/repeatable jobs.

```
 Tradeoff summary
   Dedicated cron process ........ simplest; one process = SPOF for schedule; no election code
   Redis lease election ........... automatic failover within TTL; overlap possible; needs idempotent jobs
   Queue repeatable jobs .......... durable, retries, visibility; adds the queue dependency (BullMQ library)
   Consensus lease (etcd / k8s) ... strongest guarantees; extra infrastructure
```


---

## 4.10 Pub/Sub for cross-instance communication

### 4.10.1 Definition and mechanism

Redis Pub/Sub lets any client `PUBLISH` a message to a named channel; every client currently `SUBSCRIBE`d to that channel receives it. There is no storage: Redis pushes to connected subscribers and forgets.

```
 Instance A ── PUBLISH cache:invalidate '{"key":"product:42"}' ──► Redis ──┬──► Instance A (subscriber)
                                                                          ├──► Instance B (subscriber)
                                                                          └──► Instance C (subscriber)
        PUBLISH returns the number of subscribers that received it (3)
        Instance D was restarting at that moment ──► it never sees the message
```

Properties you must internalize:

| Property | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **At-most-once** delivery | No ack, no retry. A disconnected subscriber misses messages permanently |
| **No history / replay** | Late subscribers see nothing from before |
| **Fire and forget** | A `PUBLISH` with zero subscribers succeeds (returns 0) |
| Subscriber connection is **dedicated** | A connection in subscribe mode can only run (P)SUBSCRIBE/UNSUBSCRIBE/PING-type commands (RESP2). Use a separate connection (`redis.duplicate()` in ioredis) |
| Slow subscribers are cut off | Output buffer limits for pubsub clients (`client-output-buffer-limit pubsub`, defaults of 32mb hard / 8mb over 60 s) disconnect clients that cannot keep up |
| Pattern subscriptions | `PSUBSCRIBE news:*` matches channels by glob; cost grows with the number of patterns |
| Cluster behaviour | Classic `PUBLISH` is propagated across the cluster bus to all nodes (fan-out cost grows with nodes). **Sharded Pub/Sub** [7.0+] (`SPUBLISH`/`SSUBSCRIBE`) keeps messages inside the shard that owns the channel's slot, scaling better |
| Keyspace notifications | Optional server-generated events (e.g. key expired) delivered via Pub/Sub; off by default (`notify-keyspace-events`), also at-most-once. Do not build critical logic on expiry events |

Pub/Sub is the right tool for **ephemeral, idempotent, "nudge" messages**: cache invalidation hints, config-changed signals, WebSocket fan-out, presence. It is the wrong tool when a lost message is a bug (use Streams or a queue, 4.12 and 4.13).

### 4.10.2 CLI

```bash
# Terminal 1 (subscriber)
127.0.0.1:6379> SUBSCRIBE shop:events:cache-invalidate
Reading messages... (press Ctrl-C to quit)
1) "subscribe"
2) "shop:events:cache-invalidate"
3) (integer) 1

# Terminal 2 (publisher)
127.0.0.1:6379> PUBLISH shop:events:cache-invalidate '{"key":"product:42","origin":"api-1"}'
(integer) 1

# Terminal 1 receives:
1) "message"
2) "shop:events:cache-invalidate"
3) "{\"key\":\"product:42\",\"origin\":\"api-1\"}"

127.0.0.1:6379> PUBSUB CHANNELS shop:events:*
1) "shop:events:cache-invalidate"
127.0.0.1:6379> PUBSUB NUMSUB shop:events:cache-invalidate
1) "shop:events:cache-invalidate"
2) (integer) 1
```

### 4.10.3 NestJS: cross-instance cache invalidation (two-tier cache)

Goal: an in-process L1 cache in front of Redis (Module 3, section 3.1.6). When any instance changes data, every instance must drop its L1 copy. Design:

```
 Instance A: update product 42
   1. Postgres UPDATE (commit)
   2. UNLINK product:42 in Redis (L2)
   3. evict from own L1
   4. PUBLISH invalidate {key, origin=A}
 Instances B, C: subscriber receives -> evict key from own L1
 Backstops:  L1 TTL (e.g. 5 s) bounds staleness if a message is lost
             on subscriber (re)connect: clear the whole L1
```

```bash
npm i lru-cache
```

```ts
// src/cache/l1-cache.service.ts
import { Inject, Injectable, Logger, OnModuleDestroy, OnModuleInit } from '@nestjs/common';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';
import { LRUCache } from 'lru-cache';
import { Redis } from 'ioredis';
import { REDIS_CLIENT } from '../redis/redis.constants';

const CHANNEL = 'shop:events:cache-invalidate';

interface InvalidationMessage {
  keys: string[];     // exact keys to drop; keep messages small
  origin: string;     // publisher instance id
}

@Injectable()
export class L1CacheService implements OnModuleInit, OnModuleDestroy {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(L1CacheService.name);
  private readonly instanceId = randomUUID();

  /** Bounded, short TTL: this TTL is the worst-case staleness if a message is lost. */
  private readonly l1 = new LRUCache<string, object>({ max: 1_000, ttl: 5_000 });

  private sub!: Redis;

  constructor(@Inject(REDIS_CLIENT) private readonly redis: Redis) {}

  async onModuleInit(): Promise<void> {
    // Subscriber mode monopolizes a connection: always use a dedicated duplicate.
    this.sub = this.redis.duplicate();
    this.sub.on('error', (e) => this.logger.error(`subscriber error: ${e.message}`));

    // 'ready' fires on the first connection and again after every reconnect (ioredis re-subscribes
    // automatically). Messages published during the gap are gone, so drop everything we hold.
    this.sub.on('ready', () => {
      this.l1.clear();
      this.logger.log('L1 cleared (subscriber ready)');
    });

    this.sub.on('message', (channel: string, payload: string) => {
      if (channel !== CHANNEL) return;
      try {
        const msg = JSON.parse(payload) as InvalidationMessage;
        if (msg.origin === this.instanceId) return; // we already evicted locally
        for (const k of msg.keys) this.l1.delete(k);
      } catch {
        this.l1.clear(); // unparseable message: be safe
      }
    });

    await this.sub.subscribe(CHANNEL);
  }

  async onModuleDestroy(): Promise<void> {
    await this.sub.quit();
  }

  getLocal<T extends object>(key: string): T | undefined {
    return this.l1.get(key) as T | undefined;
  }

  setLocal(key: string, value: object): void {
    this.l1.set(key, value);
  }

  /** Call after the DB commit and after the L2 delete. */
  async invalidate(...keys: string[]): Promise<void> {
    for (const k of keys) this.l1.delete(k);
    const msg: InvalidationMessage = { keys, origin: this.instanceId };
    try {
      await this.redis.publish(CHANNEL, JSON.stringify(msg));
    } catch (e) {
      this.logger.warn(`publish failed (L1 TTL will bound staleness): ${(e as Error).message}`);
    }
  }
}
```

Using it with the `CacheService` from Module 3:

```ts
// src/products/products.service.ts  (two-tier read and invalidating update)
async getProductFast(id: number): Promise<Product> {
  const key = RedisKeys.product(id);

  const local = this.l1.getLocal<Product>(key);
  if (local) return local;                                   // L1 hit: no network at all

  const p = await this.cache.wrap<Product>('product', key, () => this.repo.findById(id), {
    ttlSeconds: 600, negativeTtlSeconds: 30, distributedLock: true,
  });
  if (!p) throw new NotFoundException();
  this.l1.setLocal(key, p);
  return p;
}

async updatePrice(id: number, price: number): Promise<Product> {
  const updated = await this.repo.updatePrice(id, price);    // 1. commit
  if (!updated) throw new NotFoundException();
  await this.cache.del(RedisKeys.product(id));               // 2. L2 delete
  await this.l1.invalidate(RedisKeys.product(id));           // 3. L1 delete + broadcast to the fleet
  return updated;
}
```

Known weaknesses (say these out loud in an interview):

- A message lost during subscriber reconnect leaves stale L1 entries for at most the L1 TTL (5 s here); clearing L1 on `ready` narrows it further.
- The race from Module 3 section 3.4.2 (reader repopulating after the delete) applies to L1 as well, with the same TTL backstop.
- The invalidation is a **hint**; correctness comes from the short L1 TTL.
- Alternative with server-assisted guarantees: client-side caching with `CLIENT TRACKING` (RESP3) in node-redis [6.0+], where Redis sends invalidation pushes only for keys the client actually read.

### 4.10.4 Other Pub/Sub uses

| Use | Notes |
|---|---|
| WebSocket/Socket.IO scale-out | `@socket.io/redis-adapter` uses Pub/Sub (and a sharded variant for Cluster). Every instance broadcasts to its own local sockets on receipt |
| Config/feature-flag change signal | Message says "reload config", each instance re-reads from Redis/DB |
| Presence, typing indicators | Loss-tolerant by nature |
| Cross-service notifications of "something changed, go look" | Receiver re-queries the source of truth: message loss then costs only latency |

Design rule: **the message should say "something changed", not carry the only copy of the truth**. Then losing it is harmless.

## 4.11 Idempotency management

### 4.11.1 Why

Networks retry. Clients time out and resend; load balancers retry on a different instance; queues deliver at-least-once; users double-click. A non-idempotent operation (charge a card, create an order, send an email) executed twice causes real damage. An **idempotency key** (client-generated unique ID sent with the request) lets the server detect "I have seen this request" and return the original result instead of executing again.

### 4.11.2 State machine

```
 Request with Idempotency-Key K
        │
        ▼
  SET idem:K {state: processing, fingerprint} NX EX 60      (atomic claim)
   ├─ OK ─────────► run handler
   │                   ├─ success ──► SET idem:K {state: done, status, body} EX 24h ──► respond
   │                   └─ failure ──► DEL idem:K (so the client may retry)      ──► respond with error
   └─ nil (exists) ► GET idem:K
                       ├─ fingerprint differs ─────► 422: key reused with a different request
                       ├─ state = processing ──────► 409 Conflict (retry later)
                       └─ state = done ────────────► replay stored status and body (header: Idempotent-Replayed: true)
```

```bash
127.0.0.1:6379> SET shop:idem:u42:9c1e '{"state":"processing","fp":"a1b2"}' NX EX 60
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> SET shop:idem:u42:9c1e '{"state":"processing","fp":"a1b2"}' NX EX 60
(nil)                         # second attempt (retry or concurrent duplicate) loses the claim
127.0.0.1:6379> SET shop:idem:u42:9c1e '{"state":"done","fp":"a1b2","status":201,"body":{"orderId":991}}' EX 86400
OK
```

### 4.11.3 Where idempotency state lives, and its limits

| Approach | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|
| Redis claim key (above) | Fast, shared, TTL-based cleanup, simple | Not transactional with your DB: crash after the side effect but before recording "done" leaves "processing" until TTL, then a retry re-executes |
| DB unique constraint (`UNIQUE (idempotency_key)` written **in the same transaction** as the side effect) | Strongest: effect and record commit atomically | DB round trip, schema work |
| Both | Redis absorbs duplicate bursts cheaply; DB constraint is the final guard | More moving parts |

For payments and orders, treat Redis idempotency as a **fast front door** and enforce the real guarantee with a unique constraint or an upsert in Postgres/Mongo. Also pass the key downstream (payment providers accept their own idempotency keys).

Redis down: for payment-like endpoints, **fail closed** (reject with 503) rather than executing without protection; for low-risk endpoints you may fail open.

### 4.11.4 NestJS idempotency interceptor

```ts
// src/idempotency/idempotency.interceptor.ts
import {
  CallHandler, ConflictException, ExecutionContext, Inject, Injectable,
  NestInterceptor, ServiceUnavailableException, UnprocessableEntityException, BadRequestException,
} from '@nestjs/common';
import { createHash } from 'node:crypto';
import { Observable, from, of, throwError } from 'rxjs';
import { catchError, mergeMap } from 'rxjs/operators';
import { Redis } from 'ioredis';
import { REDIS_CLIENT } from '../redis/redis.constants';

interface IdemRecord {
  state: 'processing' | 'done';
  fp: string;               // request fingerprint
  status?: number;
  body?: unknown;
}

const PROCESSING_TTL_S = 60;       // upper bound on one handler run (tune per endpoint)
const DONE_TTL_S = 24 * 60 * 60;   // how long replays are served

@Injectable()
export class IdempotencyInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  constructor(@Inject(REDIS_CLIENT) private readonly redis: Redis) {}

  async intercept(ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler): Promise<Observable<unknown>> {
    const http = ctx.switchToHttp();
    const req = http.getRequest();
    const res = http.getResponse();

    const idemKey = req.headers['idempotency-key'] as string | undefined;
    if (!idemKey) throw new BadRequestException('Idempotency-Key header is required');
    if (!/^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{8,128}$/.test(idemKey)) throw new BadRequestException('Invalid Idempotency-Key');

    // Scope per caller so one user cannot replay or probe another user's keys.
    const scope = req.user?.id ?? req.ip;
    const redisKey = `shop:idem:${scope}:${idemKey}`;
    const fp = createHash('sha256')
      .update(`${req.method}|${req.originalUrl}|${JSON.stringify(req.body ?? {})}`)
      .digest('hex')
      .slice(0, 32);

    let claimed: 'OK' | null;
    try {
      const rec: IdemRecord = { state: 'processing', fp };
      claimed = (await this.redis.set(redisKey, JSON.stringify(rec), 'EX', PROCESSING_TTL_S, 'NX')) as 'OK' | null;
    } catch {
      // Payments-like endpoint: fail CLOSED. Use a different policy for low-risk endpoints.
      throw new ServiceUnavailableException('Idempotency store unavailable');
    }

    if (claimed !== 'OK') {
      const raw = await this.redis.get(redisKey);
      if (!raw) return this.intercept(ctx, next); // expired between SET and GET: try to claim again
      const existing = JSON.parse(raw) as IdemRecord;
      if (existing.fp !== fp) {
        throw new UnprocessableEntityException('Idempotency-Key reused with a different request');
      }
      if (existing.state === 'processing') {
        throw new ConflictException('A request with this Idempotency-Key is still being processed');
      }
      res.setHeader('Idempotent-Replayed', 'true');
      res.status(existing.status ?? 200);
      return of(existing.body);
    }

    return next.handle().pipe(
      mergeMap((body) =>
        from(
          (async () => {
            const rec: IdemRecord = { state: 'done', fp, status: res.statusCode, body };
            await this.redis.set(redisKey, JSON.stringify(rec), 'EX', DONE_TTL_S).catch(() => undefined);
            return body;
          })(),
        ),
      ),
      catchError((err) =>
        from(this.redis.unlink(redisKey).catch(() => undefined)).pipe(
          // release the claim so a legitimate client retry can run; then rethrow
          mergeMap(() => throwError(() => err)),
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}
```

```ts
// usage
@Controller('orders')
export class OrdersController {
  constructor(private readonly orders: OrdersService) {}

  @Post()
  @UseInterceptors(IdempotencyInterceptor)
  create(@Body() dto: CreateOrderDto) {
    return this.orders.create(dto); // still protect with UNIQUE(idempotency_key) inside the DB transaction
  }
}
```

Behavior notes and limitations:

- Releasing the claim on **any** error means a handler that already performed a side effect and then threw gets re-executed on retry. If errors after side effects are possible, make the handler itself idempotent (DB constraint) or keep the claim in an "unknown" state and reconcile.
- If the process crashes mid-handler, the claim lives for `PROCESSING_TTL_S`; during that window retries get `409`. After it, a retry executes again (hence the DB-level guard).
- `res.statusCode` at `mergeMap` time reflects the status Nest will send (201 for `@Post` by default).
- Cache stored bodies carefully: they may contain personal data. Keep `DONE_TTL_S` as short as the retry window really needs.
- BullMQ jobs get a similar effect for background work by passing `jobId` (duplicate IDs are ignored while the job exists); that is a BullMQ feature.

## 4.12 Event-driven architecture on Redis

### 4.12.1 Choosing the transport

| Mechanism | Delivery | Persistence | Consumers | Ordering | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Pub/Sub** | At-most-once | None | All subscribers get every message | Per publisher connection | Ephemeral signals, cache invalidation, WebSocket fan-out |
| **Streams** (`XADD`, consumer groups) | At-least-once (ack + pending list) | Yes (in memory and persisted with RDB/AOF), trimmed by you | Competing consumers per group; multiple groups each get all messages | Per stream | Lightweight durable event log, work distribution inside a service |
| **BullMQ** (library on Redis) | At-least-once with retries | Redis persistence | Workers compete for jobs | FIFO by default, with priorities/delays | Background jobs: emails, reports, webhooks, retries/backoff, scheduling |
| **Kafka / RabbitMQ / SQS** (external) | Configurable, stronger operational story | Disk-based log/queue | Rich consumer models | Partition/queue | High-volume cross-service integration, long retention, replay |

Honest trade-off: Redis Streams and BullMQ are excellent for small to mid-size workloads on infrastructure you already run. They are bounded by memory (the backlog lives in RAM), by Redis persistence guarantees (async replication, AOF fsync policy), and lack Kafka-scale retention and replay tooling.

### 4.12.2 Streams quick tour

```bash
# Produce (MAXLEN ~ trims approximately, cheaply)
127.0.0.1:6379> XADD shop:stream:orders MAXLEN ~ 100000 * orderId 991 status created
"1763540000000-0"

# Create a consumer group that starts from new messages ($); MKSTREAM creates the stream if missing
127.0.0.1:6379> XGROUP CREATE shop:stream:orders billing $ MKSTREAM
OK

# Consume as consumer "billing-1": '>' means "messages never delivered to this group"
127.0.0.1:6379> XREADGROUP GROUP billing billing-1 COUNT 10 BLOCK 5000 STREAMS shop:stream:orders >
1) 1) "shop:stream:orders"
   2) 1) 1) "1763540000000-0"
         2) 1) "orderId"
            2) "991"
            3) "status"
            4) "created"

# Acknowledge after successful processing
127.0.0.1:6379> XACK shop:stream:orders billing 1763540000000-0
(integer) 1

# Messages delivered but never acked (consumer crashed) stay in the Pending Entries List
127.0.0.1:6379> XPENDING shop:stream:orders billing
# Reclaim stuck messages from dead consumers (idle > 60 s) [6.2+]
127.0.0.1:6379> XAUTOCLAIM shop:stream:orders billing billing-2 60000 0-0 COUNT 10
```

```ts
// src/events/order-stream.consumer.ts
import { Inject, Injectable, Logger, OnApplicationBootstrap, OnApplicationShutdown } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Redis } from 'ioredis';
import { REDIS_CLIENT } from '../redis/redis.constants';

const STREAM = 'shop:stream:orders';
const GROUP = 'billing';

@Injectable()
export class OrderStreamConsumer implements OnApplicationBootstrap, OnApplicationShutdown {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(OrderStreamConsumer.name);
  private readonly consumer = `c-${process.pid}`;
  private running = false;
  private blocking!: Redis; // BLOCK ties up a connection: use a dedicated one

  constructor(@Inject(REDIS_CLIENT) private readonly redis: Redis) {}

  async onApplicationBootstrap(): Promise<void> {
    this.blocking = this.redis.duplicate();
    try {
      await this.redis.xgroup('CREATE', STREAM, GROUP, '$', 'MKSTREAM');
    } catch (e) {
      if (!(e as Error).message.includes('BUSYGROUP')) throw e; // group already exists: fine
    }
    this.running = true;
    void this.loop();
  }

  private async loop(): Promise<void> {
    while (this.running) {
      try {
        const res = (await this.blocking.xreadgroup(
          'GROUP', GROUP, this.consumer, 'COUNT', 10, 'BLOCK', 5000, 'STREAMS', STREAM, '>',
        )) as [string, [string, string[]][]][] | null;
        if (!res) continue;
        for (const [, entries] of res) {
          for (const [id, fields] of entries) {
            await this.handle(fields); // must be idempotent: redelivery is possible
            await this.redis.xack(STREAM, GROUP, id);
          }
        }
      } catch (e) {
        this.logger.error(`stream loop error: ${(e as Error).message}`);
        await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 1000));
      }
    }
  }

  private async handle(fields: string[]): Promise<void> {
    const event: Record<string, string> = {};
    for (let i = 0; i < fields.length; i += 2) event[fields[i]] = fields[i + 1];
    this.logger.log(`order event ${JSON.stringify(event)}`);
  }

  async onApplicationShutdown(): Promise<void> {
    this.running = false;
    this.blocking?.disconnect(); // aborts the pending BLOCK read
  }
}
```

This sketch omits: a periodic `XAUTOCLAIM` sweep for stuck messages, a dead-letter policy (move after N delivery attempts, visible through `XPENDING` delivery counts), and graceful drain. If you need all of those plus delays and retries, BullMQ already implements them.

## 4.13 Background jobs

### 4.13.1 Why jobs, and why Redis

Slow or unreliable work (email, PDF generation, webhooks, image processing, imports) should leave the request path: respond fast, do the work in a worker with retries, backoff, concurrency limits, and visibility. Workers are separate processes, scalable independently of the API: this is the horizontal-scaling answer for work that in-memory queues (`setImmediate`, arrays) cannot provide because they die with the process.

### 4.13.2 BullMQ overview (library, built on Redis)

BullMQ is a Node.js library; its guarantees (retries, delayed jobs, rate limiting, flows, stalled-job recovery) are implemented by the library using Redis data structures and Lua scripts. They are **not** Redis server features. Requirements you should know: it needs **ioredis**; Redis should use `maxmemory-policy noeviction` (evicting queue keys corrupts queue state); and job processing is **at-least-once**, so handlers must be idempotent. Full treatment is in the BullMQ module.

```ts
// src/jobs/email.queue.ts
import { Queue, Worker, Job } from 'bullmq';
import { Redis } from 'ioredis';

// BullMQ Workers require maxRetriesPerRequest: null on their connection (blocking commands).
const connection = new Redis(process.env.REDIS_URL!, { maxRetriesPerRequest: null });

export const emailQueue = new Queue('email', { connection });

export async function enqueueWelcomeEmail(userId: string): Promise<void> {
  await emailQueue.add(
    'welcome',
    { userId },
    {
      jobId: `welcome:${userId}`,        // duplicate adds are ignored while the job exists: cheap dedupe
      attempts: 5,
      backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 2_000 },
      removeOnComplete: { age: 3_600, count: 1_000 },
      removeOnFail: { age: 24 * 3_600 },
    },
  );
}

export const emailWorker = new Worker(
  'email',
  async (job: Job<{ userId: string }>) => {
    // Idempotent: check "already sent" in the DB or a Redis SET NX marker before sending.
    await sendWelcomeEmail(job.data.userId);
  },
  { connection, concurrency: 10 },
);

emailWorker.on('failed', (job, err) => console.error(`job ${job?.id} failed: ${err.message}`));

declare function sendWelcomeEmail(userId: string): Promise<void>;
```

Deployment shape with PM2/Docker: run the **API** and the **workers** as separate processes or containers (`pm2 start api -i 4` and `pm2 start worker -i 2`) so that CPU-heavy jobs do not block HTTP and you can scale each side independently. Scheduling ("every night at 02:00") through BullMQ's repeatable-jobs/job-scheduler feature (the exact API name depends on your BullMQ 5.x version; check the docs for the one you install) is an alternative to hand-rolled leader election: the scheduler creates one job per tick and one worker processes it.

## 4.14 Failure scenarios and operations

| Scenario | What happens | Design response |
|---|---|---|
| Redis unavailable | Sessions, rate limits, locks, idempotency, queues stall | Per-feature policy: caching fail-open; auth fail-closed; rate limit fail-open (except login/OTP); payments idempotency fail-closed; leader steps down; jobs pause and resume |
| Redis failover (Sentinel/Cluster/managed) | Seconds of errors; clients reconnect; last writes may be lost (async replication) | Retry with backoff; idempotent operations; locks/leases treated as best-effort; tolerate counter loss |
| Network partition between an instance and Redis | That instance fails alone while others work | Timeouts, circuit breaker, leader lease self-expiry |
| Pub/Sub subscriber disconnects | Misses messages | Clear L1 on reconnect; TTL backstops; "something changed" semantics |
| Eviction on a shared instance | Sessions or locks vanish silently | Separate instances by purpose; `noeviction` for queues/locks/sessions; capacity alerts |
| Hot key from a global counter | One shard/core saturated | Shard the counter, local aggregation with periodic flush |
| Clock skew between app instances | App-computed window IDs (rate limits) disagree | Use Redis server time (`TIME` command, or compute windows inside Lua with `redis.call('TIME')`) when exact agreement matters |
| Thundering reconnect after Redis restart | All instances reconnect, cold caches, retry storm | Exponential backoff with jitter (`retryStrategy`), DB bulkheads, warm-up |
| Rolling deploy with mixed versions | Old and new code share Redis keys with different shapes | Versioned key prefixes (Module 3, section 3.4.6), backward-compatible payloads |

Operational checklist for Redis as shared infrastructure:

- Separate logical roles: **cache** (evictable), **sessions/locks/idempotency** (volatile TTL data, avoid eviction), **queues** (`noeviction`, persistence on). A single instance can serve several roles for small systems, but you must size and configure for the strictest role.
- Monitor: `connected_clients`, `blocked_clients`, `used_memory` vs `maxmemory`, `evicted_keys`, `rejected_connections`, replication lag (`master_repl_offset` vs replica offset), latency (`LATENCY DOCTOR`, `SLOWLOG GET`), command stats.
- Use `connectionName` (Module 1) per role (`api`, `worker`, `subscriber`) so `CLIENT LIST` is readable.
- Set timeouts everywhere (connect, command) and bounded retries; unbounded queueing during an outage turns into memory growth in Node.
- Test failure: kill Redis in staging during load. The first time you see the failure behavior should not be production.

## 4.15 Interview Q&A

### Q1. Why do in-memory sessions or caches break when you scale an API horizontally?

**Short answer.** Each instance has its own memory, and requests are spread across instances, so state written on one is invisible to the others (and lost on restart).

**Detail.** Under PM2 cluster mode, multiple containers, or multiple servers behind Nginx, consecutive requests from one user hit different processes. Sessions disappear, rate limits multiply by instance count, caches diverge, cron jobs run N times. The fix is to keep instances stateless and move shared state into a shared store (Redis for fast ephemeral state, the database for durable state).

**Senior follow-up.** "Isn't sticky sessions enough?" It hides some symptoms but not restarts, deploys, uneven load, cron duplication, or shared limits, and it ties user state to instance health.

**Common wrong answer.** "Use a bigger server instead." That fixes capacity, not availability or the need to restart/deploy without logging users out.

### Q2. How do you make sure a cron job runs on only one of five instances?

**Short answer.** Leader election with a Redis lease (`SET NX PX` plus renewal), or a dedicated scheduler process, or queue-based repeatable jobs.

**Detail.** Lease holder renews with a compare-and-`PEXPIRE` Lua script; followers retry. The leader stops acting as soon as it cannot renew within the TTL minus a safety margin. Because pauses and partitions can produce a brief overlap, the job must be idempotent. A single dedicated scheduler process is often the simplest solution.

**Senior follow-up.** "What if the leader is paused for longer than the TTL?" Two leaders can briefly coexist. Use idempotent work, fencing tokens if the downstream resource supports them, or a consensus-based lease (etcd, Kubernetes Lease) when correctness is critical.

**Common wrong answer.** "Use `SETNX` and never release it" or "check `process.env.NODE_APP_INSTANCE === '0'`". The former blocks forever after a crash (no TTL); the latter fails when instance 0 is down and does not work across containers or hosts.

### Q3. Redis Pub/Sub vs Streams vs a queue: when each?

**Short answer.** Pub/Sub for ephemeral broadcast, Streams for a lightweight durable log with consumer groups, a queue (BullMQ) for background jobs with retries and scheduling.

**Detail.** Pub/Sub is at-most-once with no history, so it is only safe for hints where losing a message is harmless. Streams give ack/pending semantics and replay within retention. BullMQ (a library) adds retries, backoff, delays, concurrency, and stalled-job handling on top of Redis. For large-scale cross-team event streaming with long retention, consider Kafka or a managed broker.

**Senior follow-up.** "How would you invalidate distributed L1 caches reliably?" Pub/Sub for speed, short L1 TTL for correctness, clear L1 on reconnect; or client-side caching with tracking.

**Common wrong answer.** "Pub/Sub guarantees delivery to all instances." Only to those connected at that instant.

### Q4. How do you implement idempotent payment or order creation?

**Short answer.** Client sends an `Idempotency-Key`; the server atomically claims it (`SET NX EX`), executes once, stores the result, and replays it on duplicates; a DB unique constraint is the real guard.

**Detail.** Fingerprint the request to detect key reuse with a different payload (422). Return 409 while the first attempt is in flight. Scope keys per user. Choose TTLs (processing: short; result: hours to days). Redis alone cannot atomically cover the DB side effect; the unique constraint or outbox in the same DB transaction closes that gap.

**Senior follow-up.** "What if Redis is down?" For payments, fail closed; otherwise a retry could double-charge. Optionally fall back to DB-only idempotency.

**Common wrong answer.** "Check if the order exists, then create it." That is a race between concurrent retries.

### Q5. Is a Redis `SET NX PX` lock safe for correctness-critical mutual exclusion?

**Short answer.** No: it is good for efficiency (avoiding duplicate work), not for correctness.

**Detail.** Lease expiry during GC pauses or slow I/O, asynchronous replication losing the lock on failover, and clock/pause assumptions can all produce two holders. If correctness is at stake use database constraints, row locks or advisory locks within one database, fencing tokens checked by the protected resource, or a consensus system. Redlock reduces some risks and is controversial; the later locks module covers the arguments.

**Senior follow-up.** "How do fencing tokens work?" Each acquisition gets an increasing number; the resource rejects operations carrying a number lower than the highest it has seen.

**Common wrong answer.** "Redis is single-threaded so locks are always safe." Single-threaded command execution makes `SET NX` atomic on one node; it does not make distributed timing, failover, or client pauses safe.

## 4.16 Senior and Staff discussion

- **Classify every piece of Redis-held state** by loss tolerance: *rebuildable* (cache), *retryable* (OTP, rate-limit counters), *must-not-lose* (do not keep only in Redis). Each class gets its own instance policy, persistence, and alerting.
- **Define the degraded mode per feature before the incident.** A table of "if Redis is down: auth does X, rate limit does Y, locks do Z, queue does W" is one of the most valuable runbook artifacts. Fail-open vs fail-closed is a product and security decision, not a coding detail.
- **Blast radius and dependency budget.** If every service depends on one Redis, Redis availability caps everyone's SLO. Consider per-service or per-role instances, and measure whether requests truly need Redis on the critical path (JWT access tokens remove it for authentication; L1 caches remove it for hot reads).
- **Coordination minimization.** The best distributed lock is the one you avoided: unique constraints, optimistic concurrency, idempotent consumers, partitioned work (each instance owns a key range), and single-writer designs. Staff-level reviews ask "what if we removed this lock?" first.
- **Consistency vocabulary.** Be able to state, per pattern, whether it provides at-most-once, at-least-once, or effectively-once (at-least-once plus idempotency), and where the deduplication state lives.
- **Observability of coordination.** Emit metrics for lock acquisition failures and hold times, leader changes, idempotent replays, Pub/Sub subscriber reconnects, consumer lag (`XINFO GROUPS`, pending counts), queue depth and age. Coordination bugs are time-based and invisible without these.
- **When to leave Redis.** Strong consistency coordination (etcd/ZooKeeper/Postgres), very high volume durable events (Kafka), large durable queues (broker with disk), global multi-region coordination (design for eventual consistency or use a database that supports it).
- **Cost.** Memory-resident coordination state is cheap per key but accumulates: per-user session sets, idempotency bodies, per-IP rate-limit keys. Estimate cardinality x size x TTL before launch.

## 4.17 Practical exercise

**Task.** You have a NestJS API deployed with PM2 (`pm2 start dist/main.js -i 4`) behind Nginx. Today it uses `MemoryStore` sessions, an in-memory rate limiter, an L1 `Map` cache with no invalidation, and a `@Cron('*/5 * * * *')` sync job. Make it safe for horizontal scaling:

1. Move sessions to Redis (connect-redis).
2. Replace the in-memory rate limiter with a Redis fixed-window limiter (100 req/min per IP), failing open on Redis errors.
3. Add Pub/Sub invalidation for the L1 cache.
4. Ensure the cron job runs on exactly one instance at a time.
5. Add an idempotency interceptor to `POST /orders`.
6. Prove each fix with a test or command.

**Solution outline.**

| Step | Change | Verification |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `app.use(session({ store: new RedisStore({ client: redis, prefix: 'shop:session:' }), saveUninitialized: false, ... }))`, `trust proxy` set | Log in; `for i in 1..10 curl -b cookies /me` returns the same user across different `pid`s; `redis-cli --scan --pattern 'shop:session:*'` shows one key; `pm2 reload` does not log the user out |
| 2 | `RateLimitGuard` from 4.8 using `CounterService.hit` | Fire 150 requests in a minute: first 100 return 200, the rest 429, regardless of which worker answers. `redis-cli GET shop:rl:<ip>:<bucket>` shows the count. Stop Redis: requests still pass (fail open), error logged |
| 3 | `L1CacheService` from 4.10.3 | Two instances: read product on both (L1 filled); update via instance A; read via B within 100 ms returns new data. `redis-cli PUBSUB NUMSUB shop:events:cache-invalidate` equals instance count |
| 4 | `LeaderElectionService` + guard in cron | `redis-cli GET shop:leader:scheduler` shows one owner. Kill the leader (`pm2 stop` that process id); within about TTL seconds another instance owns it and the cron fires once per tick. Check logs: exactly one "sync started" per 5 minutes across all workers |
| 5 | `@UseInterceptors(IdempotencyInterceptor)` on `POST /orders` plus unique index on `orders(idempotency_key)` | `curl` the same request twice with the same `Idempotency-Key`: same body, second response has `Idempotent-Replayed: true`, one row in `orders`. Same key with a different body returns 422. Two simultaneous requests: one 201, one 409 |
| 6 | Document degraded mode per feature in the runbook | Chaos drill: `docker stop redis` under load; confirm the documented behavior, then restart and watch reconnect logs, error rate and DB load |

Test command for step 4 (counts how many instances ran the job, using a Redis counter inside the job for the exercise):

```bash
# in the job body (exercise only):  await redis.incr('shop:test:cron-runs:' + new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 16))
redis-cli --scan --pattern 'shop:test:cron-runs:*' | while read k; do echo "$k $(redis-cli GET $k)"; done
# expected: every minute-bucket that contains a tick shows exactly 1
```

**Stretch goals.** Add Streams for order events with a consumer group and `XAUTOCLAIM` sweep. Replace the cron election with a BullMQ job scheduler and compare failure behavior. Add fencing tokens to the lock helper and a Postgres `UPDATE ... WHERE fence < $n` guard.

## 4.18 Key takeaways

1. Horizontal scaling (PM2 cluster, containers, multiple hosts) makes every in-process variable per-instance. Keep services stateless and put shared state in shared stores.
2. Redis gives atomic primitives (`INCR`, `SET NX PX`, Lua, Streams, Pub/Sub) that other patterns are built from; know each pattern's actual guarantee.
3. Sessions: Redis store with idle and absolute timeouts, `saveUninitialized: false`, regenerate on login, dedicated non-evicting capacity. JWT removes the lookup but complicates revocation.
4. Counters must use atomic commands, not read-modify-write. Windowed counters and conditional decrements need Lua. Redis counters can lose recent increments on failover.
5. Locks and leader leases are **best-effort** efficiency tools; pair them with idempotent work and fencing or database constraints when correctness matters.
6. Pub/Sub is at-most-once. Use it for hints (cache invalidation, WebSocket fan-out), never as the only copy of important data. Clear local state on reconnect and keep TTL backstops.
7. Idempotency: atomic claim, fingerprint, replay, and a database unique constraint as the real guard; fail closed for payments.
8. Choose the transport by loss tolerance: Pub/Sub (ephemeral), Streams (durable log), BullMQ (jobs with retries, a library on Redis), external broker (scale and retention).
9. Decide and document the degraded mode of every Redis-backed feature (fail open vs closed) before an outage, and rehearse it.
10. The best coordination is the one you avoid: prefer unique constraints, optimistic concurrency, partitioned ownership, and idempotent consumers over distributed locks.

# Module 5: Pub/Sub, Streams & Messaging

Redis is often the first messaging system a backend team reaches for, because it is already running for caching. It ships three distinct messaging primitives with very different guarantees: **Pub/Sub** (fire-and-forget broadcast), **Lists** (simple queues) and **Streams** (a persistent, replayable log with consumer groups). On top of those, **BullMQ** (a Node.js library, not a Redis feature) builds a full job queue. Knowing which one to pick, and being able to explain why, is a classic senior-level interview topic.

This module has two parts. Part 1 covers Pub/Sub in depth. Part 2 covers Streams, the big comparison table (Redis vs RabbitMQ vs Kafka), and the Socket.IO multi-instance setup. Module 6 covers BullMQ.

> Convention used in this module: code uses the `REDIS_CLIENT` provider from Module 1, section 1.12 (an `ioredis` instance). Messaging needs extra, dedicated connections, so we add new providers next to it instead of reusing that one.

---

## 5.1 Pub/Sub Fundamentals

### 5.1.1 Definition

**Publish/Subscribe** is a messaging pattern where senders (publishers) do not send messages to specific receivers. They publish to a named **channel**, and every client currently subscribed to that channel receives a copy.

Redis implements this directly in the server:

| Command | Purpose | Version |
|---|---|---|
| `SUBSCRIBE channel [channel ...]` | Listen to exact channel names | all |
| `PSUBSCRIBE pattern [pattern ...]` | Listen to glob-style patterns (`news.*`) | all |
| `PUBLISH channel message` | Send a message; returns number of receivers | all |
| `UNSUBSCRIBE` / `PUNSUBSCRIBE` | Stop listening | all |
| `SSUBSCRIBE shardchannel` | Sharded subscribe (cluster-aware) | [7.0+] |
| `SPUBLISH shardchannel message` | Sharded publish | [7.0+] |
| `SUNSUBSCRIBE` | Sharded unsubscribe | [7.0+] |
| `PUBSUB CHANNELS [pattern]` | List active channels | all |
| `PUBSUB NUMSUB channel ...` | Subscriber count per channel | all |
| `PUBSUB NUMPAT` | Number of active pattern subscriptions | all |
| `PUBSUB SHARDCHANNELS`, `PUBSUB SHARDNUMSUB` | Sharded equivalents | [7.0+] |

### 5.1.2 Why it is needed

Typical problems where "one producer, many live listeners" fits:

- Pushing a notification to every connected WebSocket server instance (each instance holds a different subset of users).
- Cache invalidation across multiple app instances (local in-process caches must drop a key).
- Configuration reload signals ("feature flags changed, re-read them").
- Live dashboards, presence, typing indicators: data whose value expires in seconds.

In all of these, **losing a message is acceptable** because the next message, or a reconnect-and-refetch, repairs state.

### 5.1.3 Internal mechanism

Inside the Redis server, Pub/Sub is just two in-memory dictionaries:

- `pubsub_channels`: channel name to a list of subscribed clients.
- `pubsub_patterns`: a list of (pattern, client) entries.

On `PUBLISH`, the server looks up the exact channel and walks its client list, then walks **every** pattern and glob-matches the channel name against it. For each matching client it appends the message to that client's **output buffer**. The event loop later writes the buffer to the socket.

Key consequences:

1. **No storage.** Nothing is written to the keyspace, RDB, AOF, or replication backlog as data. (The `PUBLISH` command itself is propagated to replicas so replicas can deliver to their own subscribers.)
2. **At-most-once delivery.** If a subscriber is disconnected, slow, or not yet subscribed, the message is gone for that subscriber.
3. **Cost of publish is O(N + M)** where N is subscribers of that channel and M is the total number of pattern subscriptions in the server. Heavy `PSUBSCRIBE` use makes every publish slower, even on unrelated channels.
4. **Fan-out cost is paid by the server's single thread** (and memory for each output buffer copy).

### 5.1.4 Diagram

```
 Publisher A ──PUBLISH chat:room1 "hi"──┐
                                         ▼
                              ┌─────────────────────┐
 Publisher B ──PUBLISH ...───▶│     Redis server    │
                              │  channels:          │
                              │   chat:room1 ─▶ [c1,c2]
                              │  patterns:          │
                              │   chat:* ─▶ [c3]    │
                              └──────┬───────┬──────┘
                       output buf c1 │       │ output buf c3
                                     ▼       ▼
                          Subscriber c1,c2   Subscriber c3
                          (SUBSCRIBE)        (PSUBSCRIBE chat:*)

 Subscriber c4 (offline when PUBLISH happened) ──▶ never sees "hi"
```

### 5.1.5 Redis CLI examples

Open two terminals.

```text
# Terminal 1 (subscriber)
127.0.0.1:6379> SUBSCRIBE chat:room1
1) "subscribe"
2) "chat:room1"
3) (integer) 1
# ... waits. When a message arrives:
1) "message"
2) "chat:room1"
3) "hello"
```

```text
# Terminal 2 (publisher)
127.0.0.1:6379> PUBLISH chat:room1 "hello"
(integer) 1          # exactly one subscriber received it
127.0.0.1:6379> PUBLISH chat:empty "anyone?"
(integer) 0          # nobody listening: message is discarded
```

Pattern subscription (note the extra `pmessage` fields, including the matching pattern):

```text
127.0.0.1:6379> PSUBSCRIBE chat:*
1) "psubscribe"
2) "chat:*"
3) (integer) 1
1) "pmessage"
2) "chat:*"          # pattern that matched
3) "chat:room7"      # actual channel
4) "yo"              # payload
```

Introspection:

```text
127.0.0.1:6379> PUBSUB CHANNELS
1) "chat:room1"
127.0.0.1:6379> PUBSUB NUMSUB chat:room1 chat:room2
1) "chat:room1"
2) (integer) 1
3) "chat:room2"
4) (integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> PUBSUB NUMPAT
(integer) 1
```

Sharded Pub/Sub [7.0+]:

```text
127.0.0.1:6379> SSUBSCRIBE orders:eu
1) "ssubscribe"
2) "orders:eu"
3) (integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> SPUBLISH orders:eu "order-1"     # from another client
(integer) 1
```

---

## 5.2 Pub/Sub Limitations You Must Be Able to Recite

| Limitation | Detail | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| **At-most-once** | No ack, no retry. Lost if subscriber is down, reconnecting, or slow. | Use Streams or BullMQ when loss is unacceptable; or combine with "refetch on reconnect". |
| **No persistence / history** | A new subscriber sees nothing that was published earlier. No replay. | Store state in a key/stream; Pub/Sub only as a "wake up" signal. |
| **Subscribed connection is special (RESP2)** | In RESP2, a connection in subscribe mode can only run `SUBSCRIBE`, `PSUBSCRIBE`, `UNSUBSCRIBE`, `PUNSUBSCRIBE`, `PING`, `QUIT` (and `RESET`). Other commands error. | Use a **separate connection** for subscribing. With RESP3 (`HELLO 3`), push messages are out-of-band and a connection may run other commands, but a dedicated subscriber is still the safe convention. |
| **Slow subscriber kills itself** | Each subscriber has an output buffer. Default `client-output-buffer-limit pubsub 32mb 8mb 60` means: hard limit 32 MB, or soft limit 8 MB sustained for 60 s, then Redis **closes the connection**. | Keep handlers fast, offload heavy work, monitor `CLIENT LIST` (`omem`), alert on disconnects. |
| **Pattern cost** | Every `PUBLISH` is matched against all patterns. | Prefer exact channels; keep pattern count small. |
| **Cluster broadcast** | Classic `PUBLISH` in Redis Cluster is propagated to **all nodes** over the cluster bus, which scales poorly. | Use sharded Pub/Sub `SPUBLISH`/`SSUBSCRIBE` [7.0+], where messages stay within the shard that owns the channel's hash slot. |
| **No consumer groups** | Every subscriber gets every message. You cannot load-balance one message to one of N workers. | Use Streams consumer groups or BullMQ for work distribution. |
| **Not a queue** | There is no backlog, no backpressure signal to the publisher. | Same as above. |

### 5.2.1 The "subscribe mode" rule in ioredis

When you call `redis.subscribe(...)` on an `ioredis` instance, that instance enters subscriber mode. ioredis will then throw `Connection in subscriber mode, only subscriber commands may be used` if you try `GET`, `SET`, etc. on it. The fix is always the same: keep one connection for commands and one (or more) for subscribing. `redis.duplicate()` creates a new connection with the same options.

---

## 5.3 Sharded Pub/Sub [7.0+]

In classic Pub/Sub on a Redis Cluster, a `PUBLISH` to any node is relayed to **every node** in the cluster, because a subscriber might be connected anywhere. With 50 nodes, each message becomes 50 inter-node transmissions. That does not scale.

**Sharded Pub/Sub** assigns each channel to a hash slot (`CRC16(channel) mod 16384`), exactly like a key. Messages are only propagated within the shard (primary + its replicas) that owns the slot. The client connects to a node that owns the slot to `SSUBSCRIBE`.

```
 Classic Pub/Sub in Cluster                Sharded Pub/Sub [7.0+]
 --------------------------                ----------------------
 PUBLISH ch ──▶ node A                     SPUBLISH ch ──▶ node owning slot(ch)
                │ cluster bus                               │ (only to its replicas)
         ┌──────┼──────┐                              shard A: primary + replicas
         ▼      ▼      ▼                              shards B, C: untouched
       node B  node C  node D
```

Trade-offs:

- Better horizontal scalability for high-volume channels.
- You lose the "one channel visible cluster-wide with any node" simplicity: clients must subscribe on the right shard (cluster-aware clients handle this).
- Multi-channel `SSUBSCRIBE` in one command must target channels in the same slot.
- Still at-most-once, still no persistence.
- On a standalone (non-cluster) Redis, `SPUBLISH`/`SSUBSCRIBE` work but give no benefit over classic.

Client support: check that your ioredis 5.x version supports `ssubscribe` on `Cluster` before relying on it; if not, fall back to classic Pub/Sub or a Streams-based design.

---

## 5.4 Keyspace Notifications

Redis can publish Pub/Sub events when keys change or expire. It is **off by default** (it costs CPU).

Enable with the `notify-keyspace-events` config, built from flag letters:

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `K` | Keyspace events, published on `__keyspace@<db>__:<key>` (message = event name) |
| `E` | Keyevent events, published on `__keyevent@<db>__:<event>` (message = key name) |
| `g` | Generic commands (`DEL`, `EXPIRE`, `RENAME` ...) |
| `$` | String commands |
| `l` `s` `h` `z` | List, set, hash, sorted-set commands |
| `x` | **Expired** events |
| `e` | **Evicted** events |
| `t` | Stream commands |
| `A` | Alias for `g$lshzxet` (all event classes, not including `K`/`E`/`m`) |

Example: `CONFIG SET notify-keyspace-events Ex` enables keyevent notifications for expirations only.

```text
127.0.0.1:6379> CONFIG SET notify-keyspace-events Ex
OK
# Terminal 1
127.0.0.1:6379> SUBSCRIBE __keyevent@0__:expired
1) "subscribe"
2) "__keyevent@0__:expired"
3) (integer) 1
# Terminal 2
127.0.0.1:6379> SET session:42 data EX 2
OK
# ~2 seconds later, Terminal 1 receives:
1) "message"
2) "__keyevent@0__:expired"
3) "session:42"
```

### Important caveats (common interview trap)

1. **Expiry events are not delivered at the exact TTL.** They fire when Redis actually removes the key, via lazy access or the active-expire cycle. Under load there can be a delay of seconds or more.
2. **The event carries the key name only, not the value.** The value is already gone, so you cannot read it. If you need the value, store it elsewhere (for example a shadow key).
3. **Fire-and-forget.** If your listener is down at that moment, the event is lost. Do not build "reliable delayed jobs" or "booking-hold release" on expired events. Use BullMQ delayed jobs or a sorted-set scheduler instead.
4. In Cluster, notifications are local to the node that owns the key; you must subscribe on every primary.
5. Enabling `A` on a busy instance generates huge Pub/Sub traffic. Enable only what you need.

Legitimate uses: debugging, best-effort cache warming/invalidation hints, lightweight "session expired" UI hints.

---

## 5.5 Node.js / NestJS Implementation: Pub/Sub Service

### 5.5.1 Design

- One **publisher** connection (can be the shared `REDIS_CLIENT`).
- One **dedicated subscriber** connection created by `duplicate()`.
- A typed in-process event dispatcher: the service subscribes to Redis channels once, then fans out to local handlers, so 100 handlers do not create 100 Redis subscriptions.
- Re-subscribe automatically on reconnect (ioredis does this by default for channels it knows).
- Graceful shutdown: unsubscribe, then `quit()`.

### 5.5.2 Code

```ts
// src/pubsub/pubsub.constants.ts
export const REDIS_SUBSCRIBER = Symbol('REDIS_SUBSCRIBER');
```

```ts
// src/pubsub/pubsub.module.ts
import { Global, Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Redis } from 'ioredis';
import { REDIS_CLIENT } from '../redis/redis.constants';
import { REDIS_SUBSCRIBER } from './pubsub.constants';
import { PubSubService } from './pubsub.service';

@Global()
@Module({
  providers: [
    {
      provide: REDIS_SUBSCRIBER,
      inject: [REDIS_CLIENT],
      // duplicate() opens a NEW connection with the same options.
      // A subscribed connection cannot run normal commands (RESP2).
      useFactory: (base: Redis): Redis =>
        base.duplicate({ connectionName: 'pubsub-subscriber' }),
    },
    PubSubService,
  ],
  exports: [PubSubService],
})
export class PubSubModule {}
```

```ts
// src/pubsub/pubsub.service.ts
import {
  Inject, Injectable, Logger, OnApplicationShutdown, OnModuleInit,
} from '@nestjs/common';
import { Redis } from 'ioredis';
import { REDIS_CLIENT } from '../redis/redis.constants';
import { REDIS_SUBSCRIBER } from './pubsub.constants';

export type MessageHandler<T = unknown> = (payload: T, channel: string) => void | Promise<void>;

@Injectable()
export class PubSubService implements OnModuleInit, OnApplicationShutdown {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(PubSubService.name);
  private readonly exactHandlers = new Map<string, Set<MessageHandler>>();
  private readonly patternHandlers = new Map<string, Set<MessageHandler>>();

  constructor(
    @Inject(REDIS_CLIENT) private readonly publisher: Redis,
    @Inject(REDIS_SUBSCRIBER) private readonly subscriber: Redis,
  ) {}

  onModuleInit(): void {
    // 'message' for SUBSCRIBE, 'pmessage' for PSUBSCRIBE.
    this.subscriber.on('message', (channel, raw) => {
      void this.dispatch(this.exactHandlers.get(channel), channel, raw);
    });
    this.subscriber.on('pmessage', (pattern, channel, raw) => {
      void this.dispatch(this.patternHandlers.get(pattern), channel, raw);
    });
    this.subscriber.on('error', (err) =>
      this.logger.error(`subscriber error: ${err.message}`),
    );
  }

  /** Returns number of subscribers that received the message (may be 0). */
  async publish<T>(channel: string, payload: T): Promise<number> {
    return this.publisher.publish(channel, JSON.stringify(payload));
  }

  async subscribe<T>(channel: string, handler: MessageHandler<T>): Promise<() => Promise<void>> {
    let set = this.exactHandlers.get(channel);
    if (!set) {
      set = new Set();
      this.exactHandlers.set(channel, set);
      await this.subscriber.subscribe(channel); // only once per channel
    }
    set.add(handler as MessageHandler);

    return async () => {
      set!.delete(handler as MessageHandler);
      if (set!.size === 0) {
        this.exactHandlers.delete(channel);
        await this.subscriber.unsubscribe(channel);
      }
    };
  }

  async psubscribe<T>(pattern: string, handler: MessageHandler<T>): Promise<() => Promise<void>> {
    let set = this.patternHandlers.get(pattern);
    if (!set) {
      set = new Set();
      this.patternHandlers.set(pattern, set);
      await this.subscriber.psubscribe(pattern);
    }
    set.add(handler as MessageHandler);

    return async () => {
      set!.delete(handler as MessageHandler);
      if (set!.size === 0) {
        this.patternHandlers.delete(pattern);
        await this.subscriber.punsubscribe(pattern);
      }
    };
  }

  private async dispatch(
    handlers: Set<MessageHandler> | undefined,
    channel: string,
    raw: string,
  ): Promise<void> {
    if (!handlers?.size) return;
    let payload: unknown;
    try {
      payload = JSON.parse(raw);
    } catch {
      this.logger.warn(`non-JSON message on ${channel}, dropped`);
      return;
    }
    // One failing handler must not break others or the subscriber loop.
    await Promise.allSettled(
      [...handlers].map(async (h) => {
        try {
          await h(payload, channel);
        } catch (err) {
          this.logger.error(`handler failed on ${channel}: ${(err as Error).message}`);
        }
      }),
    );
  }

  async onApplicationShutdown(): Promise<void> {
    try {
      await this.subscriber.unsubscribe();
      await this.subscriber.punsubscribe();
    } finally {
      await this.subscriber.quit();
    }
  }
}
```

Usage: cross-instance local cache invalidation.

```ts
// src/catalog/catalog-cache.service.ts
import { Injectable, OnModuleInit } from '@nestjs/common';
import { PubSubService } from '../pubsub/pubsub.service';

const CHANNEL = 'cache:invalidate:product';

@Injectable()
export class CatalogCacheService implements OnModuleInit {
  private readonly local = new Map<string, { value: unknown; exp: number }>();

  constructor(private readonly pubsub: PubSubService) {}

  async onModuleInit(): Promise<void> {
    await this.pubsub.subscribe<{ id: string }>(CHANNEL, ({ id }) => {
      this.local.delete(id); // every instance drops its copy
    });
  }

  async onProductUpdated(id: string): Promise<void> {
    this.local.delete(id);
    await this.pubsub.publish(CHANNEL, { id });
  }
}
```

Failure reasoning: if one instance misses the invalidation (reconnecting), its local entry stays stale until its TTL (`exp`) expires. Always give local caches a short TTL as the safety net; Pub/Sub only makes invalidation fast, not guaranteed.

### 5.5.3 Real-time notification system (architecture)

```
 Browser A ──WS──▶ API instance 1 ─┐                       ┌─▶ API instance 1 ──WS──▶ Browser A
 Browser B ──WS──▶ API instance 2 ─┼─▶ Redis Pub/Sub ──────┼─▶ API instance 2 ──WS──▶ Browser B
 Browser C ──WS──▶ API instance 3 ─┘   channel notif:user  └─▶ API instance 3 ──WS──▶ Browser C
                         ▲
 Worker (BullMQ) ────────┘  "user 42 has a new notification"
```

Rule of thumb: the **durable record** goes into PostgreSQL/MongoDB (or a Stream); Pub/Sub is the **live push**. A client that was offline loads missed notifications from the database on reconnect. That combination gives "real-time and correct" without needing exactly-once Pub/Sub.

---

## 5.6 Pub/Sub Performance & Memory

- Throughput: Pub/Sub is among the fastest Redis features; a single node commonly handles hundreds of thousands of small messages per second. The limit is usually the fan-out (N subscribers x message size) and network bandwidth, not command parsing.
- Memory: no data is stored, but **each subscriber's output buffer** holds pending bytes. A slow consumer with a large backlog is the main memory risk. Check with `CLIENT LIST` (fields `omem`, `obl`, `oll`) and `INFO clients`.
- Keep messages small (IDs and event types, not full documents). Subscribers can fetch details from the DB or cache.
- Prefer a handful of coarse channels (`notif:user:<id>` per user is fine at moderate scale) over millions of channels; each channel is an entry in a hash table, and `PSUBSCRIBE` patterns cost CPU on every publish.

## 5.7 Common Mistakes (Pub/Sub)

1. Using the same ioredis instance to subscribe and to run `GET`/`SET`. It will throw, or in some flows silently stop doing what you expect.
2. Treating Pub/Sub as a queue for important jobs (emails, payments). A deploy restart drops messages.
3. Building delayed or "scheduled" logic on `expired` keyspace events.
4. Using `PSUBSCRIBE *` in production "to see everything". It adds load on every publish.
5. Doing slow async work (HTTP calls, DB writes) inline in the message handler, causing output buffer growth and eventual forced disconnect. Push to a queue instead.
6. Forgetting that horizontal scaling means **every** instance receives each message; if each instance acts on it (sends an email), you get N duplicates. Pub/Sub is for per-instance effects (push to local sockets, drop local cache), not for "do it once" actions.
7. Assuming `PUBLISH` returning `1` means the message was processed. It only means one client's buffer received it.

## 5.8 Pub/Sub Interview Q&A

**Q1. Is Redis Pub/Sub reliable?**
- **Short answer:** No. It is at-most-once with no persistence.
- **Detail:** The server writes each message to the output buffers of currently connected subscribers and forgets it. Disconnected or slow subscribers lose messages. There are no acks or replays.
- **Senior follow-up:** "How would you make a notification system reliable on top of it?" Persist the notification first (DB or Stream), publish only a wake-up/hint, and have clients re-sync from the durable store on reconnect.
- **Common wrong answer:** "Redis persists to disk with AOF, so Pub/Sub messages survive restarts." AOF stores data commands; published messages are not stored as data.

**Q2. Why can't I run `GET` on a subscribed connection?**
- **Short answer:** In RESP2, a connection in subscribe mode only accepts subscription-related commands, because replies and pushed messages share the same stream and would be ambiguous.
- **Detail:** Use a separate connection (`duplicate()`). RESP3 introduced typed push messages so the ambiguity is gone, but the dedicated-connection convention stays in client libraries.
- **Senior follow-up:** "What happens to subscriptions on reconnect?" ioredis re-issues `SUBSCRIBE`/`PSUBSCRIBE` for known channels (`autoResubscribe`, default true), but messages published during the gap are lost.
- **Common wrong answer:** "It is a bug in ioredis."

**Q3. What happens if a subscriber is too slow?**
- **Short answer:** Its output buffer grows; at the `client-output-buffer-limit pubsub` threshold Redis disconnects it.
- **Detail:** Default `32mb 8mb 60`. The client then reconnects and has permanently lost the buffered messages.
- **Senior follow-up:** "How do you detect it?" Alert on client disconnects, monitor `omem` in `CLIENT LIST`, and watch handler latency.
- **Common wrong answer:** "Redis applies backpressure to the publisher."

**Q4. When is sharded Pub/Sub preferable? [7.0+]**
- **Short answer:** In Redis Cluster with high-volume channels.
- **Detail:** Classic publishes are broadcast to all nodes; sharded ones stay within the owning shard.
- **Senior follow-up:** "What are the constraints?" Channel-to-slot mapping, cluster-aware client, same-slot rule for multi-channel `SSUBSCRIBE`.
- **Common wrong answer:** "Sharded Pub/Sub adds persistence."

**Q5. Can keyspace notifications drive reliable timers?**
- **Short answer:** No.
- **Detail:** Events are delayed (lazy/active expiry), carry only the key name, and are lost if no listener is connected.
- **Senior follow-up:** What instead? BullMQ delayed jobs, or a sorted-set scheduler with score = due timestamp polled by a worker.
- **Common wrong answer:** "Expired events fire exactly at TTL."

## 5.9 Senior/Staff Discussion

- **Choosing the failure mode:** Pub/Sub chooses "drop" under stress. Streams choose "buffer and retain" (memory growth). BullMQ chooses "retain and retry". Decide which failure is cheaper for the business capability.
- **Hint + source of truth pattern:** use Pub/Sub for latency, a durable store for correctness. This is how most chat and notification products are built.
- **Connection budget:** every subscriber instance holds at least one dedicated Redis connection. With 200 pods, that is 200 permanent connections; account for `maxclients`.
- **Observability:** instrument publish rate, delivered count (the return value of `PUBLISH`), and handler errors. A sustained return value of `0` on a channel that should have listeners is a useful alarm.
- **Security:** channel names are not access-controlled by default beyond ACLs (`+@pubsub` and channel patterns `&channel`). Use ACL rules to restrict which users can publish/subscribe to which channels.

## 5.10 Practical Exercise (Pub/Sub)

**Task:** Build a `/presence` feature: when a user connects/disconnects, publish `{userId, status}` on `presence:events`. Every API instance logs events. Add a `GET /presence/:userId` endpoint that returns online/offline without relying on missed events.

**Solution sketch:**

```ts
// presence.service.ts
import { Inject, Injectable, OnModuleInit } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Redis } from 'ioredis';
import { REDIS_CLIENT } from '../redis/redis.constants';
import { PubSubService } from '../pubsub/pubsub.service';

@Injectable()
export class PresenceService implements OnModuleInit {
  constructor(
    @Inject(REDIS_CLIENT) private readonly redis: Redis,
    private readonly pubsub: PubSubService,
  ) {}

  async onModuleInit(): Promise<void> {
    await this.pubsub.subscribe<{ userId: string; status: string }>(
      'presence:events',
      (e) => console.log('presence', e),
    );
  }

  async connected(userId: string): Promise<void> {
    // Source of truth: key with TTL, refreshed by heartbeat. Survives missed events.
    await this.redis.set(`presence:${userId}`, '1', 'EX', 60);
    await this.pubsub.publish('presence:events', { userId, status: 'online' });
  }

  async heartbeat(userId: string): Promise<void> {
    await this.redis.expire(`presence:${userId}`, 60);
  }

  async disconnected(userId: string): Promise<void> {
    await this.redis.del(`presence:${userId}`);
    await this.pubsub.publish('presence:events', { userId, status: 'offline' });
  }

  async isOnline(userId: string): Promise<boolean> {
    return (await this.redis.exists(`presence:${userId}`)) === 1;
  }
}
```

The key with TTL is the truth (crashes self-heal when the TTL lapses); Pub/Sub provides live updates only.

## 5.11 Key Takeaways (Pub/Sub)

- Pub/Sub = broadcast, in-memory, at-most-once, no history, no consumer groups.
- Use a dedicated subscriber connection; keep handlers fast.
- Sharded Pub/Sub [7.0+] fixes cluster-wide broadcast cost.
- Keyspace notifications are best-effort hints, never a scheduler.
- Pair Pub/Sub (speed) with durable storage (correctness).


---

## 5.12 Redis Streams as a Messaging System

### 5.12.1 Definition

A **Stream** is a Redis data type that models an **append-only log** of entries. Each entry has an auto-generated, monotonically increasing ID (`<millisecondsTime>-<sequence>`, for example `1731000000000-0`) and a set of field-value pairs. Streams were added in Redis 5.0; consumer-group features were extended in 6.2 (`XAUTOCLAIM`, `XPENDING ... IDLE`) and 7.0 (more `XINFO` detail, `entries-read`, lag). Redis 8.2 added more precise deletion semantics for consumer groups (`XDELEX`, `XACKDEL`) [8.2+].

Where Pub/Sub is "a radio broadcast", a Stream is "a durable log with bookmarks".

### 5.12.2 Why needed

Streams fill the gap between Pub/Sub (lossy) and a full broker like Kafka:

- Messages are **stored** and survive consumer downtime (and, with persistence enabled, Redis restarts, within AOF/RDB guarantees).
- Consumers can **replay** from any ID.
- **Consumer groups** distribute messages across N workers, track what each consumer has been given, and let you acknowledge completion.
- Crashed consumers' messages stay in a **Pending Entries List (PEL)** so another consumer can take them over.

### 5.12.3 Data model and internal mechanism

```
 Stream "orders" (radix tree of listpacks, ordered by ID)
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ 1731000000000-0  {orderId:1, total:10}                        │
 │ 1731000000001-0  {orderId:2, total:25}                        │
 │ 1731000000450-0  {orderId:3, total:99}                        │
 │ 1731000001200-0  {orderId:4, total:12}   ◀── last-generated-id│
 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
      ▲                           ▲
      │                           │
 Group "billing"             Group "analytics"       (independent cursors)
  last-delivered-id = ...450-0   last-delivered-id = ...1200-0
  PEL (delivered, not acked):    PEL: (empty)
    ...000-0 → consumer c1 (idle 4s, delivered 1x)
    ...001-0 → consumer c2 (idle 61s, delivered 2x)
  Consumers: c1, c2
```

- Internally: a **radix tree** keyed by ID, where each node is a compact **listpack** of many entries. This makes appends and range queries efficient (O(log N) to seek, then linear in results) and memory-dense.
- Each **consumer group** holds: `last-delivered-id` (cursor), a **PEL** (rax of message IDs to consumer and delivery time and delivery count), and a set of consumers (each with its own PEL).
- A message read via `XREADGROUP ... >` moves the group cursor forward and is added to the PEL. It leaves the PEL only on `XACK`. The entry itself stays in the stream until trimmed or deleted. **Ack does not delete data.**
- Multiple groups on the same stream each get **all** messages (fan-out between groups), while consumers **within** a group share the messages (load-balancing). This single feature gives you both Pub/Sub-like and queue-like semantics.

### 5.12.4 Core commands

| Command | Purpose | Version |
|---|---|---|
| `XADD key [MAXLEN|MINID [=|~] n] * field value ...` | Append entry; `*` = auto ID | 5.0 (`MINID` 6.2+) |
| `XLEN key` | Number of entries | 5.0 |
| `XRANGE` / `XREVRANGE` | Read by ID range | 5.0 |
| `XREAD [COUNT n] [BLOCK ms] STREAMS key id` | Read without groups (each reader tracks its own ID) | 5.0 |
| `XGROUP CREATE key group id|$ [MKSTREAM]` | Create consumer group | 5.0 |
| `XREADGROUP GROUP g c [COUNT n] [BLOCK ms] STREAMS key >` | Read new messages for a consumer; `>` = never-delivered | 5.0 |
| `XACK key group id ...` | Remove from PEL | 5.0 |
| `XPENDING key group [[IDLE ms] start end count [consumer]]` | Inspect PEL | 5.0 (`IDLE` 6.2+) |
| `XCLAIM key group consumer min-idle-ms id ...` | Take over specific pending entries | 5.0 |
| `XAUTOCLAIM key group consumer min-idle-ms start [COUNT n]` | Scan PEL and claim idle entries in one call | **[6.2+]** |
| `XTRIM key MAXLEN|MINID [~] n` | Retention | 5.0 / MINID 6.2+ |
| `XDEL key id ...` | Delete specific entries | 5.0 |
| `XINFO STREAM|GROUPS|CONSUMERS` | Introspection | 5.0 |

### 5.12.5 Redis CLI walkthrough

```text
127.0.0.1:6379> XADD orders * orderId 1 total 10
"1731000000000-0"
127.0.0.1:6379> XADD orders * orderId 2 total 25
```
