## 14.13 WebSocket communication across multiple server instances

One Node process can hold tens of thousands of WebSocket connections, but you will run several processes (PM2 cluster, multiple containers, multiple VPS). A user connected to instance A must receive an event emitted on instance B. The Socket.IO Redis adapter solves this by using Redis Pub/Sub as the message bus between instances. Presence ("is user 42 online?") needs shared state that survives instance crashes.

### Requirements

| Type | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Functional | Clients connect via Socket.IO with a JWT |
| Functional | `server.to(room).emit()` reaches clients on every instance |
| Functional | Rooms: `user:{id}` (all devices of one user), `tenant:{id}`, `chat:{roomId}` |
| Functional | Presence: online/offline per user with multi-device support |
| Functional | Any backend process (for example a BullMQ worker) can push a message to a user |
| Non-functional | Horizontal scaling with rolling deploys; clients reconnect automatically |
| Non-functional | Deliver within 100 ms across instances on the same network |

### Architecture

```
            Browsers (Socket.IO client)
                      |  wss://app.example.com/socket.io/
                      v
              +---------------+
              |    Nginx      |  sticky: ip_hash (needed for HTTP long-polling)
              +---+-------+---+
                  |       |
        +---------v-+   +-v---------+
        | Nest app A|   | Nest app B|   (Socket.IO server + redis adapter)
        +-----+-----+   +-----+-----+
              | PUBLISH/SUBSCRIBE (socket.io#/# channels)
              +-------+-------+
                      v
               +-------------+
               |   Redis     |   Pub/Sub bus + presence ZSETs
               +------+------+
                      ^
                      | @socket.io/redis-emitter (no Socket.IO server needed)
               +------+------+
               | BullMQ      |
               | worker      |
               +-------------+
```

### Redis data structures

| Key / channel | Type | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `socket.io#/#...` channels | Pub/Sub | Created by the adapter. Do not touch them. |
| `shop:presence:user:{userId}` | ZSET | member = socketId, score = expiry timestamp (ms). Online means at least one member with score in the future |
| `shop:presence:online` | ZSET (optional) | member = userId, score = last-seen ms, for "who is online now" lists |

Why a ZSET with expiry scores instead of a SET plus TTL: Redis TTL applies to the whole key, not to individual members. If instance A crashes without running `disconnect` handlers, its socket ids would remain forever in a plain SET. With scores as expiry times, stale entries are simply ignored and trimmed by `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE`.

### Key design

```ts
// src/redis/redis-keys.ts (additions)
export const WsKeys = {
  presenceUser: (userId: string) => `shop:presence:user:${userId}`,
  presenceOnline: 'shop:presence:online',
} as const;

export const WsRooms = {
  user: (userId: string) => `user:${userId}`,
  tenant: (tenantId: string) => `tenant:${tenantId}`,
  chat: (roomId: string) => `chat:${roomId}`,
} as const;
```

Socket.IO rooms are **not** Redis keys. The adapter keeps room membership in each instance's memory and uses Pub/Sub to broadcast room operations. Only presence data is stored explicitly in Redis keys.

### TTL strategy

| Data | Lifetime |
|---|---|
| Presence entry per socket | Score = `now + 90 s`, refreshed by heartbeat every 30 s |
| Presence key | `EXPIRE` 120 s on every refresh, so abandoned users vanish entirely |
| Pub/Sub messages | None; they are fire-and-forget |

### Data flow

```
CONNECT
  client --(JWT)--> Nginx --> instance A
  A: verify JWT, socket.join(user:42, tenant:7)
  A: ZADD presence:user:42 (now+90s) socketId ; ZADD presence:online now 42

HEARTBEAT (every 30 s from the server per socket, or on client ping)
  A: ZADD presence:user:42 (now+90s) socketId ; EXPIRE key 120

EVENT FROM ANOTHER INSTANCE
  B: io.to('user:42').emit('order:updated', payload)
  B --PUBLISH--> Redis --> A (subscribed) --> A delivers to local sockets in room

EVENT FROM A WORKER
  worker: new Emitter(redis).to('user:42').emit('email:sent', {...})   -> same path

DISCONNECT
  A: ZREM presence:user:42 socketId
  if no live members remain -> user is offline (ZREM presence:online 42)
```

### Code implementation

```ts
// src/ws/redis-io.adapter.ts
import { INestApplication, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { IoAdapter } from '@nestjs/platform-socket.io';
import { createAdapter } from '@socket.io/redis-adapter';
import { Redis } from 'ioredis';
import type { ServerOptions } from 'socket.io';

export class RedisIoAdapter extends IoAdapter {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(RedisIoAdapter.name);
  private adapterConstructor!: ReturnType<typeof createAdapter>;
  private pub!: Redis;
  private sub!: Redis;

  constructor(app: INestApplication, private readonly redisUrl: string) {
    super(app);
  }

  async connectToRedis(): Promise<void> {
    // Pub and sub need separate connections: a subscribed connection can run no other commands.
    this.pub = new Redis(this.redisUrl, { connectionName: 'ws-pub' });
    this.sub = this.pub.duplicate({ connectionName: 'ws-sub' });
    this.pub.on('error', (e) => this.logger.error(`pub: ${e.message}`));
    this.sub.on('error', (e) => this.logger.error(`sub: ${e.message}`));
    this.adapterConstructor = createAdapter(this.pub, this.sub);
  }

  createIOServer(port: number, options?: ServerOptions) {
    const server = super.createIOServer(port, {
      ...options,
      // websocket first; polling stays as fallback and is why sticky sessions are required
      transports: ['websocket', 'polling'],
      cors: { origin: process.env.WS_ORIGINS?.split(',') ?? [], credentials: true },
      pingInterval: 25_000,
      pingTimeout: 20_000,
      maxHttpBufferSize: 1e5, // 100 KB per message: cap abuse
    });
    server.adapter(this.adapterConstructor);
    return server;
  }

  async close(): Promise<void> {
    await Promise.allSettled([this.pub?.quit(), this.sub?.quit()]);
  }
}
```

```ts
// src/main.ts (excerpt)
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';
import { RedisIoAdapter } from './ws/redis-io.adapter';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
  app.enableShutdownHooks();

  const adapter = new RedisIoAdapter(app, process.env.REDIS_URL!);
  await adapter.connectToRedis();
  app.useWebSocketAdapter(adapter);

  await app.listen(3000);
}
bootstrap();
```

**Sharded adapter.** The classic adapter uses `PUBLISH`, which in Redis Cluster is broadcast to every node and does not scale well. [7.0+] Redis supports sharded Pub/Sub (`SPUBLISH`/`SSUBSCRIBE`), and `@socket.io/redis-adapter` ships `createShardedAdapter(pub, sub)` that uses it, so messages only travel within one shard. It needs Redis 7.0 or newer and mainly pays off when you run Redis Cluster; with a single Redis, the standard `createAdapter` is simpler. Check the adapter's docs for the exact client type it expects (for cluster, an ioredis `Cluster` instance) before switching.

```ts
// src/ws/presence.service.ts
import { Inject, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Redis } from 'ioredis';
import { REDIS_CLIENT } from '../redis/redis.constants';
import { WsKeys } from '../redis/redis-keys';

const PRESENCE_TTL_MS = 90_000;

@Injectable()
export class PresenceService {
  constructor(@Inject(REDIS_CLIENT) private readonly redis: Redis) {}

  async touch(userId: string, socketId: string): Promise<void> {
    const now = Date.now();
    const key = WsKeys.presenceUser(userId);
    await this.redis
      .multi()
      .zadd(key, now + PRESENCE_TTL_MS, socketId)
      .zremrangebyscore(key, '-inf', now)            // drop stale sockets (crashed instances)
      .expire(key, 120)
      .zadd(WsKeys.presenceOnline, now, userId)
      .exec();
  }

  /** Returns true if this was the user's last live socket (user is now offline). */
  async remove(userId: string, socketId: string): Promise<boolean> {
    const key = WsKeys.presenceUser(userId);
    await this.redis.zrem(key, socketId);
    const live = await this.redis.zcount(key, Date.now(), '+inf');
    if (live === 0) {
      await this.redis.zrem(WsKeys.presenceOnline, userId);
      return true;
    }
    return false;
  }

  async isOnline(userId: string): Promise<boolean> {
    return (await this.redis.zcount(WsKeys.presenceUser(userId), Date.now(), '+inf')) > 0;
  }

  /** Batch lookup: one pipeline for many users (e.g., a contact list). */
  async onlineMap(userIds: string[]): Promise<Record<string, boolean>> {
    const now = Date.now();
    const p = this.redis.pipeline();
    userIds.forEach((u) => p.zcount(WsKeys.presenceUser(u), now, '+inf'));
    const res = await p.exec();
    return Object.fromEntries(userIds.map((u, i) => [u, Number(res?.[i]?.[1] ?? 0) > 0]));
  }
}
```

```ts
// src/ws/app.gateway.ts
import { Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import {
  ConnectedSocket, MessageBody, OnGatewayConnection, OnGatewayDisconnect,
  SubscribeMessage, WebSocketGateway, WebSocketServer,
} from '@nestjs/websockets';
import { JwtService } from '@nestjs/jwt';
import { Server, Socket } from 'socket.io';
import { PresenceService } from './presence.service';
import { WsRooms } from '../redis/redis-keys';

interface AuthedSocket extends Socket {
  data: { userId: string; tenantId: string; hb?: NodeJS.Timeout };
}

@WebSocketGateway({ namespace: '/app' })
export class AppGateway implements OnGatewayConnection, OnGatewayDisconnect {
  @WebSocketServer() server!: Server;
  private readonly logger = new Logger(AppGateway.name);

  constructor(private readonly jwt: JwtService, private readonly presence: PresenceService) {}

  async handleConnection(client: AuthedSocket): Promise<void> {
    try {
      const token = client.handshake.auth?.token as string | undefined;
      if (!token) throw new Error('no token');
      const claims = await this.jwt.verifyAsync<{ sub: string; tenantId: string }>(token);
      client.data.userId = claims.sub;
      client.data.tenantId = claims.tenantId;
    } catch {
      client.disconnect(true); // reject unauthenticated sockets immediately
      return;
    }
    await client.join([WsRooms.user(client.data.userId), WsRooms.tenant(client.data.tenantId)]);
    await this.presence.touch(client.data.userId, client.id);
    client.data.hb = setInterval(
      () => void this.presence.touch(client.data.userId, client.id).catch(() => undefined),
      30_000,
    );
    this.server.to(WsRooms.tenant(client.data.tenantId))
      .emit('presence', { userId: client.data.userId, online: true });
  }

  async handleDisconnect(client: AuthedSocket): Promise<void> {
    if (client.data.hb) clearInterval(client.data.hb);
    if (!client.data.userId) return;
    const offline = await this.presence.remove(client.data.userId, client.id).catch(() => false);
    if (offline) {
      this.server.to(WsRooms.tenant(client.data.tenantId))
        .emit('presence', { userId: client.data.userId, online: false });
    }
  }

  @SubscribeMessage('chat:join')
  async join(@ConnectedSocket() client: AuthedSocket, @MessageBody() roomId: string) {
    // Authorize before joining: never let the client pick arbitrary rooms.
    if (!/^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}$/.test(roomId)) return { ok: false };
    // TODO: check membership in your DB here
    await client.join(WsRooms.chat(roomId));
    return { ok: true };
  }

  @SubscribeMessage('chat:send')
  send(@ConnectedSocket() client: AuthedSocket, @MessageBody() msg: { roomId: string; text: string }) {
    if (!client.rooms.has(WsRooms.chat(msg.roomId))) return { ok: false };
    // Reaches sockets on ALL instances because of the Redis adapter.
    this.server.to(WsRooms.chat(msg.roomId)).emit('chat:message', {
      from: client.data.userId, text: msg.text.slice(0, 2000), at: Date.now(),
    });
    return { ok: true };
  }

  /** Called by other Nest services, any instance. */
  notifyUser(userId: string, event: string, payload: unknown): void {
    this.server.to(WsRooms.user(userId)).emit(event, payload);
  }
}
```

Pushing from a process that has no Socket.IO server (for example a BullMQ worker) with `@socket.io/redis-emitter`:

```ts
// src/ws/ws-emitter.service.ts
import { Inject, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Emitter } from '@socket.io/redis-emitter';
import { Redis } from 'ioredis';
import { REDIS_CLIENT } from '../redis/redis.constants';
import { WsRooms } from '../redis/redis-keys';

@Injectable()
export class WsEmitterService {
  private readonly emitter: Emitter;
  constructor(@Inject(REDIS_CLIENT) redis: Redis) {
    this.emitter = new Emitter(redis);
  }
  toUser(userId: string, event: string, payload: unknown): void {
    this.emitter.of('/app').to(WsRooms.user(userId)).emit(event, payload);
  }
}
```

Nginx configuration:

```nginx
upstream socketio_backend {
    ip_hash;                       # sticky sessions for HTTP long-polling
    server 10.0.0.11:3000;
    server 10.0.0.12:3000;
}

server {
    listen 443 ssl http2;
    server_name app.example.com;

    location /socket.io/ {
        proxy_pass http://socketio_backend;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
        proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_read_timeout 120s;   # must exceed pingInterval + pingTimeout
        proxy_send_timeout 120s;
        proxy_buffering off;
    }
}
```

Why sticky sessions: with the HTTP long-polling transport, one logical Socket.IO session is made of several HTTP requests that must hit the same server. If clients are configured with `transports: ['websocket']` only, there is no polling and sticky sessions are not required. `ip_hash` is the simplest sticky mechanism but groups users behind one NAT onto one instance; a cookie-based approach (NGINX Plus `sticky`, or HAProxy cookies) distributes better.

### Failure handling

| Failure | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Redis down | Adapter stops relaying across instances. Local delivery (clients on the same instance) still works; cross-instance messages are lost while it is down. Clients stay connected. |
| Redis reconnects | The adapter resubscribes. Messages published while disconnected are gone: Pub/Sub has no persistence. Clients that need guaranteed delivery should fetch missed items by REST after reconnect (using a last-seen id), or use the Redis Streams adapter (`@socket.io/redis-streams-adapter`) with Socket.IO's connection state recovery. |
| Instance crash | Clients reconnect (through Nginx, to another instance). Its presence entries expire in at most 90 s because of the score-based expiry; reconnected sockets re-register immediately. |
| Rolling deploy | On `SIGTERM`, close the server so clients reconnect elsewhere; stagger restarts to avoid a thundering herd of reconnections. |
| Presence write fails | Treated as non-fatal (`catch`), presence may be briefly stale. |

### Security considerations

- Authenticate during the handshake (JWT in `auth`, not in a URL query string where it lands in Nginx logs).
- Authorize every room join on the server; never trust a room name from the client.
- Validate payloads and cap sizes (`maxHttpBufferSize`, text truncation). Rate limit messages per socket.
- Lock down CORS origins. Terminate TLS at Nginx (`wss://`).
- Never expose the Redis channels to untrusted code; anyone who can `PUBLISH` to the adapter channel could inject events. Use Redis ACLs and a private network.
- Revalidate tokens periodically for long-lived sockets or disconnect when a user is deactivated (emit a `force-disconnect` to `user:{id}`, then `server.in(room).disconnectSockets()`, which also works across instances with the adapter).

### Performance considerations

- Each broadcast is one `PUBLISH` regardless of recipients, and each instance fans out to its local sockets. Cost scales with instances, not clients.
- Prefer targeted rooms over `server.emit()` to everyone.
- Presence updates every 30 s per socket are cheap but not free: 100k sockets means about 3.3k small transactions per second. Increase the interval or only touch on activity if needed.
- Pub/Sub messages are not stored, so there is no memory growth; slow subscribers may be disconnected by `client-output-buffer-limit pubsub`. Keep payloads small.
- Increase file descriptor limits (`ulimit -n`, systemd `LimitNOFILE`) and tune `net.core.somaxconn` on the Ubuntu hosts.

### Testing strategy

| Test | How |
|---|---|
| Cross-instance delivery | Start two Nest apps on ports 3001/3002 with the same Redis; connect client 1 to A, client 2 to B, send a chat message from client 1, assert client 2 receives it |
| Room auth | Client attempts `chat:join` for a room it does not belong to; assert rejected |
| Presence multi-device | Connect 2 sockets for one user, disconnect one: still online; disconnect second: offline |
| Crash expiry | Add a presence entry with an expired score, assert `isOnline` is false |
| Emitter | Use `WsEmitterService` from a separate process, assert delivery |
| Load | Artillery or k6 with the Socket.IO engine against Nginx with 2 backends, verify no sticky errors (`"Session ID unknown"`) |

### Production deployment notes

- Use PM2 in fork mode with several processes on different ports (or containers), not the Node `cluster` module with one port, unless you add sticky routing between workers.
- Health check endpoint should include Redis pub/sub connection state.
- Dashboards: connected sockets per instance (`io.engine.clientsCount`), Redis `PUBSUB NUMSUB`, publish rate, reconnect rate.
- Plan capacity: roughly 20 to 50 KB memory per idle connection in Node, depending on libraries.

## 14.14 Multi-tenant application caching

In a SaaS product many tenants (companies) share one application and one Redis. Three things go wrong if you are careless: a tenant sees another tenant's data (**leakage**), one tenant's load evicts everyone else's cache or fills memory (**noisy neighbour**), and you cannot invalidate "everything for tenant X" cheaply. This project builds a tenant-aware cache layer that makes the safe path the only path.

### Requirements

| Type | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Functional | Cache get/set/delete scoped to the current tenant, taken from the authenticated context, never from client-supplied input |
| Functional | Mass invalidation of one tenant's cache in O(1) |
| Functional | Per-tenant limits: max entries, max value size, max TTL |
| Functional | Optional: separate Redis ACL user per tenant for high-isolation tenants |
| Safety | Cross-tenant reads and writes must be impossible by construction and covered by tests |
| Non-functional | Works on a single Redis now; compatible with Redis Cluster later |

### Architecture

```
 Request --JWT--> TenantMiddleware --> AsyncLocalStorage { tenantId }
                                                |
 Feature code:  tenantCache.getOrSet('product:42', loader)      (no raw keys!)
                                                |
                                      +---------v----------+
                                      |  TenantCache       |
                                      |  - key builder     |
                                      |  - version lookup  |
                                      |  - quota Lua       |
                                      +---------+----------+
                                                |
                      +-------------------------v--------------------------+
                      | Redis                                              |
                      |  t:{acme}:ver          -> 7                        |
                      |  t:{acme}:v7:product:42 -> {...json...}  EX 300    |
                      |  t:{acme}:v7:count     -> 118            EX 3600   |
                      |  t:{globex}:ver        -> 2                        |
                      |  t:{globex}:v2:...                                 |
                      +----------------------------------------------------+
```

### Redis data structures

| Key | Type | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `t:{tenantId}:ver` | STRING (integer) | Current cache version for the tenant; `INCR` invalidates everything |
| `t:{tenantId}:v{ver}:{name}` | STRING (JSON) | Cached value |
| `t:{tenantId}:v{ver}:count` | STRING (integer) | Approximate number of entries written in this version window, used for the entry quota |

### Key design

Pattern: `t:{<tenantId>}:v<version>:<logical key>`.

- The braces are a **hash tag** [Cluster]. Redis Cluster hashes only the text inside `{...}` to choose the slot, so all keys of one tenant land in the same slot. That allows multi-key operations and Lua scripts across a tenant's keys (the version key and the entry key in one script). Without a hash tag, those would fail with `CROSSSLOT` in Cluster.
- Trade-off: one tenant equals one slot equals one node. A very large tenant cannot be spread across nodes. For giant tenants, shard the tag: `{acme:3}` with the shard chosen by a hash of the logical key, at the cost of giving up cross-shard multi-key operations.
- The tenant id is validated against a strict pattern (`^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{2,31}$`). This blocks key injection: a tenant id like `acme}:v1:x{evil` could otherwise craft keys inside another tenant's namespace or break the hash tag.

```ts
// src/redis/redis-keys.ts (additions)
const TENANT_RE = /^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{2,31}$/;

export function assertTenantId(id: string): string {
  if (!TENANT_RE.test(id)) throw new Error('Invalid tenant id');
  return id;
}

export const TenantKeys = {
  version: (t: string) => `t:{${assertTenantId(t)}}:ver`,
  entry: (t: string, ver: number | string, name: string) =>
    `t:{${assertTenantId(t)}}:v${ver}:${name}`,
  count: (t: string, ver: number | string) => `t:{${assertTenantId(t)}}:v${ver}:count`,
} as const;
```

### TTL strategy

| Item | TTL |
|---|---|
| Cache entries | Caller-specified, clamped to a per-tenant maximum (for example 1 hour on the free plan, 24 h on enterprise); add 10% jitter to avoid synchronized expiry |
| Count key | Same as the max TTL, set when created; it approximates "entries written in the last max-TTL window" |
| Version key | No TTL. It is tiny, and if it vanished, versions would restart at 1 and could resurrect old entries |
| Old-version entries | Expire naturally. After `INCR ver`, nothing reads them, and their TTL (at most max-TTL) reclaims the memory |

### Data flow

```
get(name):   ver = GET t:{T}:ver (default 0)  -> GET t:{T}:v<ver>:name
set(name):   Lua( ver, entry key, count key ): reject if value too big or quota full,
             else SET EX; if key was new: INCR count (EXPIRE on creation)
invalidate:  INCR t:{T}:ver                 (O(1), old entries become unreachable)
getOrSet:    get -> miss -> loader() -> set  (+ per-key single-flight in process)
```

Fetching the version costs an extra round trip on each read. Reduce it by pipelining `GET ver` and the entry GET only when the version is known, or by caching the version in process memory for 1 to 2 seconds (accepting that invalidation takes up to 2 s to propagate; fine for most caches, not for permission changes, which should read the version fresh).

### Code implementation

```ts
// src/tenancy/tenant-context.ts
import { Injectable, NestMiddleware, UnauthorizedException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AsyncLocalStorage } from 'node:async_hooks';
import type { NextFunction, Request, Response } from 'express';
import { assertTenantId } from '../redis/redis-keys';

interface Ctx { tenantId: string }
const als = new AsyncLocalStorage<Ctx>();

@Injectable()
export class TenantContext {
  current(): string {
    const c = als.getStore();
    if (!c) throw new UnauthorizedException('No tenant context');
    return c.tenantId;
  }
}

/** Tenant comes from the verified auth token (set by your auth guard/middleware), never from query/body/headers. */
@Injectable()
export class TenantMiddleware implements NestMiddleware {
  use(req: Request, _res: Response, next: NextFunction): void {
    const tenantId = (req as any).user?.tenantId as string | undefined;
    if (!tenantId) throw new UnauthorizedException();
    als.run({ tenantId: assertTenantId(tenantId) }, next);
  }
}
```

```ts
// src/tenancy/tenant-cache.service.ts
import { Inject, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Redis } from 'ioredis';
import { REDIS_CLIENT } from '../redis/redis.constants';
import { TenantKeys } from '../redis/redis-keys';
import { TenantContext } from './tenant-context';

export interface TenantLimits {
  maxEntries: number;      // per version window
  maxValueBytes: number;
  maxTtlSec: number;
}
const DEFAULT_LIMITS: TenantLimits = { maxEntries: 10_000, maxValueBytes: 64 * 1024, maxTtlSec: 3600 };

// KEYS[1]=entry KEYS[2]=count   (same hash tag => same slot in Cluster)
// ARGV[1]=value ARGV[2]=ttl ARGV[3]=maxEntries ARGV[4]=countTtl
// Returns 1 stored, 0 quota exceeded
const SET_LUA = `
local existed = redis.call('EXISTS', KEYS[1])
if existed == 0 then
  local n = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[2]) or '0')
  if n >= tonumber(ARGV[3]) then return 0 end
end
redis.call('SET', KEYS[1], ARGV[1], 'EX', tonumber(ARGV[2]))
if existed == 0 then
  local c = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[2])
  if c == 1 then redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[2], tonumber(ARGV[4])) end
end
return 1
`;

@Injectable()
export class TenantCache {
  private readonly inflight = new Map<string, Promise<unknown>>();

  constructor(
    @Inject(REDIS_CLIENT) private readonly redis: Redis,
    private readonly ctx: TenantContext,
  ) {
    this.redis.defineCommand('tenantCacheSet', { numberOfKeys: 2, lua: SET_LUA });
  }

  private async version(tenant: string): Promise<string> {
    return (await this.redis.get(TenantKeys.version(tenant))) ?? '0';
  }

  async get<T>(name: string): Promise<T | null> {
    const t = this.ctx.current();
    const ver = await this.version(t);
    const raw = await this.redis.get(TenantKeys.entry(t, ver, name));
    return raw === null ? null : (JSON.parse(raw) as T);
  }

  async set(
    name: string, value: unknown, ttlSec: number, limits: TenantLimits = DEFAULT_LIMITS,
  ): Promise<boolean> {
    const t = this.ctx.current();
    const json = JSON.stringify(value);
    if (Buffer.byteLength(json) > limits.maxValueBytes) return false;
    const ttl = Math.min(ttlSec, limits.maxTtlSec);
    const jittered = Math.floor(ttl * (0.9 + Math.random() * 0.2));
    const ver = await this.version(t);
    const ok = await (this.redis as any).tenantCacheSet(
      TenantKeys.entry(t, ver, name), TenantKeys.count(t, ver),
      json, jittered, limits.maxEntries, limits.maxTtlSec,
    );
    return ok === 1;
  }

  async del(name: string): Promise<void> {
    const t = this.ctx.current();
    await this.redis.del(TenantKeys.entry(t, await this.version(t), name));
  }

  /** O(1) mass invalidation of the current tenant's cache. */
  async invalidateAll(): Promise<number> {
    return this.redis.incr(TenantKeys.version(this.ctx.current()));
  }

  /** Cache-aside with in-process single-flight to prevent stampedes. */
  async getOrSet<T>(name: string, ttlSec: number, loader: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
    const t = this.ctx.current();
    const hit = await this.get<T>(name).catch(() => null); // Redis down => treat as miss
    if (hit !== null) return hit;

    const flightKey = `${t}\u0000${name}`;
    const existing = this.inflight.get(flightKey);
    if (existing) return existing as Promise<T>;

    const p = (async () => {
      try {
        const value = await loader();
        await this.set(name, value, ttlSec).catch(() => false); // best effort
        return value;
      } finally {
        this.inflight.delete(flightKey);
      }
    })();
    this.inflight.set(flightKey, p);
    return p;
  }
}
```

Wiring the middleware:

```ts
// src/tenancy/tenancy.module.ts
import { MiddlewareConsumer, Module, NestModule } from '@nestjs/common';
import { TenantCache } from './tenant-cache.service';
import { TenantContext, TenantMiddleware } from './tenant-context';

@Module({
  providers: [TenantCache, TenantContext],
  exports: [TenantCache, TenantContext],
})
export class TenancyModule implements NestModule {
  configure(consumer: MiddlewareConsumer): void {
    consumer.apply(TenantMiddleware).forRoutes('*');
  }
}
```

Feature code never touches Redis keys:

```ts
// src/products/products.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { TenantCache } from '../tenancy/tenant-cache.service';
import { ProductsRepo } from './products.repo';

@Injectable()
export class ProductsService {
  constructor(private readonly cache: TenantCache, private readonly repo: ProductsRepo) {}

  find(id: string) {
    return this.cache.getOrSet(`product:${id}`, 300, () => this.repo.findById(id));
  }

  async bulkImport(rows: unknown[]) {
    await this.repo.bulkInsert(rows);
    await this.cache.invalidateAll(); // one INCR, instead of scanning and deleting
  }
}
```

**Per-tenant ACL users (optional, for strong isolation).** In the shared-app model, the application connects with one Redis user and enforces tenancy in code. If you must guarantee isolation even against application bugs (for enterprise tenants, or tenant-supplied code), create a Redis ACL user per tenant restricted to that tenant's key pattern:

```
ACL SETUSER tenant_acme on >S3cr3tFromVault ~t:{acme}:* +get +set +del +expire +incr +evalsha +eval -@dangerous
```

- `~t:{acme}:*` limits the user to matching keys (braces are literal characters in the glob). Commands touching other keys fail with `NOPERM`.
- [7.0+] ACL selectors and `%R~`/`%W~` key permissions allow read-only versus write-only patterns, for example a reporting user with `%R~t:{acme}:*`.
- Keep the user list in an ACL file (`aclfile`) rather than only in `redis.conf`, and manage secrets in a vault.
- Cost: one Redis connection (or pool) per such tenant. Use this only for a small number of high-isolation tenants; for thousands of tenants it does not scale, and the shared model plus the code-level controls above is the practical choice.

**Noisy-neighbour memory control.** Redis has a single `maxmemory` for the instance and ACLs cannot limit memory per user. You control a tenant's footprint through application-level limits:

| Control | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Entry count | Quota counter in the Lua script (above) |
| Value size | `maxValueBytes` check before write |
| TTL ceiling | `maxTtlSec`, so data cannot live forever |
| Eviction fairness | `maxmemory-policy volatile-lru` (or `allkeys-lru`) at the instance level; a heavy tenant can still cause eviction of other tenants' keys under memory pressure, so keep headroom (alert at 70% memory) |
| Audit | Periodically sample with `SCAN MATCH t:{acme}:* COUNT 1000` plus `MEMORY USAGE key` on a sample, export per-tenant bytes to metrics, and alert on outliers. Do not run `KEYS` in production |
| Hard isolation | Move large or premium tenants to a dedicated Redis instance and select it by tenant config in the client factory |

The count quota is approximate: expired entries do not decrement it, and it resets when its own TTL elapses. It limits abuse, not accounting precision.

### Failure handling

| Failure | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Redis down | `getOrSet` swallows errors and calls the loader. The system becomes slower but stays correct. Protect the database with the in-process single-flight and a concurrency limiter. |
| Version key read fails mid-operation | The operation fails safe (treated as a miss, or the write is skipped). Never fall back to a default version for writes after an error, because that could write into a stale namespace. |
| Redis restart with data loss | Version resets to 0 and old entries are gone anyway, so there is no resurrection. If only the version key is lost while entries survive (partial restore), stale data could reappear; mitigate by seeding versions from a persisted value or timestamp (for example `INCR` by a large step or using `Date.now()` as the version after a restore). |
| Invalidation race | A loader started before `invalidateAll` may write using the old version (it read the version before the INCR) and become unreachable immediately, which is harmless. |
| Quota exceeded | `set` returns false; the caller continues without caching. |

### Security considerations

- **Tenant source**: only from the verified token. A header like `X-Tenant-Id` is acceptable only if the token proves the user belongs to that tenant; otherwise it is a direct leakage vector.
- **Key injection**: strict tenant id validation (done) and never concatenating raw user input into the key prefix. Logical key names (`product:${id}`) are after the tenant prefix, so even a crafted `id` stays inside the tenant namespace; still validate `id` formats.
- **No raw Redis access in feature modules**: export only `TenantCache`. Add an ESLint `no-restricted-imports` rule for `REDIS_CLIENT` outside the infrastructure folders.
- **Cache poisoning**: scope also by user or role when the response depends on permissions (`product:42:role:admin`), otherwise a privileged user's view can be served to another user of the same tenant.
- **Serialization**: use `JSON.parse` only. Never deserialize with anything that can execute code.
- **ACL users and secrets**: per-tenant passwords come from a secrets manager, rotated; connections use TLS if Redis is not on a private network.
- **Logging**: do not log cached values; log tenant id and key name only.

### Performance considerations

- Every read costs `GET ver` then `GET entry` (2 RTTs). Use the short in-process version cache for non-sensitive data, or pipeline the version fetch together with other reads of the same request.
- Hash tags concentrate each tenant on one slot: a hot tenant can overload a single node. Monitor per-slot load (`CLUSTER` stats) and shard the tag for outliers.
- Lua script is O(1). The in-process single-flight map prevents thundering herds per process; across processes, combine with short TTL jitter or a lock (14.9) for very expensive loaders.
- JSON serialization cost matters for large values; keep entries small (the 64 KB cap helps) and consider compressing only values beyond a threshold.

### Testing strategy

| Test | How |
|---|---|
| Isolation | Run as tenant A, `set('k', 1)`; switch the context to tenant B, `get('k')` returns `null` |
| Key shape | After operations, `SCAN` all keys and assert every key matches `^t:\{[a-z0-9-]+\}:` and belongs to the expected tenant |
| Injection | `assertTenantId` rejects `a}:x{b`, `../`, empty, uppercase, over-long ids; middleware rejects missing tenant |
| Mass invalidation | Set 100 keys, `invalidateAll()`, all `get`s return `null`; TTL eventually removes the old keys |
| Quota | Set `maxEntries` to 5, insert 10 distinct keys, assert 5 stored and 5 rejected; overwriting an existing key still works at the limit |
| Value and TTL limits | Oversized value rejected; TTL clamped (`TTL` command shows at most the max) |
| ACL | With a `tenant_acme` user, `GET t:{globex}:ver` returns `NOPERM`; own keys succeed |
| Concurrency | 100 parallel `getOrSet` for the same key: loader called once per process |
| Cluster compatibility | Run the Lua script against a Redis Cluster test setup; no `CROSSSLOT` |
| Leak regression | Property-based test generating random tenant pairs and key names, asserting no cross-reads |

### Production deployment notes

- Start with one Redis (primary plus replica) for all tenants. Plan an escape hatch: a tenant-to-instance map in configuration so a noisy tenant can be moved to a dedicated instance without code changes.
- Set `maxmemory` to about 75% of RAM on the Ubuntu host, with `maxmemory-policy` chosen deliberately (`volatile-lru` for pure cache). Never share this instance with BullMQ queues (those need `noeviction`).
- Dashboards: memory used, evicted keys, hit rate overall and sampled per tenant, top tenants by sampled bytes, quota rejections per tenant.
- Runbook: "tenant says data is stale" is answered with `invalidateAll` through an admin endpoint (audited and restricted to support roles); "tenant is abusive" is answered by lowering its limits or moving it to a dedicated instance.
- Document the contract for developers: use `TenantCache` only; no raw keys; any new cached data class needs a TTL and a test.


---

# Module 15: Production Deployment & DevOps

Running Redis in production on an Ubuntu VPS is mostly about five things: install it from a trusted source, never expose it, give it a memory budget, make persistence and backups verifiable, and have a rehearsed upgrade path. This module covers each, with complete configs and scripts. Baseline is Redis 8.x; version tags like [7.0+] appear where relevant.

---

## 15.1 Deployment topology and decision overview

```text
  Internet
     |
  [Nginx :443] ---> [PM2: NestJS x4 :3000] ---+
                                              |  private network / loopback / unix socket
                                              v
                                       [Redis :6379]  (bind 127.0.0.1 or private IP)
                                              |
                              /var/lib/redis (RDB + AOF)  --->  nightly backup --> offsite (S3/B2)
```

| Decision | Single VPS default | When to change |
|---|---|---|
| Install method | APT from packages.redis.io, systemd | Docker if your whole stack is Compose-based |
| Exposure | Loopback only | Private IP + firewall if app runs on another host |
| Persistence | AOF `everysec` + RDB snapshots | Pure cache: disable both |
| HA | None (restart + backups) | Replica + Sentinel, or managed service, when downtime costs money |
| Memory | `maxmemory` ≈ 60–70% of RAM available to Redis | Higher if no persistence forks |

---

## 15.2 Installing on Ubuntu (official APT repository)

The distro `redis-server` package lags. Redis publishes signed packages at `packages.redis.io`.

```bash
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y lsb-release curl gpg

curl -fsSL https://packages.redis.io/gpg | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/redis-archive-keyring.gpg
sudo chmod 644 /usr/share/keyrings/redis-archive-keyring.gpg

echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/redis-archive-keyring.gpg] https://packages.redis.io/deb $(lsb_release -cs) main" \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/redis.list

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y redis
```

Verify:

```text
$ redis-server --version
Redis server v=8.x.x sha=00000000:0 malloc=jemalloc-5.3.0 bits=64 build=...

$ systemctl status redis-server --no-pager
● redis-server.service - Advanced key-value store
     Loaded: loaded (/lib/systemd/system/redis-server.service; enabled; ...)
     Active: active (running) since ...

$ redis-cli ping
PONG
```

Pin the major version to avoid surprise upgrades during `apt upgrade` (see 15.14):

```bash
apt-cache policy redis | head -5
sudo apt-mark hold redis redis-server redis-tools   # unhold during planned upgrade
```

File locations (Debian/Ubuntu packaging):

| Path | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `/etc/redis/redis.conf` | Main config |
| `/var/lib/redis/` | Working dir: `dump.rdb`, `appendonlydir/` |
| `/var/log/redis/redis-server.log` | Log file |
| `/etc/redis/users.acl` | ACL file (you create it, section 15.7) |
| `/lib/systemd/system/redis-server.service` | Unit shipped by the package |

---

## 15.3 systemd unit

The package ships a unit. Never edit it in `/lib/systemd/system`; use a **drop-in override**:

```bash
sudo systemctl edit redis-server
```

```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/redis-server.service.d/override.conf
[Service]
# File descriptors: must exceed maxclients + ~32 internal fds
LimitNOFILE=65535

# Restart on crash, but not forever-in-a-loop
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=3s

# Give Redis time to flush AOF / write final RDB on stop
TimeoutStopSec=120

# Sandboxing (verify Redis still starts after enabling)
NoNewPrivileges=yes
ProtectSystem=full
ProtectHome=yes
PrivateTmp=yes
ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/redis /var/log/redis /etc/redis
```

```bash
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart redis-server
systemctl show redis-server -p LimitNOFILE -p Restart
```

Expected:

```text
LimitNOFILE=65535
Restart=on-failure
```

Redis in `redis.conf` must have `supervised systemd` (the Debian package already sets it) so Redis signals readiness to systemd (`Type=notify`).

If you build from the tarball (no package), a minimal unit looks like this:

```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/redis.service
[Unit]
Description=Redis
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=notify
User=redis
Group=redis
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/redis-server /etc/redis/redis.conf --supervised systemd
ExecStop=/usr/local/bin/redis-cli shutdown
LimitNOFILE=65535
Restart=on-failure
TimeoutStopSec=120

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

Option notes: `Type=notify` waits for Redis to report ready (after loading the dataset), which orders dependent units correctly. `ExecStop` uses `SHUTDOWN` so Redis saves before exit (with `save` points configured).

---

## 15.4 Docker Compose production setup

```yaml
# docker-compose.prod.yml
services:
  redis:
    image: redis:8.2                       # pin an exact tag; avoid :latest
    container_name: redis
    command: ["redis-server", "/usr/local/etc/redis/redis.conf"]
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      # redis-cli reads REDISCLI_AUTH, so healthcheck needs no password in argv
      REDISCLI_AUTH: ${REDIS_HEALTH_PASSWORD}
      REDISCLI_USER: healthcheck           # see ACL in 15.7 (read-only: ping)
    volumes:
      - redis-data:/data                   # named volume = persistent
      - ./redis/redis.conf:/usr/local/etc/redis/redis.conf:ro
      - ./redis/users.acl:/usr/local/etc/redis/users.acl      # writable if you use ACL SAVE
    networks:
      - backend                            # internal network, no published ports
    # ports: ["127.0.0.1:6379:6379"]       # only if a host process (PM2) needs it
    ulimits:
      nofile: { soft: 65535, hard: 65535 }
    sysctls:
      net.core.somaxconn: 1024             # raise accept backlog inside the container
    mem_limit: 1536m                       # > maxmemory to leave room for fork/COW and buffers
    stop_grace_period: 60s                 # allow save-on-shutdown
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "redis-cli --no-auth-warning ping | grep -q PONG"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 30s                    # allow time to load dataset
    logging:
      driver: json-file
      options: { max-size: "10m", max-file: "5" }

networks:
  backend:
    internal: true                         # no outbound/inbound from outside Docker

volumes:
  redis-data:
```

Important points:

- **Persistent volume**: without `/data` mounted, `docker compose down -v` or container recreation deletes your data. Named volumes live in `/var/lib/docker/volumes/<project>_redis-data/_data`.
- **Docker bypasses UFW**: published ports are added via iptables before UFW rules. Never publish `6379` on `0.0.0.0`. Either use an internal network or bind to `127.0.0.1`.
- `mem_limit` must be above `maxmemory`. With RDB/AOF rewrite, `fork()` plus copy-on-write can transiently need up to ~2x for write-heavy datasets. If the cgroup limit is hit, the kernel OOM-kills Redis and you lose data since the last persist.
- If the app also runs in Compose, attach it to the `backend` network and use `redis://redis:6379`.
- Overcommit and THP are **host** kernel settings; containers cannot set them (15.9).

Terminal:

```text
$ docker compose -f docker-compose.prod.yml up -d
$ docker compose -f docker-compose.prod.yml ps
NAME    IMAGE       STATUS                    PORTS
redis   redis:8.2   Up 40 seconds (healthy)   6379/tcp
$ docker exec -it redis redis-cli ACL WHOAMI
"default"
```

---

## 15.5 Full annotated production `redis.conf`

This targets a single-node VPS with 2 GB RAM used for cache plus BullMQ. Adjust numbers to your hardware. Redis refuses to start on an unknown directive or bad argument and prints the offending line, so always validate a new file on a scratch port before restarting production (15.5.1).

```conf
################################ NETWORK ################################

# Interfaces to listen on. Loopback only is the safest default.
# For a private VLAN add its IP: bind 127.0.0.1 10.0.0.5
# The "-" prefix (e.g. -::1) means "do not fail if this address is unavailable".
bind 127.0.0.1 -::1

# Refuses connections from non-loopback clients when no password/ACL is configured.
# Keep "yes". It is a safety net, not a replacement for auth.
protected-mode yes

# Listening port. 0 disables TCP (use only unixsocket). Changing the port is NOT security.
port 6379

# Optional unix socket for same-host clients: lower latency, filesystem permissions as auth.
# unixsocket /run/redis/redis-server.sock
# unixsocketperm 770

# Length of the pending-connection queue for listen(). The kernel caps it at
# net.core.somaxconn, so raise both (15.9). Warnings appear in the log if mismatched.
tcp-backlog 511

# Close a client connection after N seconds idle. 0 = never. Use a value (e.g. 300) when
# clients leak connections; do NOT use for BullMQ/pub-sub long-lived connections unless
# those clients reconnect cleanly. Keep 0 and rely on tcp-keepalive for dead peers.
timeout 0

# Send TCP ACKs every N seconds to detect dead peers and keep NAT/LB flows alive.
tcp-keepalive 300

# Maximum simultaneous clients. Redis also needs ~32 fds for itself; if the OS
# file-descriptor limit is lower, Redis lowers this value at startup (check log).
maxclients 10000

################################ GENERAL ################################

# Let systemd supervise (readiness notification). Use "no" under Docker.
supervised systemd

# Do not daemonize under systemd or Docker.
daemonize no

pidfile /run/redis/redis-server.pid

# verbose is noisy. notice is the recommended production level.
loglevel notice

# Log file. Empty string logs to stdout (preferred in Docker).
logfile /var/log/redis/redis-server.log

# Number of logical databases. BullMQ and most apps use db 0 only. Cluster supports only db 0.
databases 16

# Server cron frequency (Hz). Higher = more precise expiry/timeouts, more CPU. dynamic-hz adapts.
hz 10
dynamic-hz yes

################################ MEMORY #################################

# Hard memory budget for dataset (not counting some overhead like replica buffers).
# Rule: 60-70% of the RAM available to Redis, leaving room for fork/COW, client buffers, OS.
maxmemory 1200mb

# What to do at the limit:
#   noeviction     -> reject writes (OOM error). REQUIRED for BullMQ / queues / primary data.
#   allkeys-lru    -> evict any key, least recently used. Pure cache.
#   allkeys-lfu    -> evict least frequently used. Cache with hot-key skew.
#   volatile-lru/lfu/ttl -> only keys with TTL are candidates; if none, behaves like noeviction.
# If one instance holds both cache and queues, choose noeviction and ensure every cache key has a TTL.
maxmemory-policy noeviction

# Sampling precision for approximated LRU/LFU. 5 is default; 10 is closer to true LRU, more CPU.
maxmemory-samples 5

################################ LAZY FREEING ###########################

# Free memory in a background thread for big keys instead of blocking the main thread.
lazyfree-lazy-eviction yes
lazyfree-lazy-expire yes
lazyfree-lazy-server-del yes
lazyfree-lazy-user-del yes
replica-lazy-flush yes

################################ THREADS ################################

# I/O threads for socket reads/writes/parsing. Command execution stays single-threaded.
# Leave at 1 (disabled) unless profiling shows the main thread saturated by network I/O.
# Rule of thumb: cores - 1, max 8; changed behaviour/performance in 8.0 so benchmark first.
# Requires restart. Do not set above the number of cores.
# io-threads 4

################################ PERSISTENCE ############################

# --- RDB snapshots ---
# save <seconds> <changes>: snapshot if at least <changes> writes in <seconds>.
# Fewer rules = less fork overhead. Use "save ''" to disable RDB entirely (pure cache).
save 3600 1
save 300 100
save 60 10000

# If a background save fails, stop accepting writes so you notice. Keep yes.
stop-writes-on-bgsave-error yes
rdbcompression yes
rdbchecksum yes
dbfilename dump.rdb

# Working directory for dump.rdb and AOF files. Must be writable by the redis user.
dir /var/lib/redis

# --- AOF ---
appendonly yes
appenddirname "appendonlydir"          # [7.0+] multi-part AOF directory under dir
appendfilename "appendonly.aof"

# fsync policy:
#   always   -> fsync every write. Safest, slowest.
#   everysec -> fsync once a second. Lose at most ~1-2 s on crash. Recommended default.
#   no       -> OS decides (~30 s). Fastest, least safe.
appendfsync everysec

# Do not fsync during a rewrite/save if it would block (trades durability for latency spikes).
no-appendfsync-on-rewrite no

# Rewrite (compact) AOF when it has doubled AND is at least 64 MB.
auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 100
auto-aof-rewrite-min-size 64mb

# New AOF rewrites begin with an RDB preamble: faster loads, smaller files.
aof-use-rdb-preamble yes

# Load a truncated AOF (unclean shutdown) and log a warning rather than refusing to start.
aof-load-truncated yes

################################ REPLICATION ############################
# Uncomment on a replica:
# replicaof 10.0.0.5 6379
# masteruser replicator
# masterauth <password>
replica-read-only yes
# Backlog lets replicas do partial resync after short disconnects. Size to cover a
# few minutes of write traffic.
repl-backlog-size 64mb

################################ SECURITY ###############################

# ACL users live in a separate file (15.7). Do NOT also use requirepass.
aclfile /etc/redis/users.acl

# Dangerous commands: prefer ACL (-@dangerous) over rename-command, which is deprecated style.

################################ TLS (optional) #########################
# Needed only if Redis crosses a network you do not control. On loopback it adds CPU cost, no benefit.
# tls-port 6380
# port 0                                  # disable plaintext when TLS is the only listener
# tls-cert-file /etc/redis/tls/redis.crt
# tls-key-file /etc/redis/tls/redis.key
# tls-ca-cert-file /etc/redis/tls/ca.crt
# tls-auth-clients yes                    # require client certs (mTLS); "optional" or "no" otherwise
# tls-protocols "TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3"
# tls-replication yes                     # encrypt replication links
# tls-cluster yes                         # only if using Cluster bus

################################ OBSERVABILITY ##########################

# Log commands slower than N microseconds (execution time only; excludes network/queue wait).
slowlog-log-slower-than 10000          # 10 ms
slowlog-max-len 256

# Record latency spikes >= N ms for LATENCY LATEST/HISTORY/DOCTOR. 0 disables.
latency-monitor-threshold 100

# Per-command latency histograms (INFO latencystats) [7.0+]
latency-tracking yes

# Keyspace notifications cost CPU; leave empty unless you need expired/evicted events.
notify-keyspace-events ""

################################ LIMITS #################################
# Client output buffer limits: <class> <hard> <soft> <soft-seconds>
# Prevent slow pub/sub subscribers or replicas from exhausting memory.
client-output-buffer-limit normal 0 0 0
client-output-buffer-limit replica 256mb 64mb 60
client-output-buffer-limit pubsub 32mb 8mb 60

# Max size of a single client query buffer (protects against runaway clients).
client-query-buffer-limit 1gb
proto-max-bulk-len 512mb
```

### 15.5.1 Validate before restarting

```bash
# Syntax / unknown directive check: Redis exits with a line number if invalid
mkdir -p /tmp/redis-conftest && chown redis:redis /tmp/redis-conftest
sudo -u redis redis-server /etc/redis/redis.conf \
  --port 6399 --pidfile /tmp/redis-conftest/r.pid --logfile "" \
  --dir /tmp/redis-conftest --appendonly no --save "" &
sleep 1
redis-cli -p 6399 --user healthcheck --pass '<health-pass>' ping   # ACLs are active, so authenticate
redis-cli -p 6399 --user admin --pass '<admin-pass>' shutdown nosave
```

Expected: `PONG`. On a typo you see `*** FATAL CONFIG FILE ERROR *** ... Bad directive or wrong number of arguments`.

Runtime inspection and edits:

```text
127.0.0.1:6379> CONFIG GET maxmemory*
1) "maxmemory"
2) "1258291200"
3) "maxmemory-policy"
4) "noeviction"
...
127.0.0.1:6379> CONFIG SET maxmemory 1500mb
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> CONFIG REWRITE      # persist runtime changes back to redis.conf
OK
```

`CONFIG REWRITE` rewrites the file in place, removing comments you wrote in some sections. Keep your annotated master copy in Git and treat the live file as generated.

### 15.5.2 Environment variables

Redis server does not read env vars for configuration. Options: (a) generate `redis.conf` from a template in your deployment (`envsubst`), (b) pass flags in `command:` in Compose (`--maxmemory ${REDIS_MAXMEMORY}`), (c) mount a secrets file. **Clients** use env vars: `REDIS_URL` for apps, `REDISCLI_AUTH` for `redis-cli` (keeps passwords out of `ps` output and shell history).

```bash
# Template -> real config at deploy time
export REDIS_MAXMEMORY=1200mb
envsubst < redis.conf.tmpl | sudo tee /etc/redis/redis.conf >/dev/null
```

## 15.6 Binding and port security

Threat model: an unauthenticated Redis reachable from the internet is compromised within minutes (attackers use `CONFIG SET dir` + `SAVE` to write SSH keys or cron jobs, or just `FLUSHALL` for ransom). Defence in depth:

| Layer | Control |
|---|---|
| Bind | `bind 127.0.0.1` (or the private NIC only) |
| Auth | ACL users, no `default` access, strong passwords |
| Firewall | `ufw default deny incoming`; allow only 22/80/443 |
| Docker | Internal network, or publish to `127.0.0.1` only |
| Command surface | ACL `-@dangerous` for app users |
| Transport | TLS if traffic leaves the host |
| Process | Non-root `redis` user, systemd sandboxing |

Verify from **another machine**:

```text
$ nmap -p 6379 your.vps.ip
PORT     STATE    SERVICE
6379/tcp filtered redis       # good: not reachable
```

And locally on the VPS:

```text
$ ss -ltnp | grep 6379
LISTEN 0 511 127.0.0.1:6379 0.0.0.0:* users:(("redis-server",pid=812,fd=6))
```

If you see `0.0.0.0:6379` or `*:6379`, fix it immediately.

---

## 15.7 Authentication and ACL

Use ACLs (Redis 6+) instead of a single `requirepass`: per-service users, least privilege, and no shared password.

Generate a password hash (store the hash in the file, never the clear password):

```bash
PASS=$(openssl rand -base64 32)
echo -n "$PASS" | sha256sum | cut -d' ' -f1
```

```conf
# /etc/redis/users.acl   (chmod 640, owner redis:redis)

# Disable the default user entirely
user default off

# Admin: all commands, all keys, all pub/sub channels. For humans and break-glass only.
user admin on #<sha256-of-admin-pass> ~* &* +@all

# App cache user: only shop:* keys, no dangerous/admin commands
user app on #<sha256-of-app-pass> ~shop:* &shop:* +@all -@dangerous -@admin

# BullMQ user: keys under the bull prefix; verify the exact commands with ACL LOG
user queue on #<sha256-of-queue-pass> ~bull:* &* +@all -@dangerous +info +client|setname

# Healthcheck / monitoring: ping and info only
user healthcheck on #<sha256-of-health-pass> ~* -@all +ping +info
# Prometheus redis_exporter (Module 16): read-only introspection. Extend if its logs show NOPERM.
user exporter on #<sha256-of-exporter-pass> ~* &* -@all +client +ping +info +config|get +slowlog|get +slowlog|len +latency|latest +memory|usage +scan +type +pttl +llen +zcard +xlen +hlen +scard +strlen
```

ACL rule syntax:

| Token | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `on` / `off` | Enable/disable user |
| `#<hex>` | SHA-256 password hash |
| `>pass` | Clear password (stored hashed in memory, **appears in file as hash after ACL SAVE**) |
| `~pattern` | Key patterns the user may touch |
| `&pattern` | Pub/Sub channel patterns |
| `+@cat` / `-@cat` | Allow/deny a command category (`ACL CAT` lists them) |
| `+cmd\|sub` | Allow a specific subcommand |

Operate and debug:

```text
127.0.0.1:6379> AUTH admin <password>
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> ACL LIST
127.0.0.1:6379> ACL GETUSER app
127.0.0.1:6379> ACL LOG 5          # recent denied commands: the first place to look for NOPERM
127.0.0.1:6379> ACL LOAD           # reload users.acl without restart
```

With `aclfile` configured, `ACL SAVE` writes the current in-memory users to the file; changing users with `ACL SETUSER` is runtime-only until saved.

The exact command list BullMQ needs depends on the BullMQ version (it uses Lua scripts and a few administrative reads). Start permissive for the queue user, run your workload, review `ACL LOG`, then tighten. Do not guess a minimal list on production first.

Application connection strings:

```bash
REDIS_URL=redis://app:URL_ENCODED_PASSWORD@127.0.0.1:6379/0
REDIS_QUEUE_URL=redis://queue:URL_ENCODED_PASSWORD@127.0.0.1:6379/0
```

URL-encode special characters in passwords (`/`, `@`, `:`, `#`, `+`), or generate alphanumeric passwords to avoid the problem.

---

## 15.8 Memory limits

Three separate limits, which must nest correctly:

```text
 VPS RAM (e.g. 2 GB)
  └─ container/cgroup limit (mem_limit 1536m)     <- hard kill by kernel OOM if exceeded
      └─ maxmemory (1200mb)                       <- Redis soft budget for data
          └─ + replication buffers, client buffers, AOF rewrite buffer, allocator fragmentation
```

Guidelines:

1. `maxmemory` ≈ 50–60% of RAM if you use RDB/AOF (fork + COW), up to ~75% for pure cache.
2. Watch `used_memory_rss` vs `used_memory`. `mem_fragmentation_ratio` consistently > 1.5 means fragmentation; `< 1` means swapping (very bad).
3. Leave RAM for Nginx, Node (PM2 instances at ~150–300 MB each), the OS page cache.
4. Alert at 80% of `maxmemory`, page at 90%.
5. `noeviction` + full memory → writes fail with `OOM command not allowed`; your BullMQ producers throw. That is the desired fail-loud behaviour for queues.

Check:

```text
127.0.0.1:6379> INFO memory
used_memory_human:312.45M
used_memory_rss_human:341.20M
used_memory_peak_human:480.01M
maxmemory_human:1.12G
mem_fragmentation_ratio:1.09
maxmemory_policy:noeviction
```


---

## 15.9 Kernel tuning (vm.overcommit_memory, THP, somaxconn)

Redis warns about these in its startup log. Fix them on the **host** (they cannot be set from a container).

| Setting | Recommended | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `vm.overcommit_memory` | `1` | `BGSAVE` and AOF rewrite `fork()` the process. With the default heuristic (`0`) the kernel can refuse the fork on a box where Redis uses >50% of free RAM, so the background save fails ("Can't save in background: fork: Cannot allocate memory"). `1` always allows it; copy-on-write means actual usage grows only as pages change. |
| Transparent Huge Pages | `never` | THP makes copy-on-write copy 2 MB pages instead of 4 KB, causing latency spikes and memory bloat after fork. |
| `net.core.somaxconn` | `1024` or higher (≥ `tcp-backlog`) | The kernel silently caps `listen()` backlog to this value (older default 128 on some systems, 4096 on newer kernels). |
| `vm.swappiness` | `1`–`10` | Avoid swapping Redis pages; swapping turns microsecond operations into milliseconds. |
| File descriptors | `LimitNOFILE=65535` (systemd) | Must exceed `maxclients`. |

Persistent sysctls:

```bash
sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-redis.conf >/dev/null <<'EOF'
vm.overcommit_memory = 1
net.core.somaxconn = 1024
vm.swappiness = 10
EOF
sudo sysctl --system
sysctl vm.overcommit_memory net.core.somaxconn
```

```text
vm.overcommit_memory = 1
net.core.somaxconn = 1024
```

THP via a small systemd unit so it survives reboots:

```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/disable-thp.service
[Unit]
Description=Disable Transparent Huge Pages for Redis
Before=redis-server.service

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/bin/sh -c 'echo never > /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled'
ExecStart=/bin/sh -c 'echo never > /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/defrag'

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

```bash
sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl enable --now disable-thp
cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled
# always madvise [never]
```

**Failure scenario:** after a VPS reboot the sysctl file is fine but the THP unit was never enabled. Redis works for weeks, then each `BGSAVE` coincides with 300 ms latency spikes. `LATENCY DOCTOR` and the startup log both mention THP. See Module 16 for diagnosis.

## 15.10 Backup automation

What to back up: the RDB snapshot is the portable, compact artifact. AOF is a multi-file directory (`appendonlydir/` with manifest) [7.0+] and copying it while Redis writes risks an inconsistent set, so use RDB for backups even if AOF is your durability mechanism.

`redis-cli --rdb <file>` asks the server for an RDB and streams it to the client over the network. It does not depend on file locks and works with remote hosts.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# /usr/local/bin/redis-backup.sh
set -Eeuo pipefail

BACKUP_DIR=/var/backups/redis
REMOTE="s3:my-bucket/redis-backups"       # rclone remote; or use: aws s3 cp
RETENTION_DAYS=14
HOST=127.0.0.1
PORT=6379
export REDISCLI_AUTH="$(cat /etc/redis/backup.pass)"   # chmod 600, owner root
REDISCLI_USER=admin; export REDISCLI_USER              # needs SYNC/PSYNC permission; use a dedicated "backup" ACL user if preferred

TS=$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)
FILE="$BACKUP_DIR/redis-$TS.rdb"
mkdir -p "$BACKUP_DIR"

# 1. Take snapshot
redis-cli -h "$HOST" -p "$PORT" --no-auth-warning --rdb "$FILE" >/dev/null

# 2. Validate: file exists, non-trivial size, passes integrity check
[ -s "$FILE" ] || { echo "empty backup"; exit 1; }
redis-check-rdb "$FILE" | tail -n 3

# 3. Compress and checksum
gzip -9 "$FILE"
sha256sum "$FILE.gz" > "$FILE.gz.sha256"

# 4. Offsite upload
rclone copy "$FILE.gz" "$REMOTE/" --s3-no-check-bucket
rclone copy "$FILE.gz.sha256" "$REMOTE/"

# 5. Local retention
find "$BACKUP_DIR" -type f -name 'redis-*.rdb.gz*' -mtime +"$RETENTION_DAYS" -delete

# 6. Heartbeat for monitoring (dead-man's switch)
touch /var/lib/redis-backup.last_ok
echo "backup OK: $FILE.gz ($(du -h "$FILE.gz" | cut -f1))"
```

```bash
sudo chmod 750 /usr/local/bin/redis-backup.sh
sudo /usr/local/bin/redis-backup.sh
```

```text
[offset 0] Checking RDB file /var/backups/redis/redis-20260115T020000Z.rdb
[offset 27] AUX FIELD redis-ver = '8.x.x'
...
\o/ RDB looks OK! \o/
backup OK: /var/backups/redis/redis-20260115T020000Z.rdb.gz (12M)
```

Schedule with a **systemd timer** (preferred over cron: logs go to journald, `Persistent=true` catches up missed runs after downtime):

```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/redis-backup.service
[Unit]
Description=Redis RDB backup
After=redis-server.service

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/redis-backup.sh
Nice=10
IOSchedulingClass=idle
```

```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/redis-backup.timer
[Unit]
Description=Nightly Redis backup

[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:00:00
RandomizedDelaySec=300
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target
```

```bash
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now redis-backup.timer
systemctl list-timers redis-backup.timer
journalctl -u redis-backup.service -n 20 --no-pager
```

Cron equivalent: `0 2 * * * /usr/local/bin/redis-backup.sh >> /var/log/redis-backup.log 2>&1`.

Backup policy table:

| Dimension | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Frequency | Match your RPO. Nightly for cache-plus-queue, hourly for primary data |
| Retention | Local 7–14 days; offsite 30 days with bucket lifecycle rules; keep a monthly copy |
| Offsite | Different provider/region than the VPS; enable bucket versioning or object lock against ransomware |
| Encryption | Server-side bucket encryption, or `gpg`/`age` before upload (RDB contains your data in plaintext) |
| Alerting | Alert if `redis-backup.last_ok` is older than 26 h |

Note the RPO reality: RDB backups lose everything since the last snapshot. If that is unacceptable, use replication plus AOF; backups are the last line of defence against operator error, not a substitute for HA.

---

## 15.11 Restore testing procedure

A backup that has never been restored is a hope, not a backup. Test monthly, automated if possible.

### Scratch restore (does not touch production)

```bash
# 1. Fetch and verify
rclone copy s3:my-bucket/redis-backups/redis-20260115T020000Z.rdb.gz /tmp/restore/
cd /tmp/restore && sha256sum -c redis-20260115T020000Z.rdb.gz.sha256
gunzip redis-20260115T020000Z.rdb.gz

# 2. Start a throwaway instance on another port, no AOF, in that directory
redis-server --port 6390 --dir /tmp/restore --dbfilename redis-20260115T020000Z.rdb \
  --appendonly no --daemonize yes --logfile /tmp/restore/redis.log

# 3. Verify
redis-cli -p 6390 DBSIZE
redis-cli -p 6390 INFO keyspace
redis-cli -p 6390 --scan --pattern 'shop:user:*' | head -3
redis-cli -p 6390 INFO persistence | grep -E 'loading|rdb_last_load_keys_loaded'

# 4. Compare with production
redis-cli -p 6379 DBSIZE      # expect roughly equal (production moved on)

# 5. Clean up
redis-cli -p 6390 shutdown nosave && rm -rf /tmp/restore
```

Record **time to restore** (download + load) as your measured RTO. A 5 GB RDB may take minutes to load.

### Real restore (production disaster)

```text
1. systemctl stop redis-server (or docker compose stop redis)
2. Move aside the damaged data: mv /var/lib/redis /var/lib/redis.broken.$(date +%s); mkdir /var/lib/redis
3. Put dump.rdb into /var/lib/redis, chown redis:redis, chmod 640
4. IMPORTANT: if redis.conf has appendonly yes and appendonlydir is empty/missing, Redis starts with an
   EMPTY dataset (it prefers AOF) and ignores dump.rdb.
   Workaround: start with --appendonly no (override), confirm data loaded, then:
     redis-cli CONFIG SET appendonly yes     # triggers a rewrite from memory
     wait until INFO persistence shows aof_rewrite_in_progress:0, then CONFIG REWRITE
5. Verify DBSIZE, run application smoke tests, re-enable traffic
```

Step 4 is the classic restore trap: people copy `dump.rdb` into place, restart, and find an empty database because the (new, empty) AOF won first.

---

## 15.12 Monitoring hooks and log inspection

Minimum viable monitoring on a VPS (full stack in Module 16):

```bash
# Liveness
redis-cli --user healthcheck --pass "$PW" ping

# One-liner snapshot
redis-cli -a "$PW" --no-auth-warning INFO | grep -E \
 '^(used_memory_human|connected_clients|blocked_clients|instantaneous_ops_per_sec|evicted_keys|keyspace_hits|keyspace_misses|rdb_last_bgsave_status|aof_last_write_status|master_link_status):'
```

Logs:

```bash
sudo tail -f /var/log/redis/redis-server.log
sudo journalctl -u redis-server -b --no-pager | tail -50      # packaged systemd output since boot
docker logs redis --since 1h                                  # Compose
```

What to grep for:

| Log line fragment | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Ready to accept connections` | Startup complete |
| `Background saving started` / `terminated with success` | RDB cycle healthy |
| `Can't save in background: fork` | overcommit or memory problem |
| `MISCONF Redis is configured to save RDB snapshots` (error to clients) | last bgsave failed with `stop-writes-on-bgsave-error yes` |
| `WARNING overcommit_memory is set to 0` | Section 15.9 not applied |
| `WARNING you have Transparent Huge Pages (THP) support enabled` | Section 15.9 not applied |
| `Asynchronous AOF fsync is taking too long` | Disk too slow; latency impact |
| `Connection with replica ... lost` / `Partial resynchronization not possible` | Replication trouble |
| `Possible SECURITY ATTACK detected` | HTTP/POST traffic sent to the Redis port: something is probing it |

Rotate the log file with logrotate (the Debian package installs `/etc/logrotate.d/redis-server`). In Docker log to stdout and cap with `max-size`.

---

## 15.13 Restart policies

| Layer | Setting | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| systemd | `Restart=on-failure`, `RestartSec=3s`, `StartLimitBurst`/`StartLimitIntervalSec` | Avoid crash loops hammering a corrupt AOF |
| Docker Compose | `restart: unless-stopped` | Container returns after reboot only if the Docker daemon is enabled: `systemctl enable docker` |
| Docker semantics | `always` restarts even if you manually stopped it after daemon restart; `unless-stopped` respects manual stops | Prefer `unless-stopped` |
| PM2 | `pm2 startup` + `pm2 save` | Otherwise apps do not return after reboot |
| Start order | Compose `depends_on: condition: service_healthy`; systemd `After=redis-server.service` + `Wants=` | App should still retry connections (13.9); ordering is best-effort |

Crash-loop trap: Redis killed by the OOM killer restarts, reloads a large dataset (tens of seconds, `LOADING` errors), is OOM-killed again as clients rush in. Fix the memory budget, not the restart policy.

---

## 15.14 Upgrade procedure (replica-based, near-zero downtime)

Goals: no data loss, rollback possible, writes paused for seconds at most.

```text
 Phase 1: old master (8.0, :6379) <--- new replica (8.2, :6380) syncs
 Phase 2: pause writes briefly, verify offsets equal
 Phase 3: promote new, repoint apps
 Phase 4: old instance kept as rollback target / then decommissioned
```

Steps (single VPS, two instances; or two hosts):

1. **Read release notes** for breaking changes and deprecations (config defaults and command behaviour change across majors). Take a fresh backup (15.10) and verify it.
2. **Install the new version** side by side (second Compose service `redis-new`, or a second host). Use a **different data dir and port**.
3. **Start it as a replica:**
   ```text
   127.0.0.1:6380> REPLICAOF 127.0.0.1 6379
   127.0.0.1:6380> CONFIG SET masterauth <password>     # and masteruser if ACLs are used
   ```
4. **Wait for sync:**
   ```text
   127.0.0.1:6380> INFO replication
   role:slave
   master_link_status:up
   master_sync_in_progress:0
   slave_repl_offset:123456789
   ```
   and on the master compare `master_repl_offset`.
5. **Smoke test the replica read-only** (a few `GET`/`SCAN`, check `DBSIZE` close to master, check module availability).
6. **Cut over:**
   ```text
   # on old master: block writers briefly (up to 10 s); pause is by write commands
   127.0.0.1:6379> CLIENT PAUSE 10000 WRITE
   # confirm offsets match: master_repl_offset == slave_repl_offset
   # on new:
   127.0.0.1:6380> REPLICAOF NO ONE
   127.0.0.1:6380> CONFIG SET appendonly yes          # if it was off for the sync
   # repoint application (env/Compose network alias/DNS), reload apps (pm2 reload)
   ```
   Writes paused by `CLIENT PAUSE` time out automatically after the duration, so a forgotten step does not leave the old master frozen. Make sure applications are repointed **before** the pause expires, or they will write to the old master again and diverge.
7. **Keep the old instance** (read-only, unreferenced) for 24–48 h as rollback. Rolling back after new writes means losing them unless you reverse-replicate, so decide your window consciously.
8. **Decommission**, `apt-mark unhold` as needed, update monitoring.

Compatibility notes:

- A newer replica can replicate from an older master (the normal upgrade direction). The reverse is not guaranteed, so after cutover you cannot simply downgrade by replicating back.
- RDB format version increases with Redis versions: an RDB produced by 8.x may not load in 7.x.
- If you run Sentinel, upgrade replicas first, fail over, then upgrade the former master. Sentinel handles the repointing for clients that support it (ioredis `sentinels` option).
- With a single node and no replica, the honest options are: accept a restart window (stop, upgrade, start, ~seconds plus dataset load time), or build the replica as above.

Rolling upgrade of the packaged install:

```bash
sudo apt-mark unhold redis redis-server redis-tools
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install --only-upgrade redis
sudo apt-mark hold redis redis-server redis-tools
redis-server --version
```

Do not do an in-place upgrade without a verified backup. Package upgrades restart the service, so schedule it like a deploy.

---

## 15.15 PM2 + NestJS ecosystem file talking to Redis

```js
// ecosystem.config.js
module.exports = {
  apps: [
    {
      name: 'api',
      script: 'dist/main.js',
      exec_mode: 'cluster',          // Node cluster module: instances share the HTTP port
      instances: 'max',              // or a fixed number such as 4 (leave a core for Redis/Nginx)
      max_memory_restart: '400M',    // restart worker if it leaks beyond this
      kill_timeout: 15000,           // ms between SIGINT and SIGKILL; > longest request/job
      wait_ready: true,              // wait for process.send('ready') before routing traffic on reload
      listen_timeout: 20000,         // max wait for 'ready' (covers Redis connect at boot)
      env_production: {
        NODE_ENV: 'production',
        PORT: 3000,
        APP_NAME: 'api',
        REDIS_URL: 'redis://app:CHANGEME@127.0.0.1:6379/0',
        REDIS_QUEUE_URL: 'redis://queue:CHANGEME@127.0.0.1:6379/0',
        REDIS_COMMAND_TIMEOUT_MS: '1500',
      },
    },
    {
      name: 'worker',               // BullMQ workers as a separate process type
      script: 'dist/worker.js',
      exec_mode: 'fork',
      instances: 1,
      kill_timeout: 30000,           // let active jobs finish (worker.close())
      env_production: { NODE_ENV: 'production', APP_NAME: 'worker', REDIS_QUEUE_URL: 'redis://queue:CHANGEME@127.0.0.1:6379/0' },
    },
  ],
};
```

Signal readiness to PM2 from Nest after Redis is ready:

```ts
// src/main.ts (excerpt)
const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
app.enableShutdownHooks();          // PM2 sends SIGINT first; Nest listens to it
await app.listen(Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000));
if (process.send) process.send('ready');
```

```bash
pm2 start ecosystem.config.js --env production
pm2 save && pm2 startup             # follow the printed sudo command
pm2 reload api                      # zero-downtime rolling reload (cluster mode)
pm2 logs api --lines 50
```

Do not commit real secrets in `ecosystem.config.js`. Load them from an `.env` file outside Git, from systemd `EnvironmentFile`, or from your secret manager.

Connection math with PM2 cluster: 4 `api` instances x 4 clients each (default, cache, queue, subscriber) + BullMQ's own duplicates = ~20–30 connections. Trivial for `maxclients 10000`, but multiply by your instance count when scaling horizontally.
