## 15.16 Nginx context

Nginx (open source) does **not** speak the Redis protocol and should never proxy raw Redis in production. Where it relates to Redis:

| Topic | Guidance |
|---|---|
| Edge rate limiting | `limit_req_zone` is per Nginx node, in shared memory, and resets on reload. It stops floods cheaply before Node. Use **Redis-based** limits (13.23) for per-user/per-API-key limits shared across nodes. Use both. |
| Sessions / sticky | Store sessions in Redis so Nginx round-robin works without `ip_hash`. |
| Exposing Redis | Never `stream { proxy_pass redis }` to the internet. If remote access is needed, use an SSH tunnel or WireGuard. |
| Caching | `proxy_cache` caches HTTP responses on local disk. Redis caches data objects. They stack; do not replace one with the other blindly. |
| Graceful reload | `nginx -s reload` keeps connections; combined with `pm2 reload` there is no dropped request. |

```nginx
upstream api {
    server 127.0.0.1:3000;
    keepalive 32;
}

limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=perip:10m rate=20r/s;

server {
    listen 443 ssl http2;
    server_name api.example.com;

    location / {
        limit_req zone=perip burst=40 nodelay;
        proxy_pass http://api;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Connection "";
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    }
}
```

For SSH-tunnel debugging: `ssh -L 6380:127.0.0.1:6379 user@vps`, then `redis-cli -p 6380` locally.

---

## 15.17 VPS vs managed Redis

| | Self-hosted on VPS | AWS ElastiCache (Redis OSS/Valkey) | AWS MemoryDB | Redis Cloud (Redis Inc.) | Upstash | Valkey (self-hosted or managed) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Model | You run everything | Managed cache, Multi-AZ, optional replicas | Managed **durable** primary database (Multi-AZ transaction log) | Managed Redis with latest features/modules | Serverless, pay per request, REST + Redis protocol | Linux Foundation fork of Redis 7.2 |
| Ops burden | High: patching, backups, monitoring, failover | Low | Low | Low | Lowest | Same as Redis if self-hosted |
| HA / failover | You build (replica + Sentinel) | Built in | Built in | Built in | Built in | Same options as Redis |
| Durability | RDB/AOF, your discipline | Snapshots, not primary-store grade | Strong (synchronous multi-AZ log) | Persistence options | Persistent storage | Same as Redis |
| Cost shape | Cheapest at steady load | Instance-hours | Higher, instance-hours | Tiered subscription | Per command; **can be expensive for chatty/BullMQ polling workloads** | Free |
| Latency | Loopback: lowest | Same VPC: sub-ms to ms | Same | Depends on region/peering | Higher (network/HTTP) | Same as Redis |
| BullMQ | Great | Works; disable eviction via parameter group (`noeviction`) | Good fit (durable queue) | Works | Poll-heavy costs; check pricing model | Works (Redis-protocol compatible) |
| Version / modules | Redis 8 with bundled JSON/Search/etc. (subject to license) | Redis OSS/Valkey versions chosen by AWS | Redis OSS/Valkey compatible | Latest Redis and modules | Subset of commands | Valkey versions and its own module set |
| Lock-in | None | AWS | AWS | Redis Inc. | Upstash | Open-source governance |
| Best for | Single product, small team comfortable with Linux; cost-sensitive | AWS-native cache | Redis as system of record on AWS | Redis feature set, multi-cloud | Serverless/edge, spiky low traffic | License-sensitive orgs wanting BSD code |

Licensing note: Redis changed licenses in 2024 (source-available RSALv2/SSPL), then added an **AGPLv3** option with Redis 8, which led to the Valkey fork (BSD-3, under the Linux Foundation) from Redis 7.2.4 and to managed vendors offering Valkey. Check legal implications for your use, especially if you distribute Redis or offer it as a service.

Decision heuristics:

- VPS is reasonable when: one region, one product, you can tolerate minutes of downtime during incidents, and someone owns patching and backups.
- Move to managed when: you need automatic failover and compliance evidence, the team lacks an on-call Redis owner, or the data is a system of record (consider MemoryDB-style durability).
- Do not choose Upstash for polling-heavy BullMQ without modelling request cost.
- Application code stays portable if you only rely on the Redis protocol and keep the client config environment-driven (Module 13).

---

## 15.18 Real-world use case

A SaaS on one Ubuntu 24.04 VPS (4 vCPU, 8 GB): Nginx, 4 PM2 API instances, 1 PM2 worker, Postgres on a separate managed instance, Redis on the VPS. Redis: `maxmemory 3gb`, `noeviction`, AOF `everysec`, ACL users (`app`, `queue`, `exporter`, `admin`), bound to loopback, UFW allowing only 22/80/443. Nightly RDB backup to an object store with 30-day retention and a monthly automated restore drill. Upgrade done once a year via replica on port 6380. When traffic grows past one box, the same config moves to a private-network Redis host by changing `bind`, the firewall rule, and `REDIS_URL`.

## 15.19 Performance and memory considerations

- Fork cost: `BGSAVE` duration and COW memory grow with dataset size and write rate. On a VM, fork of a 10 GB process can pause the main thread for tens to hundreds of ms (`latest_fork_usec` in `INFO stats`).
- AOF `always` costs one fsync per write batch and can cut throughput drastically on cheap VPS disks. `everysec` is the sane default.
- Disk: put `dir` on SSD; never on network storage with unpredictable latency.
- `io-threads` helps only when network I/O (not command execution) saturates the main thread; benchmark with `redis-benchmark` before enabling.
- CPU pinning is rarely worth it on a VPS; noisy neighbours matter more (check steal time with `top`/`vmstat`).

## 15.20 Limitations and alternatives

- Single node = single point of failure; restart plus dataset load is your RTO.
- Replica + Sentinel gives automatic failover but adds client complexity and split-brain considerations (`min-replicas-to-write`).
- Redis Cluster is for horizontal scale, not for HA of a small dataset.
- Backups via RDB have an RPO equal to the interval; AOF narrows it but is not a backup.

## 15.21 Common mistakes

1. Publishing `6379` through Docker on `0.0.0.0` and assuming UFW protects it.
2. Disabling `protected-mode` as a "fix" for connection errors.
3. No `maxmemory`, so Redis grows until the OOM killer ends it.
4. `mem_limit` equal to or below `maxmemory`.
5. Using `allkeys-lru` on an instance that holds BullMQ queues (jobs get evicted silently).
6. Persistent volume missing, so recreating the container wipes data.
7. Backups that are never test-restored; or restores that hit the empty-AOF trap.
8. Copying `appendonlydir` or `dump.rdb` live as a "backup" without validating.
9. Forgetting THP/overcommit after reboot because they were set only at runtime.
10. `apt upgrade` silently upgrading Redis across a minor/major version at 3 AM.
11. Password in `ecosystem.config.js` committed to Git.
12. Putting Redis behind liveness probes, or restarting Redis on a loop while it reloads a big dataset.

## 15.22 Interview Q&A

**Q1. What are the minimum steps to secure a self-hosted Redis?**
Bind to loopback or a private interface, keep protected mode on, disable the default user and use ACL users with least privilege, firewall the port (and remember Docker bypasses UFW), use TLS if traffic crosses an untrusted network, run as non-root, and monitor `ACL LOG`.

**Q2. Why `vm.overcommit_memory=1`?**
Background persistence forks the process. Under heuristic overcommit the kernel may refuse the fork if it looks like it needs a full copy of Redis' memory, even though copy-on-write means it rarely will. Setting `1` lets the fork succeed.

**Q3. Why disable THP?**
With THP the kernel copies 2 MB pages on write during a fork, which amplifies latency and memory use. Redis also warns about it at startup.

**Q4. How do you back up Redis and prove it works?**
Scheduled `redis-cli --rdb` snapshot, validated with `redis-check-rdb`, compressed, checksummed, uploaded offsite, with retention and a dead-man's alert. Prove it with a periodic restore into a scratch instance, comparing `DBSIZE` and sample keys and measuring restore time.

**Q5. You copied `dump.rdb` into `/var/lib/redis` and Redis started empty. Why?**
`appendonly yes` is set and the AOF directory is empty, so Redis loaded the (empty) AOF rather than the RDB. Start with AOF off, load the RDB, then enable AOF with `CONFIG SET appendonly yes`.

**Q6. Describe a near-zero-downtime upgrade.**
Install the new version beside the old, make it a replica, wait for sync and equal offsets, `CLIENT PAUSE ... WRITE` the old master, promote the replica with `REPLICAOF NO ONE`, repoint applications, keep the old node as a short-lived rollback.

**Q7. `maxmemory` vs container `mem_limit`?**
`maxmemory` is Redis' own data budget and triggers eviction or errors; the cgroup limit is a hard kill by the kernel. The latter must be higher to cover buffers, fragmentation, and copy-on-write during persistence.

**Q8. When would you choose managed Redis?**
When failover, patching, and compliance evidence are more expensive than the premium, when no one owns Redis operations, or when Redis is a system of record that needs multi-AZ durability.

## 15.23 Senior / Staff discussion

- **RPO/RTO as numbers.** Write down: "lose at most X seconds of Redis data, restore within Y minutes", then check the architecture meets it (AOF `everysec` = ~1 s RPO on crash; restore time = download + load).
- **Separate instances per workload.** Cache (`allkeys-lfu`, TTLs, disposable) and queues (`noeviction`, durable) have opposite policies. Prefer two instances over one compromise config.
- **Blast radius and dependency mapping.** What breaks if Redis is down: login (sessions)? checkout (locks)? Define degradation modes per feature and test them with a game day (stop Redis, watch dashboards).
- **Configuration as code.** Keep `redis.conf`, ACL file (hashes only), systemd overrides, and sysctl in Git with an Ansible/shell bootstrap so a replacement VPS is minutes, not hours.
- **Security posture beyond loopback.** If you add a second app host, evaluate WireGuard or a private VLAN plus TLS plus per-service ACL users instead of "open port with a password".
- **Cost model.** VPS cost is flat; managed cost grows with memory and replicas; serverless grows with requests. Model your workload before migrating.

## 15.24 Practical exercise

**Task.** On a fresh Ubuntu VM: install Redis from the official repository, bind to loopback, create `app` and `admin` ACL users, set `maxmemory 256mb` with `noeviction`, enable AOF, configure THP/overcommit persistently, create a nightly backup timer, then perform a restore drill.

**Solution outline (commands).**

```bash
# 1. Install (15.2), then:
sudo sed -i 's/^# *bind .*/bind 127.0.0.1 -::1/' /etc/redis/redis.conf
sudo tee -a /etc/redis/redis.conf >/dev/null <<'EOF'
maxmemory 256mb
maxmemory-policy noeviction
appendonly yes
appendfsync everysec
aclfile /etc/redis/users.acl
EOF

# 2. ACL file
APP_HASH=$(echo -n 'appPass123' | sha256sum | cut -d' ' -f1)
ADM_HASH=$(echo -n 'adminPass123' | sha256sum | cut -d' ' -f1)
sudo tee /etc/redis/users.acl >/dev/null <<EOF
user default off
user admin on #$ADM_HASH ~* &* +@all
user app on #$APP_HASH ~app:* +@all -@dangerous -@admin
EOF
sudo chown redis:redis /etc/redis/users.acl && sudo chmod 640 /etc/redis/users.acl
sudo systemctl restart redis-server

# 3. Verify
redis-cli ping                                   # (error) NOAUTH Authentication required
redis-cli --user app --pass appPass123 SET app:x 1   # OK
redis-cli --user app --pass appPass123 CONFIG GET maxmemory   # (error) NOPERM
redis-cli --user admin --pass adminPass123 CONFIG GET maxmemory

# 4. Kernel (15.9), backup script + timer (15.10)
# 5. Restore drill (15.11): compare DBSIZE in the scratch instance.
```

Check yourself: `ss -ltnp | grep 6379` shows only `127.0.0.1`; `systemctl list-timers` lists the backup; the scratch restore reports the same key count; `ACL LOG` shows the NOPERM attempt.

## 15.25 Key takeaways

- Install from the official APT repo, hold the version, and upgrade deliberately via a replica.
- Never expose Redis: loopback or private network, ACL users, firewall, and remember Docker bypasses UFW.
- Budget memory in three nested layers: VM, cgroup, `maxmemory`; choose the eviction policy per workload (`noeviction` for queues).
- Kernel settings (overcommit, THP, somaxconn) must be persistent, not runtime-only.
- Back up with RDB, validate, ship offsite, alert on staleness, and drill restores (beware the empty-AOF trap).
- Keep config in Git, log what matters, and decide VPS vs managed with a clear RPO/RTO and cost model.


---

# Module 16: Monitoring & Troubleshooting

Redis rarely fails silently if you know where to look. This module gives you the observability toolbox (INFO, SLOWLOG, LATENCY, CLIENT, MEMORY), the formulas that matter (hit ratio, fragmentation, eviction rate), a Prometheus + Grafana setup, and ten troubleshooting playbooks in the form **symptoms, systematic debugging, root causes, fixes**.

Conventions: examples assume `redis-cli` can authenticate (via `REDISCLI_AUTH` / `--user`). Output values are illustrative.

---

## 16.1 The observability toolbox at a glance

| Tool | Answers | Cost / risk |
|---|---|---|
| `INFO` (sections) | What is the state right now? Counters since boot | Cheap. Safe |
| `INFO commandstats` / `latencystats` | Which commands are used and how slow? | Cheap |
| `SLOWLOG` | Which individual commands were slow (server execution time)? | Cheap |
| `LATENCY` (monitor) | When did the server stall, and why (event class)? | Needs threshold configured |
| `CLIENT LIST/INFO/KILL` | Who is connected, doing what, using what memory? | Moderate on huge client counts |
| `MEMORY STATS/USAGE/DOCTOR` | Where is memory going? | `USAGE` is O(N) sampled per key |
| `SCAN` | Enumerate keys safely | Safe, incremental |
| `KEYS` | Enumerate keys | **Blocks server. Never in production** |
| `MONITOR` | Stream every command | **Heavy. Debug only, briefly** |
| Logs | Persistence, replication, OOM, config warnings | Free |
| Prometheus exporter | History, alerting | Small |

---

## 16.2 INFO sections

`INFO` returns text grouped by section. Request one with `INFO <section>`; `INFO everything` (or `all`) returns all, including `commandstats` and `errorstats`; plain `INFO` returns the defaults only.

| Section | Key fields | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `server` | `redis_version`, `uptime_in_seconds`, `tcp_port`, `config_file`, `hz` | Did it restart? (`uptime_in_seconds` small) |
| `clients` | `connected_clients`, `blocked_clients`, `maxclients`, `client_recent_max_input_buffer`, `client_recent_max_output_buffer` | Connection pressure, leaks |
| `memory` | `used_memory`, `used_memory_rss`, `used_memory_peak`, `maxmemory`, `maxmemory_policy`, `mem_fragmentation_ratio`, `used_memory_dataset`, `mem_clients_normal`, `mem_replication_backlog` | Capacity, fragmentation |
| `persistence` | `loading`, `rdb_last_bgsave_status`, `rdb_last_save_time`, `aof_enabled`, `aof_last_write_status`, `aof_rewrite_in_progress`, `rdb_changes_since_last_save`, `latest_fork_usec` | Durability health |
| `stats` | `total_connections_received`, `rejected_connections`, `instantaneous_ops_per_sec`, `keyspace_hits`, `keyspace_misses`, `expired_keys`, `evicted_keys`, `total_net_input_bytes`, `sync_full`, `sync_partial_ok` | Throughput, hit ratio, eviction |
| `replication` | `role`, `connected_slaves`, `master_link_status`, `master_last_io_seconds_ago`, `master_repl_offset`, `slave_repl_offset`, `repl_backlog_size` | Replica health |
| `cpu` | `used_cpu_sys`, `used_cpu_user` (cumulative seconds) | CPU rate via deltas |
| `commandstats` | `cmdstat_get:calls=...,usec=...,usec_per_call=...,rejected_calls=...,failed_calls=...` | Hot and slow commands |
| `errorstats` | `errorstat_NOPERM:count=...` | Error classes (ACL, OOM, WRONGTYPE) |
| `latencystats` | `latency_percentiles_usec_get:p50=...,p99=...,p99.9=...` [7.0+] | Server-side percentiles per command |
| `keyspace` | `db0:keys=1000,expires=900,avg_ttl=...` | Keys and expiring keys |
| `modules`, `cluster` | Loaded modules; `cluster_enabled` | Context |

Example:

```text
$ redis-cli INFO stats | grep -E 'keyspace|evicted|expired|rejected|ops_per_sec'
instantaneous_ops_per_sec:1850
rejected_connections:0
expired_keys:48211
evicted_keys:0
keyspace_hits:9123456
keyspace_misses:1203344
```

Remember that counters are cumulative since process start (or `CONFIG RESETSTAT`); monitoring systems compute **rates** from them.

---

## 16.3 MONITOR and its production risks

`MONITOR` streams every command processed by the server to your client in real time:

```text
$ redis-cli MONITOR
OK
1736899000.123456 [0 10.0.0.12:51234] "SET" "shop:user:1" "Tareq" "EX" "3600"
1736899000.124001 [0 10.0.0.12:51236] "GET" "shop:product:7"
```

Format: unix timestamp with microseconds, `[db client-addr]`, then the command and arguments (arguments for `AUTH` are redacted).

Risks:

| Risk | Detail |
|---|---|
| Throughput loss | Every command is duplicated to the monitoring client; Redis documentation cites a throughput reduction that can exceed 50% with one monitor client |
| Memory growth | If the monitor client reads slowly, its output buffer grows until limits kill it (or memory pressure builds) |
| Data exposure | Full keys and values pass through; secrets and PII can leak to terminal logs |
| False sense | It shows commands received, not their latency |

Safer usage: run it for seconds (`timeout 10 redis-cli monitor | head -200`), filter on the client side (`| grep -E '"(SET|DEL)"'`), do it on a replica when possible, and prefer SLOWLOG, `INFO commandstats`, or `redis-cli --hotkeys` (requires an LFU policy) for questions that do not need a full firehose. Restrict `MONITOR` via ACL (`-monitor` or the `@dangerous` category) for application users.

---

## 16.4 SLOWLOG

Records commands whose **execution time inside Redis** exceeded a threshold. It excludes network time and time spent waiting in the queue, which is why a slow client can still have latency despite an empty slowlog.

```conf
slowlog-log-slower-than 10000   # microseconds; 0 logs everything, -1 disables
slowlog-max-len 256             # ring buffer entries
```

```text
127.0.0.1:6379> SLOWLOG GET 2
1) 1) (integer) 14              # unique id
   2) (integer) 1736899123      # unix time
   3) (integer) 54321           # duration in microseconds
   4) 1) "KEYS"
      2) "shop:session:*"
   5) "10.0.0.12:51234"         # client address
   6) "api:cache"               # client name (from connectionName)
127.0.0.1:6379> SLOWLOG LEN
(integer) 14
127.0.0.1:6379> SLOWLOG RESET
OK
```

What typically shows up: `KEYS`, `SMEMBERS`/`HGETALL`/`LRANGE 0 -1` on huge collections, `SORT`, `ZUNIONSTORE`, `SUNION`, big `DEL` of a large key (use `UNLINK`), long Lua scripts, `FLUSHALL`. Because logged entries truncate long arguments, they are safe to read, but still contain key names.

The client name (field 6) is why `connectionName` in Module 13 pays off: you immediately see which service issued the culprit.

---

## 16.5 MEMORY commands

```text
127.0.0.1:6379> MEMORY USAGE shop:user:1 SAMPLES 5
(integer) 72                    # bytes for key + value + overhead; SAMPLES for aggregates

127.0.0.1:6379> MEMORY STATS
 1) "peak.allocated"            2) (integer) 502660128
 3) "total.allocated"           4) (integer) 327651840
 5) "startup.allocated"         6) (integer) 1048576
 7) "replication.backlog"       8) (integer) 0
 9) "clients.normal"           10) (integer) 1048576
...
    "keys.count"                 (integer) 1200345
    "keys.bytes-per-key"         (integer) 270
    "dataset.bytes"              (integer) 310121472
    "dataset.percentage"         "94.66"
    "fragmentation"              "1.04"

127.0.0.1:6379> MEMORY DOCTOR
"Hi Sam, I can't find any memory issue in your instance..."

127.0.0.1:6379> MEMORY PURGE      # ask allocator to release dirty pages (jemalloc)
OK
```

Reading the output:

- `dataset.bytes` vs `total.allocated`: the rest is overhead (client buffers, replication backlog, AOF buffers, internal structures).
- High `clients.normal` / `clients.slaves` / `replication.backlog` means non-data memory is the problem.
- `keys.bytes-per-key` high (> a few hundred) suggests fat values or many small keys with high overhead; consider hashes, shorter key names, compression.

Finding big keys:

```bash
redis-cli --bigkeys          # samples keys with SCAN per type, reports the biggest by length/elements
redis-cli --memkeys          # biggest keys by memory (uses MEMORY USAGE)
```

Both iterate with SCAN and are safe, but they generate load; use `-i 0.1` to sleep between batches and run during low traffic or against a replica.

---

## 16.6 CLIENT LIST, CLIENT INFO, CLIENT KILL

```text
127.0.0.1:6379> CLIENT LIST
id=412 addr=10.0.0.12:51234 laddr=10.0.0.5:6379 fd=9 name=api:cache age=3600 idle=0 flags=N db=0 sub=0 psub=0 ssub=0 multi=-1 qbuf=26 qbuf-free=20448 argv-mem=10 multi-mem=0 obl=0 oll=0 omem=0 tot-mem=22298 events=r cmd=get user=app redir=-1 resp=2
```

| Field | Meaning | Red flag |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | `CLIENT SETNAME` (ioredis `connectionName`) | Empty names: unattributable |
| `age` / `idle` | Seconds connected / idle | Thousands of old idle sockets = leak |
| `flags` | `N` normal, `b` blocked, `S` replica, `P` pubsub, `M` master | `b` with BullMQ is normal |
| `qbuf` | Query buffer bytes | Large, growing = huge pipeline or stuck client |
| `obl` / `oll` / `omem` | Output buffer length/list/mem | Large `omem` = slow consumer (pub/sub) |
| `tot-mem` | Total memory used by this client | Rank by it |
| `cmd` | Last command | Helps identify behaviour |
| `multi` | Queued commands in MULTI (`-1` if none) | Large = unfinished transaction |
| `user` | ACL user | |

```bash
# Group connections by IP (leak detection):
redis-cli CLIENT LIST | awk '{print $2}' | cut -d= -f2 | cut -d: -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
# Group by name:
redis-cli CLIENT LIST | grep -o 'name=[^ ]*' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
# Top memory consumers:
redis-cli CLIENT LIST | awk '{for(i=1;i<=NF;i++) if($i ~ /^tot-mem=/){split($i,a,"="); print a[2], $0}}' | sort -rn | head -5
```

```text
127.0.0.1:6379> CLIENT INFO                      # your own connection
127.0.0.1:6379> CLIENT LIST TYPE pubsub
127.0.0.1:6379> CLIENT KILL ID 412
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> CLIENT KILL ADDR 10.0.0.12:51234
127.0.0.1:6379> CLIENT KILL USER app             # kills all connections of a user
127.0.0.1:6379> CLIENT KILL TYPE pubsub MAXAGE 3600   # [7.4+] older than an hour
127.0.0.1:6379> CLIENT NO-EVICT on               # protect your admin connection from client eviction
```

Killing a client only closes its socket. A well-behaved client reconnects, so fix the code or configuration, not just the symptom. `maxmemory-clients` (client eviction) can also cap aggregate client memory.

---

## 16.7 LATENCY commands

Enable the monitor with a threshold, in ms:

```text
127.0.0.1:6379> CONFIG SET latency-monitor-threshold 100
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> LATENCY LATEST
1) 1) "fork"                 # event name
   2) (integer) 1736899200   # last occurrence
   3) (integer) 312          # latest latency (ms)
   4) (integer) 540          # max latency (ms)
127.0.0.1:6379> LATENCY HISTORY fork
127.0.0.1:6379> LATENCY DOCTOR
127.0.0.1:6379> LATENCY GRAPH fork
127.0.0.1:6379> LATENCY RESET
```

Event names you will see: `command`, `fast-command`, `fork`, `aof-write`, `aof-fsync-always`, `aof-write-pending-fsync`, `rdb-unlink-temp-file`, `expire-cycle`, `eviction-cycle`, `eviction-del`.

| Event | Typical cause |
|---|---|
| `fork` | Big dataset + slow VM fork + THP enabled |
| `aof-write*` / `aof-fsync-always` | Slow disk, `appendfsync always` |
| `expire-cycle` | Many keys expiring at the same instant; spread TTLs with jitter |
| `command` / `fast-command` | Slow O(N) commands |
| `eviction-cycle` | Heavy eviction at maxmemory |

Client-side measurement (distinguishes server vs network):

```bash
redis-cli --latency                 # continuous min/max/avg RTT in ms
redis-cli --latency-history -i 5    # windows of 5 s
redis-cli --intrinsic-latency 10    # run ON the server: baseline scheduling latency of the host (10 s test), independent of Redis
```

If `--intrinsic-latency` shows 10+ ms maxima, the VM is the problem (noisy neighbour, CPU steal), not Redis.

**Latency budget reasoning:** application p99 = network RTT + queueing behind other commands (single-threaded!) + execution time + client library overhead (event loop delay in Node). SLOWLOG only covers execution time. When Redis looks healthy but the app is slow, check Node event-loop lag too.

---

## 16.8 SCAN vs KEYS

| | `KEYS pattern` | `SCAN cursor MATCH pattern COUNT n` |
|---|---|---|
| Complexity | O(N) in a single blocking call | O(1) per call, O(N) total across calls |
| Blocks server | **Yes**, for the whole keyspace | No |
| Consistency | Snapshot at call time | Elements that exist the whole iteration are returned; may return **duplicates**; keys added/removed during iteration may or may not appear |
| Use | Never in production | Maintenance, migrations, audits |

```text
127.0.0.1:6379> SCAN 0 MATCH shop:session:* COUNT 500
1) "1048"                       # next cursor; "0" means done
2) 1) "shop:session:a1"
   2) "shop:session:b2"
```

Notes: `COUNT` is a hint (work per call), not a guarantee of result count; `MATCH` filters after fetching, so a rare pattern may return empty pages with a non-zero cursor. Keep calling until the cursor returns `0`. De-duplicate in the client. Variants: `SSCAN`, `HSCAN`, `ZSCAN` for big collections; `SCAN ... TYPE string`.

```ts
// Safe deletion by pattern in Node (ioredis): scanStream + UNLINK in batches
import { Redis } from 'ioredis';

export async function deleteByPattern(redis: Redis, pattern: string): Promise<number> {
  let deleted = 0;
  const stream = redis.scanStream({ match: pattern, count: 500 });
  for await (const keys of stream as AsyncIterable<string[]>) {
    if (keys.length === 0) continue;
    deleted += await redis.unlink(...keys);   // non-blocking free; may be cross-slot unsafe on Cluster
  }
  return deleted;
}
```

On Redis Cluster, `SCAN` is per node and multi-key commands require same-slot keys, so iterate each primary and delete one key at a time (or pipeline per slot).

Design rule: if you need "all keys for X", maintain an index (a Set `shop:user:1:sessions`) instead of scanning.

---

## 16.9 Redis logs

Where: `/var/log/redis/redis-server.log`, `journalctl -u redis-server`, or `docker logs`. Level `notice` for production; temporarily `CONFIG SET loglevel verbose` during an investigation.

```text
12345:M 15 Jan 2026 02:00:01.123 * 100 changes in 300 seconds. Saving...
12345:M 15 Jan 2026 02:00:01.130 * Background saving started by pid 2345
2345:C  15 Jan 2026 02:00:03.500 * DB saved on disk
12345:M 15 Jan 2026 02:00:03.600 * Background saving terminated with success
```

Process markers: `M` master, `S` replica, `C` child (fork), `X` sentinel. Log level markers: `.` debug, `-` verbose, `*` notice, `#` warning. Warnings (`#`) are the ones to alert on.

Useful greps:

```bash
sudo grep -E ' # ' /var/log/redis/redis-server.log | tail -20          # warnings
sudo grep -iE 'oom|fork|MISCONF|loading|replica|sync' /var/log/redis/redis-server.log | tail -50
sudo journalctl -u redis-server --since "1 hour ago" -p warning
```

---

## 16.10 Connection monitoring

Metrics: `connected_clients`, `blocked_clients`, `total_connections_received` (rate = connection churn), `rejected_connections` (should be 0; non-zero means `maxclients` hit), `maxclients`.

```bash
watch -n 2 "redis-cli INFO clients | grep -E 'connected|blocked|maxclients'"
```

Healthy signals: `connected_clients` is flat in steady state and roughly equals `instances x clients-per-instance`. Warning signs: a staircase growth (leak), high `total_connections_received` rate (connection-per-request anti-pattern: each reconnect costs a TCP+AUTH+SELECT handshake), `connected_clients` close to `maxclients` or near the OS fd limit.

OS-level cross-check:

```bash
ss -tn state established '( sport = :6379 )' | wc -l
ss -tn state established '( sport = :6379 )' | awk '{print $4}' | cut -d: -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
```

---

## 16.11 Memory monitoring

| Metric | Formula / source | Alert |
|---|---|---|
| Used vs limit | `used_memory / maxmemory` | warn 80%, page 90% |
| Fragmentation ratio | `used_memory_rss / used_memory` | > 1.5 sustained (fragmentation) or < 1.0 (swapping) |
| Peak vs current | `used_memory_peak` | Peak close to limit = headroom risk |
| Non-data memory | `mem_clients_normal`, `mem_replication_backlog`, `mem_aof_buffer` | Growing = buffer problem |
| Keys growth | `db0:keys` trend | Unexpected steady growth = missing TTL |
| Keys without TTL | `keys - expires` in `INFO keyspace` | Rising on a cache instance |

Fragmentation notes: for tiny datasets (a few MB) the ratio is meaningless. Active defragmentation (`activedefrag yes`, jemalloc builds) can reduce fragmentation at CPU cost; test on staging. A restart also compacts memory, but is disruptive.

Linux side:

```bash
free -h
vmstat 1 5          # si/so columns > 0 means swapping
dmesg -T | grep -iE 'killed process|out of memory'
```

---

## 16.12 Hit/miss ratio and eviction metrics

```text
hit_ratio = keyspace_hits / (keyspace_hits + keyspace_misses)
```

Compute over a **window** with rates, not lifetime counters:

```text
PromQL: rate(redis_keyspace_hits_total[5m]) /
        (rate(redis_keyspace_hits_total[5m]) + rate(redis_keyspace_misses_total[5m]))
```

```bash
redis-cli INFO stats | awk -F: '/keyspace_hits/{h=$2} /keyspace_misses/{m=$2} END{printf "hit ratio: %.2f%%\n", 100*h/(h+m)}'
```

Interpretation: a cache with < 80% hit ratio may be too small, TTLs too short, or keys poorly designed; but a 100% ratio can also mean you cache too little variety. Misses from `GET` on nonexistent keys used for existence checks or rate-limiter first hits are expected; counters include them. Note that hits/misses count only key lookups by read commands, not every command.

Eviction and expiry:

| Metric | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `expired_keys` | Keys removed because TTL passed (normal) |
| `evicted_keys` | Keys removed because of `maxmemory` (cache: normal at low rate; queue: **incident**) |
| `evicted_clients` | Clients dropped by `maxmemory-clients` |
| `expired_stale_perc` | Estimated share of logically expired keys not yet deleted (active expire cycle lag) |
| `expire_cycle_cpu_milliseconds` | CPU spent on active expiry |

Rule: sustained `rate(evicted_keys) > 0` with falling hit ratio means the working set does not fit; add memory, shorten TTLs, shrink values, or shard. Any eviction on an instance holding BullMQ data means the policy is wrong.

---

## 16.13 Replication monitoring

Master:

```text
127.0.0.1:6379> INFO replication
role:master
connected_slaves:1
slave0:ip=10.0.0.6,port=6379,state=online,offset=123456789,lag=0
master_repl_offset:123456789
repl_backlog_active:1
repl_backlog_size:67108864
```

Replica:

```text
role:slave
master_host:10.0.0.5
master_link_status:up                 # must be "up"
master_last_io_seconds_ago:0          # growing = link stalled
master_sync_in_progress:0
slave_repl_offset:123456700
slave_read_repl_offset:123456700
```

Compute **replication lag in bytes** = `master_repl_offset - slave_repl_offset`; in seconds use `slave0:...lag=` (seconds since last ack). Watch `sync_full` (full resyncs, expensive, usually after backlog overflow or replica restart) and `sync_partial_ok`/`sync_partial_err` in `INFO stats`. If `sync_full` climbs, increase `repl-backlog-size` and check network.

Safety knobs: `min-replicas-to-write` and `min-replicas-max-lag` stop a master from accepting writes when it has no healthy replicas (reduces data loss on failover at an availability cost).

---

## 16.14 Health checks

Layered health, from cheapest to richest:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# redis-health.sh: exit 0 healthy, 1 unhealthy; prints reason
set -u
R="redis-cli --no-auth-warning -h ${REDIS_HOST:-127.0.0.1} -p ${REDIS_PORT:-6379}"

[ "$($R PING 2>/dev/null)" = "PONG" ] || { echo "FAIL: ping"; exit 1; }
INFO=$($R INFO everything 2>/dev/null)
get() { echo "$INFO" | awk -F: -v k="$1" '$1==k{gsub(/\r/,"",$2); print $2}'; }

[ "$(get loading)" = "0" ]                      || { echo "FAIL: loading dataset"; exit 1; }
[ "$(get rdb_last_bgsave_status)" = "ok" ]      || { echo "FAIL: last bgsave"; exit 1; }
[ "$(get aof_last_write_status)" = "ok" ] || [ -z "$(get aof_last_write_status)" ] || { echo "FAIL: aof write"; exit 1; }
if [ "$(get role)" = "slave" ]; then
  [ "$(get master_link_status)" = "up" ]        || { echo "FAIL: replica link down"; exit 1; }
fi
MAX=$(get maxmemory); USED=$(get used_memory)
if [ "${MAX:-0}" -gt 0 ] && [ $((USED * 100 / MAX)) -gt 90 ]; then echo "FAIL: memory >90%"; exit 1; fi
echo "OK"
```

A `PING` that returns `PONG` while a replica link is down or a persistence write fails tells you little. Use PING for liveness and the composite check for readiness and alerts. In Node use the Terminus indicator from Module 13 (13.13).

## 16.15 Prometheus, redis_exporter, and Grafana

```text
 Redis :6379 <--- redis_exporter :9121 <--- Prometheus :9090 ---> Alertmanager ---> Slack/PagerDuty
                                                  ^
                                               Grafana :3001
```

`docker-compose.monitoring.yml` (joins the same backend network as Redis; no host ports except Grafana behind your reverse proxy):

```yaml
services:
  redis_exporter:
    image: oliver006/redis_exporter:latest      # pin a specific version tag in production
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      REDIS_ADDR: redis://redis:6379
      REDIS_USER: exporter
      REDIS_PASSWORD: ${REDIS_EXPORTER_PASSWORD}
    networks: [backend, monitoring]
    # Optional extra: --check-keys, --check-single-keys for specific queue lengths (see below)

  prometheus:
    image: prom/prometheus:v2.55.1
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - ./prometheus/prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml:ro
      - ./prometheus/alerts.yml:/etc/prometheus/alerts.yml:ro
      - prom-data:/prometheus
    command:
      - --config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml
      - --storage.tsdb.retention.time=15d
    networks: [monitoring]

  grafana:
    image: grafana/grafana:11.3.0
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports: ["127.0.0.1:3001:3000"]
    environment:
      GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD: ${GRAFANA_ADMIN_PASSWORD}
    volumes: [grafana-data:/var/lib/grafana]
    networks: [monitoring]

networks:
  backend: { external: true }      # same network as the redis service
  monitoring: {}
volumes:
  prom-data:
  grafana-data:
```

```yaml
# prometheus/prometheus.yml
global:
  scrape_interval: 15s
  evaluation_interval: 15s
rule_files: [/etc/prometheus/alerts.yml]
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: redis
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['redis_exporter:9121']
        labels: { instance: redis-main }
```

Verify:

```text
$ curl -s localhost:9121/metrics | grep -E '^redis_(up|connected_clients|memory_used_bytes)'
redis_up 1
redis_connected_clients 24
redis_memory_used_bytes 3.2765184e+08
```

(Run it from inside the Compose network or publish the port on loopback temporarily.) Grafana: add Prometheus as a data source (`http://prometheus:9090`) and import a community Redis dashboard (the Redis exporter project ships one; verify the ID/JSON in its README) or build panels from the table below.

### Key metrics (redis_exporter names)

| Metric | Why |
|---|---|
| `redis_up` | Exporter can reach Redis |
| `redis_uptime_in_seconds` | Detect restarts |
| `redis_memory_used_bytes`, `redis_memory_max_bytes` | Capacity |
| `redis_mem_fragmentation_ratio` | Fragmentation/swap |
| `redis_connected_clients`, `redis_blocked_clients`, `redis_rejected_connections_total` | Connection health |
| `redis_commands_processed_total` | Throughput (use `rate`) |
| `redis_commands_duration_seconds_total` / `redis_commands_total` | Average latency per command |
| `redis_keyspace_hits_total`, `redis_keyspace_misses_total` | Hit ratio |
| `redis_evicted_keys_total`, `redis_expired_keys_total` | Eviction/expiry rates |
| `redis_db_keys`, `redis_db_keys_expiring` | Keyspace size |
| `redis_connected_slaves`, `redis_master_link_up`, `redis_master_repl_offset`, `redis_slave_repl_offset` | Replication |
| `redis_rdb_last_bgsave_status`, `redis_aof_last_write_status` (where exposed) | Persistence |
| `redis_slowlog_length` | Slow command trend |
| `redis_cpu_user_seconds_total`, `redis_cpu_sys_seconds_total` | CPU via `rate()` |
| `redis_total_error_replies` / `redis_errors_total` (name varies by exporter version) | Error classes |

Metric names vary slightly between exporter versions; check `/metrics` for exact names before writing rules.

For BullMQ and queue depth monitoring, the exporter can report key lengths (`--check-single-keys` / `REDIS_EXPORTER_CHECK_SINGLE_KEYS`, for example `bull:emails:wait,bull:emails:active`; `--check-keys` takes patterns), or use BullMQ's own metrics APIs in your app and expose them via your Prometheus client. Verify flag names against your exporter version.

### Example alert rules

```yaml
# prometheus/alerts.yml
groups:
  - name: redis
    rules:
      - alert: RedisDown
        expr: redis_up == 0
        for: 1m
        labels: { severity: critical }
        annotations: { summary: "Redis {{ $labels.instance }} is down" }

      - alert: RedisRestarted
        expr: redis_uptime_in_seconds < 300
        for: 0m
        labels: { severity: warning }
        annotations: { summary: "Redis restarted within the last 5 minutes" }

      - alert: RedisMemoryHigh
        expr: redis_memory_used_bytes / redis_memory_max_bytes > 0.85 and redis_memory_max_bytes > 0
        for: 10m
        labels: { severity: warning }
        annotations: { summary: "Redis memory > 85% of maxmemory" }

      - alert: RedisMemoryNoLimit
        expr: redis_memory_max_bytes == 0
        for: 5m
        labels: { severity: warning }
        annotations: { summary: "maxmemory is not set; OOM killer risk" }

      - alert: RedisEvictingKeys
        expr: rate(redis_evicted_keys_total[5m]) > 0
        for: 10m
        labels: { severity: warning }
        annotations: { summary: "Redis is evicting keys (critical if this instance holds queues)" }

      - alert: RedisLowHitRatio
        expr: |
          rate(redis_keyspace_hits_total[10m]) /
          (rate(redis_keyspace_hits_total[10m]) + rate(redis_keyspace_misses_total[10m])) < 0.8
        for: 15m
        labels: { severity: warning }
        annotations: { summary: "Cache hit ratio below 80%" }

      - alert: RedisRejectedConnections
        expr: increase(redis_rejected_connections_total[5m]) > 0
        labels: { severity: critical }
        annotations: { summary: "Redis rejecting connections (maxclients reached)" }

      - alert: RedisTooManyConnections
        expr: redis_connected_clients > 5000
        for: 5m
        labels: { severity: warning }
        annotations: { summary: "High client count, possible connection leak" }

      - alert: RedisReplicaLinkDown
        expr: redis_master_link_up == 0
        for: 2m
        labels: { severity: critical }
        annotations: { summary: "Replica lost link to master" }

      - alert: RedisBgsaveFailing
        expr: redis_rdb_last_bgsave_status == 0
        for: 1m
        labels: { severity: critical }
        annotations: { summary: "Last RDB save failed; writes may be blocked (MISCONF)" }

      - alert: RedisSlowCommands
        expr: increase(redis_slowlog_length[10m]) > 20
        labels: { severity: warning }
        annotations: { summary: "Slowlog growing quickly" }

      - alert: RedisHighCPU
        expr: rate(redis_cpu_user_seconds_total[5m]) + rate(redis_cpu_sys_seconds_total[5m]) > 0.8
        for: 10m
        labels: { severity: warning }
        annotations: { summary: "Redis main thread near saturation (single-threaded: 1.0 = one full core)" }
```

Staff-level note: alert on **symptoms** (hit ratio, latency, errors seen by the application) as well as causes (memory, CPU). A single-threaded server hits a ceiling around 1 CPU core; sustained user+sys CPU above ~0.8 means you are close to saturation even when the host shows plenty of idle cores. Verify the `redis_rdb_last_bgsave_status` value mapping (1 = ok) in your exporter version.


---

## 16.16 Troubleshooting method

A repeatable order beats intuition during an incident.

```text
 1. Is Redis up and reachable?         (systemctl, redis-cli ping, ss)
 2. Did it restart?                    (INFO server uptime_in_seconds, journal, dmesg OOM)
 3. Is it healthy internally?          (INFO: memory, persistence, clients, replication)
 4. Is it busy or blocked?             (INFO stats ops/sec, SLOWLOG, LATENCY, CLIENT LIST flags)
 5. Is the problem the client/network? (client logs, ss, intrinsic latency, Node event-loop lag)
 6. What changed?                      (deploy, traffic, config, cron, kernel, disk)
```

First-minute command pack (save it in your runbook):

```bash
systemctl status redis-server --no-pager | head -15
redis-cli ping
redis-cli INFO server | grep -E 'uptime_in_seconds|redis_version'
redis-cli INFO clients | grep -E 'connected|blocked|maxclients'
redis-cli INFO memory  | grep -E 'used_memory_human|maxmemory_human|maxmemory_policy|fragmentation_ratio'
redis-cli INFO stats   | grep -E 'ops_per_sec|rejected|evicted|expired|keyspace_'
redis-cli INFO persistence | grep -E 'loading|rdb_last_bgsave_status|aof_last_write_status'
redis-cli SLOWLOG GET 5
redis-cli LATENCY LATEST
sudo tail -n 50 /var/log/redis/redis-server.log
df -h /var/lib/redis; free -h; dmesg -T | grep -iE 'oom|killed' | tail -3
```

---

## 16.17 Scenario 1: Connection refused

**Symptoms.** App logs `connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:6379`; `redis-cli` prints `Could not connect to Redis at 127.0.0.1:6379: Connection refused`.

**Debug steps.**

```bash
systemctl status redis-server --no-pager          # running? failed? restarting?
sudo ss -ltnp | grep -E '6379|redis'              # listening, and on which address?
sudo journalctl -u redis-server -n 50 --no-pager  # why did it stop?
sudo tail -n 50 /var/log/redis/redis-server.log
redis-cli -h <host> -p <port> ping                # from the same host as the app
docker ps -a --filter name=redis; docker logs redis --tail 50   # Compose
sudo ufw status; sudo iptables -S | grep 6379     # firewall (remote clients)
```

**Root causes and fixes.**

| Cause | Evidence | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Service stopped / crashed | `inactive`/`failed`; OOM kill in `dmesg` | Fix memory (16.19), `systemctl start`, enable `Restart=on-failure` |
| Config error after edit | Log: `FATAL CONFIG FILE ERROR` | Fix line; validate on a scratch port (15.5.1) |
| Bound to loopback but app is remote | `ss` shows `127.0.0.1:6379` only | Add private IP to `bind`, open firewall to that source only |
| Wrong host/port (Compose: using `localhost` inside a container) | App container's `localhost` is itself | Use service name `redis`, same network |
| Port in use / permission | Log: `Address already in use` | Stop duplicate instance (`ss -ltnp`) |
| Firewall drops (timeout rather than refusal) | `nc -vz host 6379` hangs | Fix security group / UFW rule |
| Still loading dataset | Connection accepted but `-LOADING` errors | Wait; see scenario 10 |

Note: "refused" means the host answered with a TCP reset (nothing listening); a **timeout** means packets are dropped or the host is unreachable, which is a different branch (scenario 2).

---

## 16.18 Scenario 2: Timeouts

**Symptoms.** `Command timed out`, `ETIMEDOUT`, sporadic p99 spikes, `MaxRetriesPerRequestError`.

**Debug steps.**

```bash
redis-cli --latency -i 1                 # network + server RTT
redis-cli --intrinsic-latency 10         # (on server) host jitter
redis-cli SLOWLOG GET 10                 # long executions that block others
redis-cli LATENCY LATEST; redis-cli LATENCY DOCTOR
redis-cli INFO commandstats | sort -t= -k3 -rn | head      # heavy commands (by usec)
redis-cli CLIENT LIST | grep -E 'cmd=(keys|sort|smembers|hgetall|lrange)'
redis-cli INFO persistence | grep -E 'latest_fork_usec|rdb_bgsave_in_progress|aof_rewrite_in_progress'
redis-cli INFO stats | grep -E 'instantaneous_ops_per_sec|instantaneous_input_kbps|instantaneous_output_kbps'
```

Timeline correlation: do timeouts line up with `BGSAVE` times in the log, cron jobs, deploys, or traffic peaks?

**Root causes and fixes.**

| Root cause | Evidence | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Slow O(N) command blocking the single thread | SLOWLOG entries; `LATENCY` `command` | Replace `KEYS` with `SCAN`, paginate `LRANGE`, `UNLINK` instead of `DEL`, cap collection sizes |
| Fork latency during BGSAVE/AOF rewrite | `latest_fork_usec` high, `fork` latency event, THP warning | Disable THP, shrink dataset, schedule saves off-peak, consider disabling RDB on replicas only |
| Slow disk with AOF `always`/rewrite | `aof-write`/`aof-fsync-always` events, log warning | `everysec`, faster disk, `no-appendfsync-on-rewrite yes` (accepts durability risk) |
| Large values / big pipelines | Big `qbuf`/`omem`, network saturation | Split payloads, compress, limit batch size |
| Network issue / NAT idle drops | `--latency` spikes only remotely, resets after idle | `tcp-keepalive`, client `keepAlive`, same AZ/private network |
| Client-side: Node event loop blocked | Redis metrics fine, app p99 high | Profile; move CPU work (large `JSON.parse`) off request path |
| Too-aggressive client timeout | Timeouts at exactly the configured value | Raise from 500 ms to ~1–2 s only after confirming server is fine |
| CPU saturation (single core at 100%) | `top` shows redis-server at ~100% | Scenario 5 |
| Swap or host steal | `vmstat` `si/so`, `st` | Remove swapping, bigger/dedicated VM |

---

## 16.19 Scenario 3: Memory full / OOM

Two different failures share the name: **Redis' own** OOM replies (`maxmemory` reached) and the **kernel OOM killer** terminating Redis.

**Symptoms.** (a) Writes fail: `OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'`. (b) Redis vanishes, service restarts, `dmesg` shows `Out of memory: Killed process ... redis-server`.

**Debug steps.**

```bash
redis-cli INFO memory | grep -E 'used_memory_human|used_memory_rss_human|used_memory_peak_human|maxmemory_human|maxmemory_policy|mem_fragmentation_ratio|mem_clients|mem_replication_backlog|mem_aof_buffer'
redis-cli MEMORY STATS | head -40
redis-cli MEMORY DOCTOR
redis-cli INFO keyspace                          # keys vs expires
redis-cli --bigkeys -i 0.05                      # large keys
redis-cli --memkeys -i 0.05
redis-cli CLIENT LIST | sort -t= -k18 -rn | head # large buffers (omem/qbuf)
redis-cli INFO stats | grep -E 'evicted_keys|expired_keys'
sudo dmesg -T | grep -iE 'out of memory|killed process'
```

**Root causes and fixes.**

| Cause | Evidence | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Keys without TTL accumulating | `keys` grows, `expires` flat | Add TTLs at write time, code review `SET` without `EX`, one-off cleanup with `SCAN` + `EXPIRE` |
| `maxmemory` unset on a small VPS | `maxmemory:0`; kernel OOM kill | Set `maxmemory` to ~60% RAM |
| `noeviction` on a cache | OOM errors under load | Cache instance: `allkeys-lru`/`allkeys-lfu`; or raise memory |
| Big keys (giant hash/list/stream) | `--bigkeys` | Split, trim (`XTRIM`, `LTRIM`), TTL, redesign |
| Buffers: slow pub/sub subscriber, replica lag, huge pipelines | Large `mem_clients_*`, `omem` | `client-output-buffer-limit`, kill client, fix consumer |
| Fork copy-on-write at high write rate | RSS ≫ `used_memory` during BGSAVE | More headroom, lower `maxmemory`, avoid frequent saves, THP off |
| Fragmentation | ratio > 1.5 | `activedefrag yes` (test), `MEMORY PURGE`, planned restart |
| Container/cgroup limit < needs | Docker `OOMKilled: true` | Raise `mem_limit`, lower `maxmemory` |
| BullMQ completed/failed jobs kept forever | huge `bull:*:completed` zsets | `removeOnComplete`/`removeOnFail` (age/count) |

Emergency actions (in order of least harm): raise `maxmemory` if the host has RAM (`CONFIG SET maxmemory`), delete known-disposable keys with `UNLINK` in batches via `SCAN`, trim queues' completed history, then restart as a last resort. Do **not** run `FLUSHALL` on an instance that has queues or sessions.

```text
docker inspect redis --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}}'
true
```

---

## 16.20 Scenario 4: Unexpected key expiration

**Symptoms.** Keys disappear sooner than intended; sessions log users out; locks vanish; `TTL` returns smaller values than expected.

**Debug steps.**

```bash
redis-cli TTL shop:session:abc               # -2 = missing, -1 = no expiry, else seconds
redis-cli PTTL shop:session:abc
redis-cli OBJECT FREQ shop:session:abc       # only with LFU policy
redis-cli INFO stats | grep -E 'expired_keys|evicted_keys'
redis-cli INFO keyspace
redis-cli CONFIG GET notify-keyspace-events
redis-cli --user admin MONITOR | grep -E 'EXPIRE|SET|PERSIST|GETEX'   # briefly; see 16.3
```

Enable keyspace events temporarily to see *who* expires what: `CONFIG SET notify-keyspace-events Ex`, then `redis-cli PSUBSCRIBE '__keyevent@0__:expired'`.

**Root causes and fixes.**

| Cause | Detail | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Units mixed up | `EX` seconds vs `PX` milliseconds; JS `Date.now()` ms passed to `EX` (huge) or seconds to `PX` (instant) | Centralize TTL constants in seconds, name them `ttlSec` |
| `SET` overwrote TTL | A plain `SET key value` **removes** an existing TTL (keeps none); `SET ... KEEPTTL` preserves it | Use `KEEPTTL` or re-apply TTL; `HSET`/`INCR` do not change TTL, `RENAME` keeps it |
| `EXPIRE` not re-applied on rewrite | Rolling TTL pattern forgotten | Use `GETEX key EX n` or `SET ... EX` each write |
| Evicted, not expired | `evicted_keys` rising; policy `allkeys-*`/`volatile-*` | Memory pressure: fix capacity, see scenario 3 |
| Different Redis / DB index | Writer uses db 1, reader db 0; or pointing to a different instance | Verify `INFO keyspace` and URL in both services |
| Clock jump on replica/master | Expiry uses wall-clock time; large clock changes cause mass expiry | NTP/chrony, avoid manual date changes |
| Replica reads | Replicas do not expire independently but hide logically-expired keys | Expect to see the same TTL semantics; check replication lag |
| Key prefix / naming mismatch | Looks like expiry, actually a miss | Use `RedisKeys` builders (Module 1/13) |
| Another job calls `EXPIRE`/`DEL`/`UNLINK` | Visible in MONITOR | Find the code path |

Semantics worth knowing: Redis expires keys lazily on access plus an active sampling cycle, so a key may physically exist slightly after its TTL but is never returned once logically expired. TTL precision is milliseconds; a TTL of `0` or negative deletes the key immediately.

---

## 16.21 Scenario 5: High CPU

**Symptoms.** `redis-server` at ~100% of one core; latency rises with load; `top` shows other cores idle.

**Debug steps.**

```bash
top -H -p $(pidof redis-server)               # per-thread view (main, bio, io threads)
redis-cli INFO cpu
redis-cli INFO stats | grep -E 'instantaneous_ops_per_sec|total_connections_received|expire_cycle'
redis-cli INFO commandstats | sort -t= -k3 -rn | head -10       # most total time (usec) by command
redis-cli --latency-history -i 2
redis-cli SLOWLOG GET 20
redis-cli CLIENT LIST | wc -l
redis-benchmark -q -n 20000 -t get,set -c 50      # on a staging box only
```

Compute rates by sampling `used_cpu_user + used_cpu_sys` twice (delta CPU seconds / delta wall seconds ≈ cores used).

**Root causes and fixes.**

| Cause | Evidence | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| One expensive command pattern | `commandstats` shows huge `usec` for one command | Fix query/data structure; cache results; limit ranges |
| Simply too many ops/sec for one thread | Ops/sec high, no slow commands | Pipeline/batch, reduce chattiness, local in-process cache for hot keys, shard (Cluster), consider `io-threads` if network-bound (benchmark) |
| Connection churn | `total_connections_received` rate high | Reuse connections (Module 13); AUTH/TLS handshakes are CPU heavy |
| Mass expiry | `expire_cycle_cpu_milliseconds` rising, many keys with identical TTL | Add jitter to TTLs |
| Lua scripts doing heavy work | Slowlog `EVAL`/`EVALSHA` | Make scripts O(1)/small, move work to app |
| TLS everywhere on loopback | CPU in crypto | Drop TLS on loopback/private link |
| Eviction storm | `evicted_keys` rate high | Capacity |
| `KEYS`, `SMEMBERS` loops, `SORT` | Slowlog | Replace |
| Background threads (AOF rewrite, bgsave child) | Child process CPU | Not main-thread issue; check disk and schedule |
| Hot key | One key receives most traffic (`redis-cli --hotkeys` with LFU) | Local cache with short TTL, replicate key across N suffixes (`key:{0..N}`) |

---

## 16.22 Scenario 6: Slow commands

**Symptoms.** Specific operations are slow; SLOWLOG fills; p99 high though average looks fine.

**Debug steps.**

```bash
redis-cli CONFIG GET slowlog-log-slower-than
redis-cli SLOWLOG GET 25
redis-cli INFO latencystats | grep -E 'get|set|hgetall|zrange'
redis-cli --bigkeys -i 0.05
redis-cli MEMORY USAGE <suspect-key>
redis-cli TYPE <key>; redis-cli LLEN <key>; redis-cli SCARD <key>; redis-cli HLEN <key>; redis-cli ZCARD <key>; redis-cli XLEN <key>
```

**Complexity cheat sheet for review.**

| Command | Complexity | Safer approach |
|---|---|---|
| `KEYS` | O(N) all keys | `SCAN` |
| `SMEMBERS`, `HGETALL`, `LRANGE 0 -1` | O(size) | `SSCAN`/`HSCAN`, `LRANGE` with windows, `HMGET` for needed fields |
| `DEL bigkey` | O(size) | `UNLINK` (async free) |
| `SORT` | O(N+M log M) | Pre-sorted structures (ZSET) |
| `ZUNIONSTORE`, `SUNION` | Sum of sizes | Cache result with TTL |
| `FLUSHALL`/`FLUSHDB` | O(keys) | `FLUSHALL ASYNC` and avoid |
| `ZRANGE` w/ large ranges | O(log N + M) | Paginate with `LIMIT` |
| `EVAL` | Script-defined | Keep short |

**Fixes.** Replace pattern, cap collection sizes at write time (`LTRIM`, `ZREMRANGEBYRANK`, `XADD MAXLEN ~`), enable `lazyfree-*`, add application-level timeouts, add an alert on `redis_slowlog_length` growth. Treat any command whose cost grows with data size as a latent incident.

---

## 16.23 Scenario 7: Too many client connections

**Symptoms.** `ERR max number of clients reached`; `rejected_connections` increments; app errors at peak; or `EMFILE` / `too many open files` in Redis log.

**Debug steps.**

```bash
redis-cli INFO clients                      # connected_clients vs maxclients
redis-cli CONFIG GET maxclients
redis-cli INFO stats | grep -E 'rejected_connections|total_connections_received'
redis-cli CLIENT LIST | grep -o 'name=[^ ]*' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
redis-cli CLIENT LIST | awk '{print $2}' | cut -d= -f2 | cut -d: -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
redis-cli CLIENT LIST | awk '{for(i=1;i<=NF;i++) if($i ~ /^idle=/){split($i,a,"="); if(a[2]>3600) c++}} END{print c " idle > 1h"}'
cat /proc/$(pidof redis-server)/limits | grep 'open files'
grep -i 'maxclients\|file descriptor' /var/log/redis/redis-server.log | tail
```

**Root causes and fixes.**

| Cause | Evidence | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Client created per request/job | High `total_connections_received` rate; thousands of young connections | One shared client per role (Module 13); never `new Redis()` in handlers |
| Leak: clients created but never closed (tests, scripts, hot-reload) | Old `age`, `idle` large, same names | `quit()` in shutdown/teardown; set server `timeout 300` as a safety net **only** if no long-lived idle connections are needed (BullMQ and subscribers are long-lived but not idle at the TCP layer when keepalive is on) |
| Too many app instances x clients | `connected_clients` = instances x N | Fewer clients per process; central proxy only if truly necessary |
| FD limit lower than `maxclients` | Log: "Your maximum number of open files is X... maxclients reduced" | `LimitNOFILE` in systemd drop-in (15.3), `ulimits` in Compose |
| BullMQ connection multiplication | Many queues x many workers each creating connections | Reuse a shared `connection` (ioredis instance) for Queues; note Workers still need their own blocking connection |
| Pub/Sub subscribers per user request | Many `flags=P` | One subscriber per process, fan out in-process |

Emergency: `CLIENT KILL` idle old connections (`CLIENT KILL MAXAGE`), temporarily `CONFIG SET maxclients` higher (bounded by fds), then fix the leak. Raising `maxclients` alone only delays the incident.

---

## 16.24 Scenario 8: Data unexpectedly disappearing

**Symptoms.** Keys that should exist are gone; `DBSIZE` drops to near zero; data returns after restore; or after restart the database is empty or old.

**Debug steps.**

```bash
redis-cli INFO server | grep uptime_in_seconds          # restart?
redis-cli INFO stats | grep -E 'expired_keys|evicted_keys'
redis-cli INFO keyspace
redis-cli INFO persistence | grep -E 'rdb_last_save_time|rdb_changes_since_last_save|aof_enabled|rdb_last_bgsave_status'
redis-cli INFO commandstats | grep -E 'cmdstat_(flushall|flushdb|del|unlink|expire|config|debug)'
redis-cli ACL LOG 20
redis-cli CONFIG GET dir; redis-cli CONFIG GET dbfilename; redis-cli CONFIG GET appendonly
redis-cli CONFIG GET save
sudo grep -iE 'flush|DB loaded|loading|AOF|RDB' /var/log/redis/redis-server.log | tail -30
docker inspect redis --format '{{json .Mounts}}'        # volume really mounted?
```

`INFO commandstats` is the key forensic: `cmdstat_flushall:calls=1` proves someone flushed. Non-zero `flushdb`/`flushall` calls on a prod instance are rarely innocent: they come from test suites pointed at the wrong URL (very common: Jest teardown doing `flushall` with `REDIS_URL` loaded from the production `.env`), admin tools, or an attacker.

**Root causes and fixes.**

| Cause | Fix |
|---|---|
| Test suite or script ran `FLUSHALL`/`FLUSHDB` against prod | Separate DB/instance per env, ACL-deny `flushall|flushdb` for app users (`-@dangerous`), use `rename`-free ACL control; add boot guard that refuses to run tests when URL host is not localhost |
| Expired/evicted (not deleted) | Scenarios 3 and 4 |
| Restart with no persistence | Enable AOF/RDB; verify `dir` is writable and on a persistent volume |
| Container recreated without volume | Mount `/data`; use named volume; `docker inspect` mounts |
| Wrong `dir`/`dbfilename` after config change | Redis starts empty because it reads a different path |
| Empty AOF preferred over RDB at startup | See restore trap (15.11) |
| Failed bgsave then restart | `rdb_last_bgsave_status:err`; fix disk/permissions; stop-writes protection exists for this reason |
| Failover to a stale/empty replica | Check replication offsets before promotion; use `min-replicas-to-write` |
| Attack (exposed Redis, `CONFIG SET dir` + `SAVE`, ransom note key) | Rotate credentials, lock down network (15.6), restore from backup, audit `ACL LOG` and logs |
| Different DB index / instance | Verify config of every service |
| Cluster resharding / different shard | `CLUSTER INFO`, `MOVED` handling in the client |

Prevention: `FLUSHALL`/`FLUSHDB` denied by ACL for application users, separate instance per environment, backups with drills, and alerts on `redis_uptime_in_seconds` resets and sudden drops in `redis_db_keys`.

---

## 16.25 Scenario 9: BullMQ jobs stuck

**Symptoms.** Jobs sit in `waiting` or `active` forever, delayed jobs never run, `failed` count grows, queue appears empty but work is not done, or jobs are processed twice.

BullMQ stores each queue under `bull:<queueName>:*` keys (for example `wait`, `active`, `delayed`, `failed`, `completed`, `paused`, `stalled`, `id`, `meta`, per-job hashes `bull:<queue>:<jobId>`). Exact key types and names are version-dependent, so inspect with `SCAN` and `TYPE`.

**Debug steps.**

```bash
# 1. Which keys exist for this queue?
redis-cli --scan --pattern 'bull:emails:*' | head -30

# 2. Counts (commands depend on type; check with TYPE first)
redis-cli TYPE bull:emails:wait
redis-cli LLEN bull:emails:wait             # waiting (list)
redis-cli LLEN bull:emails:active           # active (list)
redis-cli ZCARD bull:emails:delayed         # delayed (sorted set)
redis-cli ZCARD bull:emails:failed
redis-cli ZCARD bull:emails:completed
redis-cli LLEN bull:emails:paused           # paused queue?

# 3. Is anyone consuming? Look for blocked clients and worker connection names
redis-cli CLIENT LIST | grep -E 'flags=b|bull'
redis-cli INFO clients | grep blocked_clients

# 4. Redis-side problems that break BullMQ
redis-cli CONFIG GET maxmemory-policy       # must be noeviction
redis-cli INFO stats | grep evicted_keys    # must be 0
redis-cli INFO memory | grep -E 'used_memory_human|maxmemory_human'

# 5. Application side
pm2 status; pm2 logs worker --lines 100
```

In code, use the queue API for authoritative state:

```ts
const counts = await queue.getJobCounts('waiting', 'active', 'delayed', 'failed', 'completed', 'paused');
const isPaused = await queue.isPaused();
const workers = await queue.getWorkers();            // connected workers (via CLIENT LIST names)
const failed = await queue.getFailed(0, 5);          // inspect failedReason and stacktrace
```

**Root causes and fixes.**

| Cause | Evidence | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| No worker process running (crashed, wrong PM2 app, deployed only API) | `getWorkers()` empty; no `b` clients | Start worker; `pm2 startup`; alert on worker count |
| Queue paused | `isPaused()` true, items in `paused` | `queue.resume()` |
| Eviction removed BullMQ keys | `evicted_keys > 0`, `allkeys-lru`, missing job hashes, "Missing key for job" errors | Set `noeviction`; dedicated Redis for queues; cannot recover evicted jobs |
| Wrong Redis/DB/prefix between producer and worker | Producer's keys not visible to worker | Same `connection`, `prefix`, queue name; check `REDIS_QUEUE_URL` in both |
| Worker event loop blocked (CPU-heavy job) so lock renewal fails | Jobs become `stalled`, retried, double processing | Keep jobs async/chunked, raise `lockDuration`, use sandboxed processors for CPU work |
| Worker crashed mid-job | Job stays `active` until stalled check moves it back (`stalledInterval`, `maxStalledCount`) | Tune stall settings; make jobs idempotent |
| `maxRetriesPerRequest` not `null` on worker connection | Worker errors/exits during Redis blips | `maxRetriesPerRequest: null` (Module 13) |
| Concurrency too low for backlog | Waiting grows steadily, workers busy | Raise `concurrency`, scale workers, check job duration |
| Rate limiter configured | `limiter` option throttling | Review limiter settings |
| Delayed jobs not firing | `delayed` zset has past scores; no worker | Worker must be running to promote delayed jobs; check system clock/NTP |
| Completed/failed history huge, memory pressure | Large `completed` zset | `removeOnComplete: { age, count }`, `removeOnFail` |
| Redis restarted without persistence | Queue empty after reboot | AOF `everysec`, volume |
| Job throws before ack / unhandled promise | `failed` entries | Handle errors; use `attempts` + `backoff` |
| Redis restarted with different version/prefix upgrade | Version-specific key layouts | Follow BullMQ migration notes when upgrading BullMQ |

Fix stuck state safely: prefer API methods (`job.retry()`, `queue.retryJobs()`, `queue.clean()`, `queue.obliterate()` for last resort) over editing keys by hand, because BullMQ maintains several structures atomically via Lua scripts. Manual `DEL` of internal keys corrupts queue state.

---

## 16.26 Scenario 10: Redis unavailable after VPS reboot

**Symptoms.** After a reboot (kernel patch, provider maintenance, crash) the app returns 500s; `redis-cli` says connection refused, `LOADING`, or the data is gone/old.

**Debug steps.**

```bash
uptime; who -b                                   # confirm reboot time
systemctl is-enabled redis-server                # "enabled"?
systemctl status redis-server --no-pager
sudo journalctl -u redis-server -b --no-pager | tail -60       # -b = this boot
sudo journalctl -b -p err --no-pager | tail -30
sudo tail -n 80 /var/log/redis/redis-server.log
df -h /var/lib/redis; df -i /var/lib/redis       # disk/inodes full?
ls -la /var/lib/redis /var/lib/redis/appendonlydir
sudo -u redis test -w /var/lib/redis && echo writable
redis-cli INFO persistence | grep -E 'loading|loading_loaded_perc|loading_eta_seconds'
systemctl is-enabled docker; docker ps -a        # Compose installs
docker inspect redis --format '{{.HostConfig.RestartPolicy.Name}} {{.State.Status}}'
pm2 list                                          # app processes returned?
```

**Root causes and fixes.**

| Cause | Evidence | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Service not enabled | `is-enabled` → `disabled` | `systemctl enable --now redis-server` |
| Docker daemon not enabled, or restart policy `no` | `docker ps` empty | `systemctl enable docker`; `restart: unless-stopped` |
| Dataset still loading | `-LOADING Redis is loading the dataset in memory`, `loading:1` | Wait (see `loading_eta_seconds`); app clients should retry (ready check); consider smaller AOF/RDB, faster disk |
| Corrupt/truncated AOF after hard power-off | Log: `Bad file format reading the append only file` | `redis-check-aof --fix` on a **copy** first, then replace; `aof-load-truncated yes` handles clean truncation; restore from backup if needed |
| Disk full or permission change | Log `Permission denied`/`No space left` | Free space, `chown -R redis:redis /var/lib/redis` |
| Config edited but never tested | `FATAL CONFIG FILE ERROR` | Fix, validate (15.5.1) |
| Bind to an IP that is not up yet at boot | `Could not create server TCP listening socket` | Use `bind 127.0.0.1 -<ip>` style tolerant address, add `After=network-online.target` + `Wants=` |
| sysctl/THP settings lost | Startup warnings again; latency | Persist in `/etc/sysctl.d`, enable THP unit (15.9) |
| Volume path changed / not mounted at boot | Empty `/var/lib/redis`, started empty | Mount ordering (`RequiresMountsFor=/var/lib/redis` in the drop-in), `fstab` `nofail` caveats |
| App started before Redis and gave up | App logs show errors only at boot | Client retry/backoff (13.9), PM2 `restart_delay`, readiness checks |
| Redis healthy but Nginx/PM2 not started | `pm2 list` empty | `pm2 startup && pm2 save`, `systemctl enable nginx` |

Post-reboot checklist to bake into a runbook: `systemctl is-enabled` for redis/docker/nginx/pm2, `INFO persistence` loaded, `DBSIZE` sane vs last known, sysctl and THP values, monitoring alert history for gap, backup timer (`systemctl list-timers`) still scheduled. Run a **reboot test** during a maintenance window before you need it for real.

---

## 16.27 Real-world use case: a latency incident, end to end

Alert: API p99 jumps from 80 ms to 2 s at 02:00 each night. Hit ratio normal, CPU low.

1. `LATENCY LATEST` shows `fork` events of ~900 ms at 02:00. `INFO stats` `latest_fork_usec:870000`.
2. Log shows `Background saving started` at 02:00 and a startup-era warning about THP.
3. `cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled` shows `[always]`: the THP unit was never enabled after the last reboot.
4. Fix: disable THP (15.9) and move the heaviest cron off the 02:00 window. Fork latency drops to ~60 ms.
5. Follow-up: alert on `rate(redis_latest_fork_usec)` / `latest_fork_usec > 200000`, add THP check to the post-reboot runbook, add a game-day item.

Lesson: nightly latency with a correlated background persistence event is a kernel or dataset-size problem, not an application problem; SLOWLOG would have been empty because fork time is not command execution time.

## 16.28 Performance considerations of monitoring itself

- Scraping every 15 s with `INFO` is cheap; avoid scrapers that call `MEMORY USAGE`/`--bigkeys` regularly on large datasets.
- `CLIENT LIST` is O(clients); do not poll it every second on 10k clients.
- `MONITOR` and verbose logging add load when you are already in trouble; use them surgically.
- Exporter key-checks (`--check-keys`) run `SCAN`; restrict patterns and use `--check-single-keys` for known queue keys.
- Prefer rates over absolute values and keep dashboards to ~12 panels: memory, clients, ops/sec, hit ratio, evictions/expirations, latency percentiles, replication lag, persistence status, CPU, slowlog length, keys, network.

## 16.29 Limitations and alternatives

- `INFO` counters are instance-level; they cannot tell you which service or endpoint caused load. Use `connectionName`, client-side metrics, and tracing for attribution.
- SLOWLOG omits network and queue wait. LATENCY needs a threshold set *before* the event.
- Redis Insight (GUI) offers a slow-log viewer, profiler, and memory analysis; it uses the same commands (including MONITOR for its profiler) so the same risks apply.
- Commercial APMs (Datadog, New Relic) offer Redis integrations; they scrape the same `INFO` data. Managed Redis exposes CloudWatch/metrics in place of direct `INFO` access, sometimes with restricted commands.
- Valkey exposes the same `INFO`/`SLOWLOG`/`LATENCY` surface, so these tools work unchanged.

## 16.30 Common mistakes

1. Running `KEYS *` or `MONITOR` on production "just to check".
2. Reading lifetime counters (hit ratio since boot) instead of windowed rates.
3. Alerting only on `redis_up` and missing evictions, memory, persistence failures, and replication lag.
4. Ignoring the startup log warnings (THP, overcommit, somaxconn).
5. Raising `maxclients` or timeouts instead of finding the leak or the slow command.
6. Restarting Redis as the first reaction, destroying evidence (`SLOWLOG`, `LATENCY` history, client list) and risking a long reload.
7. Using `SLOWLOG` as proof Redis is fine when the problem is network or event-loop lag.
8. Keeping BullMQ on a cache-policy instance (`allkeys-lru`).
9. Unnamed clients that cannot be attributed in `CLIENT LIST`.
10. Never testing reboot behaviour, restore, or failover until the incident.

## 16.31 Interview Q&A

**Q1. Redis is slow. Walk me through diagnosis.**
Confirm whether it is the server or the path: `redis-cli --latency` locally and remotely, `--intrinsic-latency` for host jitter. Server side: SLOWLOG for blocking commands, `LATENCY LATEST/DOCTOR` for fork/AOF/expire events, `INFO commandstats` for heavy commands, `INFO persistence` for fork time, `CLIENT LIST` for blocked or fat clients, CPU for saturation. Then client side: connection churn, event-loop lag, timeouts configuration.

**Q2. Why is `KEYS` dangerous and what do you use instead?**
It is O(N) and blocks the single command thread, so all clients stall. `SCAN` iterates incrementally with a cursor (may return duplicates and has weak guarantees for keys modified during iteration). Better still: keep an index set so you never need to scan.

**Q3. How do you calculate the cache hit ratio and what is a good value?**
`hits / (hits + misses)` from `keyspace_hits` and `keyspace_misses`, using windowed rates in Prometheus. "Good" depends on the workload; sustained decline plus rising `evicted_keys` signals an undersized cache or poor TTL/key design.

**Q4. Memory is fine according to `used_memory` but the box is OOM. Why?**
RSS includes fragmentation, copy-on-write pages during fork, client and replication buffers, and the allocator's retention. Compare `used_memory_rss`, fork activity, and `maxmemory` vs the VM/cgroup limit.

**Q5. What does `MONITOR` cost and when would you use it?**
It echoes every command to the client and can halve throughput; it can also leak data. Use it for a few seconds to see which client/key pattern is misbehaving, preferably on a replica, otherwise prefer SLOWLOG, commandstats, or client names.

**Q6. How do you find which service is creating too many connections?**
Name clients (`CLIENT SETNAME` / `connectionName`), then group `CLIENT LIST` by `name` and `addr`, look at `age`/`idle`, and compare `total_connections_received` rate with `connected_clients`.

**Q7. Replica shows `master_link_status:down`. What do you check?**
Replica log for the reason (auth failure `masterauth`, network, `protected-mode`, memory/`client-output-buffer-limit replica` disconnect during sync), master `INFO replication` for backlog and `sync_full`, firewall/bind, and TLS settings.

**Q8. BullMQ jobs are stuck waiting. First three checks?**
Is a worker connected (`queue.getWorkers()`, blocked clients)? Is the queue paused? Is Redis evicting keys (`maxmemory-policy`, `evicted_keys`)? Then look at worker event-loop blocking, prefix/connection mismatches, and stalled settings.

## 16.32 Senior / Staff discussion

- **SLIs for Redis as a platform dependency.** Define SLOs from the caller's perspective: p99 command latency measured in the client, error rate, and cache hit ratio per feature. Server metrics are for diagnosis, not for SLOs.
- **Capacity planning.** Track growth of `used_memory`, keys, and ops/sec; project time to 80%. Single-thread CPU headroom (user+sys) is the scaling ceiling; plan sharding or workload splitting before you hit 70%.
- **Incident hygiene.** Capture evidence first (`SLOWLOG GET`, `LATENCY HISTORY`, `CLIENT LIST`, `INFO everything` to a file), then mitigate. Make a script `redis-snapshot-diagnostics.sh` that dumps these to a timestamped file for postmortems.
- **Guardrails over heroics.** ACL-deny `KEYS`, `FLUSHALL`, `FLUSHDB`, `DEBUG`, `CONFIG` for apps; per-environment instances; CI check that scans for `redis.keys(` and `flushall` in code; load tests that assert hit ratio and tail latency.
- **Failure-mode testing.** Quarterly game days: stop Redis, kill -9 it, fill the disk, reboot the VPS, restore from backup, fail over. Measure RTO/RPO, then fix the findings.
- **Observability cost.** Metrics cardinality in exporters (per-key checks) can explode; budget it deliberately.

## 16.33 Practical exercise

**Task.** In a lab Redis, reproduce and diagnose three faults: (1) a slow command, (2) memory full under `noeviction`, (3) connection leak. For each, show the metric that reveals it and the fix.

**Solution.**

```bash
# (1) Slow command
redis-cli CONFIG SET slowlog-log-slower-than 1000
redis-cli DEBUG POPULATE 2000000 big 10            # needs enable-debug-command local/yes in lab only
redis-cli KEYS 'big:*' > /dev/null
redis-cli SLOWLOG GET 1                             # shows KEYS with duration in microseconds
# Fix: SCAN-based iteration; deny KEYS via ACL (-keys) for the app user.

# (2) Memory full
redis-cli CONFIG SET maxmemory 50mb
redis-cli CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy noeviction
redis-benchmark -n 1000000 -t set -r 1000000 -d 100 -q
redis-cli SET x 1                                   # (error) OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'.
redis-cli INFO memory | grep -E 'used_memory_human|maxmemory_human'
# Fix: CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru (cache) or raise maxmemory (data); add TTLs.

# (3) Connection leak: 200 idle clients that never close
for i in $(seq 1 200); do (redis-cli --no-raw BLPOP never 0 >/dev/null 2>&1 &) ; done
redis-cli INFO clients | grep -E 'connected_clients|blocked_clients'
redis-cli CLIENT LIST | awk '{print $2}' | cut -d= -f2 | cut -d: -f1 | sort | uniq -c
redis-cli CLIENT KILL TYPE normal MAXAGE 1          # [7.4+] drop connections older than 1 s (careful: kills yours elsewhere)
# Fix: reuse clients, close on shutdown, name connections, alert on connected_clients.
```

Reset the lab afterwards: `redis-cli FLUSHALL; redis-cli CONFIG SET maxmemory 0; redis-cli CONFIG RESETSTAT`. Never run these on shared or production instances; `DEBUG POPULATE` additionally requires the debug command to be enabled.

Then add to your answer: write the Prometheus alert that would have caught each (`RedisSlowCommands`, `RedisMemoryHigh`, `RedisTooManyConnections` from 16.15).

## 16.34 Key takeaways

- INFO for state, SLOWLOG for slow executions, LATENCY for server stalls, CLIENT for attribution, MEMORY for capacity; MONITOR and KEYS are not production tools.
- Hit ratio, eviction rate, fragmentation, replication lag, and persistence status are the metrics that matter; use windowed rates.
- Prometheus + redis_exporter + Grafana, with alerts on symptoms and causes, gives you history that incidents need.
- Troubleshoot in a fixed order: reachable, restarted, healthy, busy, client/network, what changed.
- Most real incidents trace back to a short list: missing TTLs, wrong eviction policy, O(N) commands, connection churn, THP/overcommit, un-persisted data, and untested restart or restore paths.
