# Module 17: Advanced Interview Question Bank

This bank is organized by topic. Every question has the same five parts: a **short interview answer** (what you say in the first 20 seconds), a **detailed technical explanation**, a **practical example**, a **senior-level follow-up with its answer**, and **common incorrect answers** (what loses points). Each question is tagged `[Intermediate]`, `[Senior]`, or `[Staff]` to show the depth an interviewer expects at that level.

How to use it: cover the answer, say yours out loud, then compare. Interviewers at Senior and Staff level care less about definitions and more about trade-offs, failure modes, and how you would verify a claim in production.

Version tags: unless marked, behavior applies to Redis 7.x and 8.x. Features that are newer are tagged (7.0+), (7.2+), (8.0+), and so on.

| Section | Questions |
|---|---|
| A. Fundamentals | Q1–Q10 |
| B. Data structures | Q11–Q20 |
| C. Caching | Q21–Q30 |
| D. Distributed systems | Q31–Q40 |
| E. Messaging and BullMQ | Q41–Q48 |
| F. Transactions and Lua | Q49–Q54 |
| G. Performance and production | Q55–Q62 |
| H. High availability and Cluster | Q63–Q67 |
| I. Security | Q68–Q70 |
| J. System design prompts | S1–S6 |

---

## 17.1 Section A: Fundamentals

### Q1. [Intermediate] Why is Redis fast, and what does "fast" actually depend on?

- **Short answer:** Data lives in RAM, commands run on one thread with no lock contention, I/O uses epoll multiplexing, the data structures are compact C code, and the protocol (RESP) is trivial to parse. In practice, network round trips dominate latency, not Redis itself.
- **Detailed explanation:** A typical `GET` costs a few microseconds of CPU. A network round trip inside one data center costs 100–500 µs. So the client-side pattern (pipelining, connection reuse, avoiding chatty loops) usually matters more than server tuning. Redis is fast only for commands with low algorithmic cost. `KEYS *`, `SMEMBERS` on a 5M-member set, `LRANGE 0 -1` on a long list, or a huge Lua script are slow because everything shares the single command thread.
- **Practical example:**

```ts
// 1,000 sequential awaits: ~1,000 RTTs
for (const id of ids) await redis.get(`user:${id}`);

// One pipeline: ~1 RTT plus server time
const pipe = redis.pipeline();
ids.forEach((id) => pipe.get(`user:${id}`));
const results = await pipe.exec(); // [[err, value], ...]
```

```bash
redis-benchmark -t get -n 100000 -P 1    # no pipelining
redis-benchmark -t get -n 100000 -P 16   # pipelined, usually many times higher rps
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"Redis p99 is 40 ms but SLOWLOG is empty. Where is the time going?"* **Answer:** SLOWLOG records only command execution time, not queueing, network, client-side event loop delay, or fork pauses. Check `LATENCY DOCTOR`, `INFO persistence` (`latest_fork_usec`), client-side event loop lag, network path, CPU steal, and whether the Node process itself is blocked.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Because it's NoSQL." "Because it's multi-threaded." "Because it never touches disk" (AOF and RDB do touch disk, just off the hot path).

### Q2. [Intermediate] Is Redis single-threaded? How do you use a multi-core machine?

- **Short answer:** Command execution is single-threaded. Redis also has background threads (lazy free, fsync, close), optional I/O threads for socket read/write (6.0+), and forked children for RDB/AOF rewrite. To use many cores you run multiple instances or a Cluster.
- **Detailed explanation:** A single execution thread gives atomic commands without locks and predictable ordering. The cost: one slow command blocks everyone. I/O threads (`io-threads N`) parallelize reading and writing sockets, not command execution. Redis 8.0 reworked and improved I/O threading, so large throughput gains are possible on many-core machines, but execution is still serialized per instance. Redis Query Engine (search, vector) in 8.x runs queries on additional threads, but that is a module-style subsystem, not general command execution.
- **Practical example:**

```bash
redis-cli CONFIG GET io-threads
# 1) "io-threads"
# 2) "1"
# Typical rule: leave at 1 unless a single instance is CPU-bound on network I/O.
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"One shard is at 100% of one core, others are idle. Will io-threads help?"* **Answer:** Only if the time is spent in socket I/O. If it is command execution (hot key, O(N) commands, Lua), more I/O threads do nothing. Fix the hot key or split the workload across shards.
- **Common incorrect answers:** A flat "yes, single-threaded" with no nuance; "Redis uses all cores automatically".

### Q3. [Intermediate] Why does Redis offer many data structures instead of just key-value strings?

- **Short answer:** Server-side structures let you do atomic, efficient operations next to the data (increment a field, push to a list, add to a sorted set) without read-modify-write round trips from the client.
- **Detailed explanation:** If you store a leaderboard as a JSON string, every update is GET, parse, modify, serialize, SET, with a race window. As a sorted set it is one `ZINCRBY` that is O(log N) and atomic. Structures also expose operations a blob cannot: range by score, pop from the head, set intersections, bit counting. The trade-off is that structures are Redis-specific modeling, and some (large sets, long lists) have O(N) hazards.
- **Practical example:**

```bash
ZINCRBY leaderboard:2026-11 25 user:42
ZREVRANGE leaderboard:2026-11 0 9 WITHSCORES
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"When is a plain String the right choice?"* **Answer:** For opaque cached values read as a whole (serialized view models, HTML fragments), counters (`INCR`), and flags. If you always read and write the whole object, a hash gives you no benefit and costs more per-field overhead on small objects.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "So that it can replace the database."

### Q4. [Intermediate] `SET user:1 '{json}'` versus `HSET user:1 name ... age ...`. How do you choose?

- **Short answer:** Use a String with serialized JSON when you read and write the whole object. Use a Hash when you update or read individual fields frequently and want atomic field-level operations.
- **Detailed explanation:** A Hash allows `HINCRBY`, `HGET` of one field, and per-field `HEXPIRE` (7.4+ for field-level TTL; verify your server version). Small hashes use a compact listpack encoding and are memory-efficient. Hash values are strings only, so nested objects require flattening or JSON inside a field. A JSON String needs no flattening, but any partial update is read-modify-write and races with other writers. Redis JSON (included in Redis 8) provides `JSON.SET`/`JSON.GET` with path updates, which solves partial updates for nested documents.
- **Practical example:**

```bash
HSET user:1 name "Ana" plan "pro" logins 0
HINCRBY user:1 logins 1
HGET user:1 plan
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"Does a hash TTL expire individual fields?"* **Answer:** A key TTL expires the whole hash. Per-field expiration exists only in newer versions (7.4+ with `HEXPIRE`). On older versions you model field expiry yourself (separate keys or a sorted set of expirations).
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Hashes are always more memory efficient" (not true past the listpack thresholds, `hash-max-listpack-entries`/`hash-max-listpack-value`).

### Q5. [Intermediate] How does key expiry work? Is a key deleted exactly at its TTL?

- **Short answer:** No. Redis uses lazy expiration (a key is checked when accessed) plus an active expiration cycle that samples keys with TTLs. Expired keys can occupy memory briefly after their TTL.
- **Detailed explanation:** The active cycle runs about 10 times per second. It samples keys from the expires dictionary, deletes expired ones, and repeats if more than about 25% of the sample was expired, within a CPU time budget. On replicas, expiry is driven by the primary: the primary emits `DEL`/`UNLINK` to replicas, though replicas hide logically expired keys from reads. Inside a Lua script, time is frozen at script start.
- **Practical example:**

```bash
SET session:abc "x" EX 30
TTL session:abc        # (integer) 29
PTTL session:abc       # milliseconds
SET session:abc "y"    # removes the TTL (no KEEPTTL)
TTL session:abc        # (integer) -1
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"A million keys were set with TTL = 3600 at the same minute. What happens at the one-hour mark?"* **Answer:** An expiry wave. The active cycle may loop heavily, causing latency spikes, and a cache miss wave hits the database (avalanche). Add jitter to TTLs (for example `3600 + random(0, 300)`), and consider lazy-free settings so deletions are off the main thread.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "A timer per key deletes it exactly on time." "A TTL of -1 means expired" (it means no expiry; -2 means the key does not exist).

### Q6. [Intermediate] Persistence versus replication: what is the difference?

- **Short answer:** Persistence (RDB/AOF) lets a single node recover data after restart. Replication copies data to other nodes for failover and read scaling. They solve different failure modes and are not substitutes for each other or for backups.
- **Detailed explanation:** Replication is asynchronous by default, so a primary can acknowledge a write and crash before replicas receive it. `WAIT` can reduce that window but does not make Redis strongly consistent. A `FLUSHALL` or a bad deploy that deletes keys replicates instantly. A primary with persistence off that restarts empty will make its replicas empty too if they resync from it. Backups (RDB snapshots copied off-box) protect against logical errors.
- **Practical example:**

```bash
redis-cli INFO persistence | grep -E "rdb_last_save_time|aof_enabled|aof_last_write_status"
redis-cli INFO replication | grep -E "role|connected_slaves|master_repl_offset"
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"Your primary restarts under systemd with persistence disabled and Sentinel is running. What can go wrong?"* **Answer:** If systemd restarts it quickly, before Sentinel's failover timeout, the primary comes back empty and replicas resync from it, wiping their data. Either keep persistence on, or prevent automatic restart so Sentinel can promote a replica first.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Replication is my backup." "AOF always means zero data loss" (only `appendfsync always` approaches that, with a heavy throughput cost).

### Q7. [Intermediate] RDB versus AOF: which would you use for a cache, and which for a job queue?

- **Short answer:** A pure cache can run with persistence off or RDB only. A queue (BullMQ) should use AOF with `everysec` (accepting up to about one second of loss) plus replicas, because losing jobs is a business problem.
- **Detailed explanation:** RDB is a compact point-in-time snapshot (fork plus copy-on-write). It is fast to load but loses data since the last snapshot. AOF logs every write and is replayed on startup. The `everysec` policy fsyncs once per second in a background thread. Since 7.0, AOF is a multi-part (base plus incremental) set of files, and rewrite compacts it. Many production setups enable both: AOF for durability, RDB for backups. Persistence costs: fork latency with large datasets and disk I/O pressure.
- **Practical example:**

```bash
redis-cli CONFIG SET appendonly yes
redis-cli CONFIG SET appendfsync everysec
redis-cli INFO persistence | grep aof_rewrite_in_progress
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"Why can a fork on a 30 GB instance freeze Redis for hundreds of milliseconds?"* **Answer:** `fork()` copies page tables, which scale with resident memory, and on virtualized hosts this is slower. Transparent Huge Pages make copy-on-write worse. Disable THP, keep the dataset smaller per node, and monitor `latest_fork_usec`.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "AOF is always better." "RDB blocks the server while saving" (the child process does the save; only the fork itself blocks).

### Q8. [Intermediate] What are the main memory eviction policies, and when do you set `noeviction`?

- **Short answer:** When `maxmemory` is reached, the policy decides what happens: `noeviction` rejects writes, `allkeys-lru`/`allkeys-lfu` evict any key, and `volatile-*` policies evict only keys with a TTL. Caches use `allkeys-lru` or `allkeys-lfu`. Queues and primary data use `noeviction`.
- **Detailed explanation:** Redis LRU/LFU are approximate (sampled with `maxmemory-samples`, default 5). `volatile-*` policies fall back to errors if no keys have TTLs. `allkeys-lfu` is often better for skewed access patterns because it keeps frequently used keys even if they were not touched recently. BullMQ requires `noeviction`; evicting queue keys corrupts queue state, and BullMQ logs a warning if the policy is different.
- **Practical example:**

```bash
redis-cli CONFIG SET maxmemory 2gb
redis-cli CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy allkeys-lfu
redis-cli INFO stats | grep evicted_keys
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"The same Redis holds the cache and BullMQ queues. What policy?"* **Answer:** There is no safe single choice: `noeviction` protects queues but makes the cache reject writes when full; `allkeys-lru` could evict queue keys. Split them into separate instances, or at minimum use `volatile-lru` with TTLs only on cache keys and accept the risk. Separate instances is the right answer.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "`allkeys-lru` is a safe default everywhere."

### Q9. [Intermediate] `KEYS` versus `SCAN`; `DEL` versus `UNLINK`.

- **Short answer:** `KEYS` is O(N) and blocks the server; use `SCAN` for incremental iteration. `DEL` frees memory synchronously; `UNLINK` unlinks in O(1) and frees memory in a background thread.
- **Detailed explanation:** `SCAN` can return duplicates and its `COUNT` is a hint. Elements present for the whole iteration are guaranteed to be returned. In Cluster, `SCAN` works per node, so you iterate every primary. Deleting a hash with millions of fields via `DEL` blocks; `UNLINK` avoids that, and for incremental cleanup you can use `HSCAN` plus `HDEL`.
- **Practical example:**

```ts
async function deleteByPattern(redis: Redis, pattern: string) {
  let cursor = '0';
  do {
    const [next, keys] = await redis.scan(cursor, 'MATCH', pattern, 'COUNT', 500);
    cursor = next;
    if (keys.length) await redis.unlink(...keys);
  } while (cursor !== '0');
}
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"Even with SCAN, why is pattern-delete a bad invalidation strategy at scale?"* **Answer:** It still touches every key in the keyspace (cost proportional to total keys, not matches). Better: maintain index sets of keys per entity, use versioned key namespaces, or use tags.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "`SCAN` returns exactly COUNT keys." "`SCAN` is a snapshot."

### Q10. [Senior] Redis versus Memcached versus a relational database cache table. When does each win?

- **Short answer:** Redis wins when you need data structures, atomic operations, persistence, replication, or pub/sub. Memcached wins for a simple multi-threaded blob cache. A database table wins when you need transactional consistency with source data and traffic is low.
- **Detailed explanation:** Memcached scales across cores in one process and has simple slab memory management, but no persistence, replication, or rich types. A DB-backed cache avoids a new dependency but puts load on the same database you are trying to protect. Also consider the license landscape: Redis moved licensing across versions (Redis 8 offers an AGPL option), and Valkey is a Linux Foundation fork; some orgs choose based on licensing and managed-service support.
- **Practical example:** Decision for a NestJS stack: sessions, rate limits, BullMQ, leaderboards, and cache all in Redis (separate logical roles, ideally separate instances for cache and queues).
- **Senior follow-up:** *"Why not just use one big Redis for everything?"* **Answer:** Blast radius and policy conflicts. A cache stampede or memory overflow in the cache workload can take down queues and sessions. Different durability and eviction needs call for separate instances.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Redis is always faster than Memcached" (Memcached can match it for simple GET/SET across many cores).

## 17.2 Section B: Data structures

### Q11. [Intermediate] How do you choose among List, Set, Sorted Set, and Stream for a "recent activity" feature?

- **Short answer:** A List with `LPUSH` and `LTRIM` is the simplest capped feed. A Sorted Set (timestamp as score) supports range queries by time and removal by score. A Stream adds consumer groups, acknowledgement, and IDs, and is best when multiple consumers process the events.
- **Detailed explanation:** Lists are O(1) at the ends but O(N) in the middle and have no uniqueness. Sorted Sets are O(log N) per write and deduplicate by member. Streams (5.0+) are append-only logs with `MAXLEN`/`MINID` trimming, with fields per entry, and with consumer groups and a pending entries list.
- **Practical example:**

```bash
LPUSH feed:u42 "post:9001"
LTRIM feed:u42 0 99          # keep latest 100
ZADD feed:u42:ts 1763500000 "post:9001"
ZREMRANGEBYSCORE feed:u42:ts -inf 1760000000
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"The list feed has 5M entries for a celebrity user. What breaks?"* **Answer:** Unbounded keys are a big-key problem (slow `LRANGE`, slow `DEL`, replication spikes). Always cap with `LTRIM`, or shard the feed into time buckets, and read with bounded ranges.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Use a Set because it's unordered and fast" for an ordered feed.

### Q12. [Intermediate] How does a Sorted Set work internally and what are its costs?

- **Short answer:** It combines a hash table (member to score) with a skip list (ordered by score), giving O(log N) insert and rank operations. Small sorted sets use a compact listpack.
- **Detailed explanation:** `ZADD`, `ZREM`, `ZRANK`, `ZINCRBY` are O(log N). `ZRANGE` is O(log N + M). Ties in score are ordered lexicographically by member. `ZRANGE` in 6.2+ unifies `BYSCORE`, `BYLEX`, `REV`, `LIMIT` options. Scores are double-precision floats, so integers above 2^53 lose precision.
- **Practical example:**

```bash
ZADD board 1500 "ana" 1200 "bo" 1500 "cy"
ZREVRANGE board 0 -1 WITHSCORES
# 1) "cy" 2) "1500" 3) "ana" 4) "1500" 5) "bo" 6) "1200"
ZREVRANK board "ana"      # (integer) 1
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"How do you rank users by score with ties broken by earliest achievement?"* **Answer:** Encode a composite score such as `score * 1e6 + (MAX_TS - ts)` while staying below 2^53, or keep a secondary hash for timestamps and break ties in the application. Verify precision limits first.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "It's a balanced binary tree" or "a heap".

### Q13. [Intermediate] When would you use a Hash with a million fields, and why might that be a mistake?

- **Short answer:** Rarely. A Hash of that size is a big key: operations like `HGETALL` and `DEL` are O(N), it cannot be split across Cluster shards, and it becomes a hot key.
- **Detailed explanation:** Redis keys are the unit of sharding, replication, and expiry. A single huge hash lives on one shard and is deleted all-or-nothing. Splitting into buckets (`user:{id/1000}` with field `id%1000`) is the classic memory optimization for small objects and also bounds key size. Use `HSCAN` for iteration instead of `HGETALL`.
- **Practical example:**

```ts
const bucket = Math.floor(id / 1000);
await redis.hset(`profile:${bucket}`, String(id), json);
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"How do you find big keys safely in production?"* **Answer:** `redis-cli --bigkeys` or `--memkeys` run SCAN-based sampling and add load; run against a replica off peak. `MEMORY USAGE key SAMPLES 0` gives exact size for one key.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Redis handles big values fine because it's in memory."

### Q14. [Senior] What are HyperLogLog, Bitmaps, and Bloom filters, and what error or trade-off does each carry?

- **Short answer:** HyperLogLog counts unique items using about 12 KB with a standard error near 0.81%. Bitmaps store one bit per integer ID (exact). Bloom filters (in Redis 8 core, previously RedisBloom) test set membership with possible false positives but no false negatives.
- **Detailed explanation:** HLL cannot list members or remove them; it merges with `PFMERGE`. Bitmaps are efficient for dense, small integer ID spaces (daily active users with sequential IDs) and wasteful for sparse ones: a bit at offset 4 billion allocates about 512 MB. Bloom filters are used to avoid cache or database lookups for nonexistent keys.
- **Practical example:**

```bash
PFADD uv:2026-11-19 user:1 user:2 user:1
PFCOUNT uv:2026-11-19          # (integer) 2
SETBIT dau:2026-11-19 42 1
BITCOUNT dau:2026-11-19
BF.ADD seen:emails "a@x.com"   # (8.0+ core Bloom)
BF.EXISTS seen:emails "a@x.com"
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"Can you remove an element from a Bloom filter?"* **Answer:** Not in a standard one. Use a Cuckoo filter (`CF.DEL`), or rebuild the Bloom filter periodically.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "HyperLogLog is exact", "Bitmaps are always memory efficient".

### Q15. [Senior] Redis Streams versus Lists versus Pub/Sub as a message mechanism.

- **Short answer:** Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget with no storage. Lists give a simple queue where a popped message is gone if the consumer crashes. Streams give a durable log with consumer groups, acknowledgement, and recovery of unacknowledged messages.
- **Detailed explanation:** A `BRPOPLPUSH`/`BLMOVE` reliable-queue pattern improves lists but requires manual recovery. Streams track a Pending Entries List per consumer; `XAUTOCLAIM` (6.2+) reassigns stale messages. Streams still sit in a single node's memory and are subject to `maxmemory`, so trimming policy matters.
- **Practical example:**

```bash
XGROUP CREATE orders workers $ MKSTREAM
XADD orders * orderId 1001 total 49.90
XREADGROUP GROUP workers w1 COUNT 10 BLOCK 5000 STREAMS orders >
XACK orders workers 1763500000000-0
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"A consumer died after reading but before XACK. How is the message recovered?"* **Answer:** The entry stays in the PEL. Another consumer runs `XAUTOCLAIM orders workers w2 60000 0-0` to claim entries idle for more than 60 s. Handlers must be idempotent because delivery is at-least-once.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Streams give exactly-once delivery."

### Q16. [Intermediate] What is the difference between `INCR` and a GET-then-SET counter in Node.js?

- **Short answer:** `INCR` is atomic on the server. GET then SET from the client is a race: two instances can read the same value and both write value+1, losing an update.
- **Detailed explanation:** Atomicity is per command (or per Lua script/transaction). Any read-modify-write you do across the network is not atomic unless protected by `WATCH`, a Lua script, or a lock.
- **Practical example:**

```ts
// Buggy
const v = Number(await redis.get('hits')) || 0;
await redis.set('hits', String(v + 1));

// Correct
await redis.incr('hits');
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"How do you make 'increment but cap at 100' atomic?"* **Answer:** A Lua script: read, compare, `INCR` only if below the cap, return the result. `INCR` plus a post-check is not a cap, since the value has already moved.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Node is single-threaded so there's no race" (multiple Node instances and clusters exist).

### Q17. [Senior] What are listpack/quicklist/intset encodings and why do they matter?

- **Short answer:** Redis stores small collections in compact contiguous encodings (listpack, intset) and converts them to hash tables, skip lists, or quicklists when they grow past configured thresholds. This is the main lever for memory efficiency.
- **Detailed explanation:** Small hashes, sorted sets, and lists use listpack (Redis 7.0 replaced ziplist). Sets of integers use intset. Conversion is one-way in practice: once converted to a hash table, a collection does not go back automatically after shrinking. Compact encodings trade CPU (linear scan within the blob) for memory, which is fine at small sizes.
- **Practical example:**

```bash
HSET small a 1 b 2
OBJECT ENCODING small           # "listpack"
CONFIG GET hash-max-listpack-entries   # default 128
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"Memory doubled after you raised `hash-max-listpack-value`. Why?"* **Answer:** Raising the threshold too far makes large linear-scan blobs; CPU rises, and the reallocation behavior on updates can hurt. Verify with `MEMORY USAGE` and benchmarks, not intuition.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Encodings are chosen by the client."

### Q18. [Senior] How would you store and query geospatial data, and what are the limits?

- **Short answer:** Use `GEOADD` and `GEOSEARCH` (6.2+). Internally it is a sorted set with geohash scores. Good for nearby lookups, not for polygons or complex spatial queries.
- **Detailed explanation:** Precision is limited (about 0.6 m error range is typical for the 52-bit geohash), and latitude is limited to roughly ±85.05°. `GEOSEARCH` is O(N+log M) where N is the number of items in the bounding area. A single huge geo key is a hot key; shard by region.
- **Practical example:**

```bash
GEOADD drivers 13.361389 38.115556 "d1" 15.087269 37.502669 "d2"
GEOSEARCH drivers FROMLONLAT 15 37 BYRADIUS 200 km ASC WITHDIST
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"Millions of drivers update location every few seconds. Design considerations?"* **Answer:** Shard by city or grid cell, apply TTL or cleanup of inactive drivers (a geo set has no per-member TTL), batch updates through pipelines, and consider whether updates need to be durable at all.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Redis geo supports polygon queries" (not natively in core geo commands).

### Q19. [Senior] How do you model a many-to-many relationship (users and groups) in Redis, and what are the consistency problems?

- **Short answer:** Keep two sets: `group:{id}:members` and `user:{id}:groups`, and update both in one transaction or Lua script. Redis has no referential integrity, so the application owns consistency.
- **Detailed explanation:** If both sets are updated in separate commands, a crash between them leaves them inconsistent. `MULTI/EXEC` makes both writes atomic with respect to other clients (not rollback-on-error). In Cluster, both keys must share a hash tag (`{group:7}`) to be in one transaction, which may force data placement compromises.
- **Practical example:**

```ts
await redis
  .multi()
  .sadd('group:7:members', 'u42')
  .sadd('user:42:groups', 'g7')
  .exec();
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"Why not use hash tags for everything?"* **Answer:** Hash tags pin keys to one slot, and over-using them concentrates data and load on one shard, creating hotspots.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "MULTI rolls back if one command fails" (it does not roll back runtime errors).

### Q20. [Staff] You must choose a data model for 50M user sessions with per-session attributes, TTL, and "list all sessions for a user". Walk through it.

- **Short answer:** One Hash per session (`sess:{sid}`) with TTL, and a per-user Set (`user:{uid}:sessions`) of session IDs for listing. Clean up the user set lazily because set members have no TTL.
- **Detailed explanation:** Memory per session must be measured (hash overhead plus key name). The user set can drift (stale IDs after session expiry); either verify membership with `EXISTS` when listing, use a sorted set with expiry timestamp as the score and prune with `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE`, or subscribe to keyspace expiry events (best effort only; they are not guaranteed delivery). At 50M sessions, shard by session ID (Cluster or client-side), and keep the user index sharded by user ID, accepting that session creation is then a two-shard write.
- **Practical example:**

```ts
await redis.multi()
  .hset(`sess:${sid}`, { uid, ua, createdAt: Date.now() })
  .expire(`sess:${sid}`, 86400)
  .zadd(`user:${uid}:sessions`, Date.now() + 86400_000, sid)
  .exec();
// List active: ZRANGEBYSCORE user:{uid}:sessions <now> +inf
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"In Cluster those three keys are on different slots. What now?"* **Answer:** `MULTI/EXEC` will fail with CROSSSLOT. Use two separate operations with an idempotent repair path (the sorted set is self-healing by score), or use a hash tag on the user ID for both keys if the per-user fan-out is small.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Rely on keyspace notifications to remove session IDs from the set" (not reliable; notifications are fire-and-forget).

## 17.3 Section C: Caching

### Q21. [Intermediate] Explain cache-aside, read-through, write-through, and write-behind.

- **Short answer:** Cache-aside: the app checks the cache, then the DB on a miss, then fills the cache. Read-through: the cache layer loads from the DB itself. Write-through: writes go to cache and DB synchronously. Write-behind: writes go to cache and are flushed to the DB asynchronously.
- **Detailed explanation:** Redis itself does not do read-through; your application or a library does. Cache-aside is the default in Node/NestJS because it is simple and tolerates cache outages. Write-through keeps the cache fresh but doubles write latency. Write-behind is fast but risks data loss if Redis dies before the flush, so it needs durable queues and idempotent flushes.
- **Practical example:**

```ts
async function getProduct(id: string): Promise<Product> {
  const key = `product:v1:${id}`;
  const hit = await redis.get(key);
  if (hit) return JSON.parse(hit);
  const row = await db.product.findById(id);
  if (row) await redis.set(key, JSON.stringify(row), 'EX', 300 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 60));
  return row;
}
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"Which pattern risks a stale cache after a write race?"* **Answer:** Cache-aside. Reader A misses and reads old DB data; writer updates DB and deletes the key; reader A then writes the old value to the cache. Mitigations: short TTLs, versioned values, or a delayed double-delete. The race is rare but real.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Write-through means Redis writes to the DB by itself."

### Q22. [Senior] How do you prevent a cache stampede (thundering herd)?

- **Short answer:** Make only one request regenerate a missing hot key. Use a per-key lock or single-flight, serve stale data while refreshing, add TTL jitter, and consider probabilistic early refresh.
- **Detailed explanation:** When a hot key expires, thousands of requests miss simultaneously and hit the database. Defenses stack: (1) in-process single-flight so one instance sends one DB query; (2) a Redis lock (`SET NX PX`) so one instance across the fleet regenerates; (3) stale-while-revalidate, storing a soft expiry in the value and serving the old value while a background refresh runs; (4) jittered TTLs so keys do not expire together; (5) early recomputation (XFetch algorithm).
- **Practical example:**

```ts
const inflight = new Map<string, Promise<any>>();

async function getWithLock(key: string, load: () => Promise<any>) {
  const cached = await redis.get(key);
  if (cached) return JSON.parse(cached);

  if (inflight.has(key)) return inflight.get(key);       // single-flight (per process)
  const p = (async () => {
    const lockKey = `lock:${key}`;
    const token = crypto.randomUUID();
    const got = await redis.set(lockKey, token, 'PX', 5000, 'NX');
    if (!got) {                                          // someone else is loading
      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 50));
      const again = await redis.get(key);
      if (again) return JSON.parse(again);
    }
    const value = await load();
    await redis.set(key, JSON.stringify(value), 'EX', 300);
    return value;
  })().finally(() => inflight.delete(key));
  inflight.set(key, p);
  return p;
}
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"The lock holder crashes. What happens to waiters?"* **Answer:** The lock expires after its TTL (5 s here). Waiters retry and one acquires it. The TTL must exceed the typical load time; fallback behavior if the lock is never acquired is to load anyway, accepting limited duplication.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Increase the TTL" (delays, doesn't remove, the stampede); "Use a bigger Redis".

### Q23. [Senior] What are cache penetration and cache avalanche, and how do they differ from a stampede?

- **Short answer:** Penetration: requests for keys that do not exist anywhere bypass the cache every time. Avalanche: many keys expire at once, or the cache goes down, flooding the DB. Stampede: many concurrent requests for the same expired hot key.
- **Detailed explanation:** Penetration defenses: cache negative results (`null` markers with short TTL), validate input, and use a Bloom filter of valid IDs. Avalanche defenses: TTL jitter, multi-layer caching, rate limiting and circuit breakers on the DB, and warming. Stampede defenses are in Q22.
- **Practical example:**

```ts
const NULL_MARK = '__null__';
const hit = await redis.get(key);
if (hit === NULL_MARK) return null;           // negative cache hit
if (hit) return JSON.parse(hit);
const row = await db.find(id);
await redis.set(key, row ? JSON.stringify(row) : NULL_MARK, 'EX', row ? 300 : 30);
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"Why keep the negative TTL short?"* **Answer:** An item created later would remain invisible until the negative entry expires. Creation paths should delete the negative marker explicitly.
- **Common incorrect answers:** Using the three terms interchangeably.

### Q24. [Senior] What is your cache invalidation strategy, and why is it considered hard?

- **Short answer:** Prefer TTL as the safety net plus explicit invalidation on write. Delete (not update) cache entries on writes, and accept a short staleness window. For groups of keys, use versioned namespaces or index sets.
- **Detailed explanation:** The difficulty is knowing every cached view that derives from a changed entity. Techniques: (1) key-per-entity with delete on update; (2) namespace versions: `catalog:v{N}:...`, bumping `N` invalidates everything logically with O(1) work and old keys expire by TTL; (3) tag sets mapping an entity to dependent keys; (4) event-driven invalidation from the DB (change streams, outbox, CDC). Delete-on-write beats update-on-write because it avoids writing stale data under races.
- **Practical example:**

```ts
const ver = await redis.get('ns:catalog') ?? '1';
const key = `catalog:v${ver}:list:page:${page}`;
// Invalidate everything:
await redis.incr('ns:catalog');
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"What is the cost of version namespaces?"* **Answer:** Old versions linger until TTL expiry and consume memory; there is one extra GET per read (cacheable in-process for a second or so); and the version key itself is a hot key.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Just flush the DB (`FLUSHALL`) on every change."

### Q25. [Senior] What happens if Redis goes down, and how should the application behave?

- **Short answer:** For a cache, the app should degrade gracefully: fail open to the database with timeouts, circuit breaking, and rate limiting to protect the DB. For queues and sessions, Redis is a critical dependency and needs HA.
- **Detailed explanation:** Design per use case: cache (bypass, protect DB), rate limiter (decide fail-open vs fail-closed; auth endpoints often fail-closed), distributed lock (fail closed: do not proceed without mutual exclusion if correctness matters), sessions (fall back to signed stateless tokens or force re-login), BullMQ (producers fail or buffer; use `enableOfflineQueue` carefully). Configure ioredis timeouts and retry strategy to avoid unbounded queues of commands in the Node process.
- **Practical example:**

```ts
const redis = new Redis({
  host, port,
  connectTimeout: 2000,
  commandTimeout: 500,
  maxRetriesPerRequest: 1,       // fail fast instead of queueing forever
  enableOfflineQueue: false,     // reject commands while disconnected
  retryStrategy: (times) => Math.min(times * 200, 3000),
});
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"When Redis comes back, the cache is cold. How do you avoid the DB melting?"* **Answer:** Rate-limit or queue DB access, use request coalescing, warm the hottest keys before routing traffic, and ramp traffic gradually. Persistence (RDB) on the cache primary shortens the cold period.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Catch the error and return 500." "Retry forever."

### Q26. [Intermediate] How do you design cache keys?

- **Short answer:** Use a stable, readable convention: `service:entity:version:id[:variant]`. Include everything that changes the value (tenant, locale, filters) and a schema version, keep keys short, and avoid unbounded user-provided input.
- **Detailed explanation:** Missing a dimension (tenant, language) causes cross-user data leaks, a serious bug. Including too many dimensions fragments the cache and lowers hit rate. Hash long or complex parameters (sorted JSON, then SHA-1) to a fixed length. Use `{}` hash tags only when you need multi-key operations in Cluster. A version segment lets you change serialization format safely.
- **Practical example:**

```ts
const key = `shop:product:v2:${tenantId}:${id}:${locale}`;
const listKey = `shop:list:v2:${tenantId}:${sha1(stableStringify(filters))}`;
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"Why is user-provided input in a key dangerous?"* **Answer:** Attackers can create unlimited distinct keys (memory exhaustion and cache pollution). Normalize and whitelist parameters, cap cardinality, and use short TTLs for low-value variants.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Use the raw URL as the key."

### Q27. [Senior] How do you handle stale data and consistency between cache and DB?

- **Short answer:** Accept eventual consistency within a defined staleness budget. Reduce it with delete-on-write, short TTLs on volatile data, versioned values, and event-driven invalidation. For data that must be strongly consistent, do not cache it, or read from the DB in that code path.
- **Detailed explanation:** Define the SLA first: "price may be stale for 60 s; stock must not". Use per-data-class TTLs. Include an `updatedAt` or version in the cached value and reject older writes with a Lua compare-and-set. The "write DB then delete cache" ordering is safer than the reverse, but with replicas lagging, a reader may re-cache stale replica data; read from primary right after writes or use a short delayed second delete.
- **Practical example:**

```lua
-- cas-set.lua: only write if incoming version is newer
local cur = redis.call('HGET', KEYS[1], 'v')
if (not cur) or (tonumber(ARGV[1]) > tonumber(cur)) then
  redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'v', ARGV[1], 'data', ARGV[2])
  redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[3])
  return 1
end
return 0
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"Why is delete-after-DB-write still racy with MongoDB or Postgres replicas?"* **Answer:** A read from a lagging replica after the delete can repopulate the cache with the pre-write value. Route post-write reads to the primary, or delay the second invalidation beyond the typical replica lag.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Write to cache first, then DB" (a failed DB write leaves phantom data).

### Q28. [Staff] Design a multi-layer cache (CDN, in-process, Redis). What are the invalidation challenges?

- **Short answer:** A request checks the CDN, then an in-process LRU (L1), then Redis (L2), then the DB. Invalidation uses short L1 TTLs plus Pub/Sub or client-side caching invalidation messages to evict L1 across instances.
- **Detailed explanation:** L1 absorbs hot keys and removes network latency but multiplies staleness by the number of instances. Redis supports client-side caching (6.0+, RESP3 tracking) where the server tells clients when a key changes. With ioredis you can implement your own invalidation channel using Pub/Sub, accepting that missed messages leave L1 stale until TTL. CDN invalidation is slower (purge APIs, `stale-while-revalidate`).
- **Practical example:**

```ts
const l1 = new Map<string, { v: any; exp: number }>();
sub.subscribe('cache:invalidate');
sub.on('message', (_ch, key) => l1.delete(key));
// writer: await redis.del(key); await redis.publish('cache:invalidate', key);
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"Pub/Sub dropped a message during a reconnect. How do you bound the damage?"* **Answer:** Keep L1 TTL short (for example 1–5 s), and on reconnect clear the entire L1. Correctness comes from the TTL bound, not from message delivery.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Pub/Sub guarantees invalidation."

### Q29. [Senior] How do you cache a paginated list or search result safely?

- **Short answer:** Cache IDs (or small page objects) with a bounded number of pages, version the namespace, and avoid caching deep pages. Cache entities separately so one entity change does not force rebuilding every list.
- **Detailed explanation:** Caching whole pages couples list freshness to every entity in it. A two-level approach stores list = array of IDs and `MGET`s entities. Deep pagination (page 5000) is rarely requested and pollutes memory; use cursor pagination and cache only the first few pages. Include sort and filter in the key.
- **Practical example:**

```ts
const ids: string[] = JSON.parse((await redis.get(listKey)) ?? '[]');
const items = ids.length ? await redis.mget(ids.map((i) => `product:v2:${i}`)) : [];
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"`MGET` in Cluster across slots?"* **Answer:** `MGET` requires one slot; ioredis `Cluster` does not split it for you automatically. Group keys by slot and send per-slot commands in a pipeline, or use hash tags if the group is small.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Cache every page forever."

### Q30. [Staff] A catalog gets 100k reads/sec and Redis CPU is saturated. What is your plan?

- **Short answer:** Measure first for hot keys, then add an in-process L1 cache, replicate hot keys (key suffixes), use read replicas, pipeline, shard with Cluster, and shrink payloads.
- **Detailed explanation:** Check `INFO commandstats`, `redis-cli --hotkeys` (needs an LFU policy), and `MONITOR` only briefly. Reduce per-request commands (one `MGET` instead of 20 `GET`s), compress values, use `GETEX` or avoid extra `EXPIRE` calls. For hot keys: L1 with 1–2 s TTL typically removes 90%+ of reads; or write the value to N copies (`product:123#0..N`) and read a random copy. Use replicas for reads when staleness is acceptable (async lag). Consider io-threads if network I/O dominates.
- **Practical example:**

```bash
redis-cli INFO commandstats | sort -t= -k3 -nr | head
redis-cli --hotkeys        # requires maxmemory-policy *lfu*
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"What do you lose with read replicas?"* **Answer:** Read-your-writes consistency and sometimes correctness after failover (a replica may be behind). Fine for catalogs, wrong for balances.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Just scale the VM vertically" (a single execution thread does not scale with cores).

## 17.4 Section D: Distributed systems

### Q31. [Senior] Implement a correct single-instance distributed lock with Redis.

- **Short answer:** `SET lock:key <random-token> NX PX <ttl>` to acquire, and a Lua compare-and-delete to release only if the token still matches. Use a TTL so a crashed holder does not block forever.
- **Detailed explanation:** The random token prevents deleting someone else's lock after your own lock expired. The TTL needs to be larger than the critical section, and long operations need renewal (watchdog) or a fencing token. A lock built on one Redis node is only as safe as that node: with async replication a failover can lose the lock and allow two holders.
- **Practical example:**

```ts
const RELEASE = `
if redis.call('get', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call('del', KEYS[1])
else return 0 end`;

async function withLock<T>(name: string, ttlMs: number, fn: () => Promise<T>) {
  const token = crypto.randomUUID();
  const ok = await redis.set(`lock:${name}`, token, 'PX', ttlMs, 'NX');
  if (!ok) throw new Error('lock busy');
  try { return await fn(); }
  finally { await redis.eval(RELEASE, 1, `lock:${name}`, token); }
}
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"The critical section takes longer than the TTL. What happens?"* **Answer:** Two clients can hold the lock. Extend the TTL periodically only if still the owner (Lua), and protect the downstream resource with a fencing token (monotonic counter checked by the resource) so a stale holder's write is rejected.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "`SETNX` then `EXPIRE`" (not atomic; a crash between them leaves a permanent lock). "`DEL` the key to release" (may delete another owner's lock).

### Q32. [Staff] Is Redlock safe? When would you not use it?

- **Short answer:** Redlock acquires locks on a majority of N independent Redis nodes. It improves availability but relies on bounded clock drift and process pauses, so it does not provide strict safety. For correctness-critical mutual exclusion, use a consensus-based system or fencing tokens with a datastore that enforces ordering.
- **Detailed explanation:** The well-known critique: a client can pause (GC, VM stall) after acquiring the lock, and the lock expires; another client acquires it; the first client resumes and writes. Fencing tokens fix this only if the resource checks them, and Redlock itself does not generate monotonic tokens. For efficiency-only locks (avoid duplicate work), a single-node lock is usually enough. For correctness (money), prefer database constraints, optimistic concurrency, or a consensus store (etcd, ZooKeeper).
- **Practical example:** Prefer a DB-level guarantee over any lock:

```sql
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100, version = version + 1
WHERE id = 7 AND version = 12 AND balance >= 100;  -- optimistic check, atomic
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"How would you decide between lock-for-efficiency and lock-for-correctness?"* **Answer:** Ask what happens if two holders run at once. If the result is wasted work, a simple Redis lock is fine. If the result is data corruption, the lock must not be your only defense.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Redlock is perfectly safe." "Redlock is useless."

### Q33. [Senior] How do you prevent duplicate job execution?

- **Short answer:** Make the job idempotent and deduplicate at the producer and consumer. Use stable job IDs, an idempotency key stored with `SET NX`, and database unique constraints. Assume at-least-once delivery.
- **Detailed explanation:** Duplicates arise from retries, producer retries after timeouts, stalled-job recovery, and double clicks. Exactly-once processing is not achievable end to end; you get effectively-once through idempotent effects. In BullMQ, a custom `jobId` makes `queue.add` ignore a job with an existing ID (while the earlier job is still stored); the consumer must still be idempotent.
- **Practical example:**

```ts
await queue.add('send-invoice', { invoiceId }, { jobId: `invoice:${invoiceId}` });

// Consumer side idempotency
const first = await redis.set(`done:invoice:${invoiceId}`, '1', 'EX', 86400, 'NX');
if (!first) return;                 // already processed
await sendInvoice(invoiceId);       // ideally also guarded by a DB unique constraint
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"The consumer sends the email, then crashes before writing the `done` key. What happens on retry?"* **Answer:** A duplicate email. Fully avoiding it needs the external system to support idempotency keys. Otherwise write the done-marker before sending (risking a lost send) and choose which failure is cheaper.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "BullMQ guarantees exactly-once."

### Q34. [Senior] Redis is a cache in front of a primary DB. How do you reason about consistency?

- **Short answer:** The DB is the source of truth. The cache is allowed to be stale within a stated bound. Redis offers eventual consistency under async replication, and you design reads and writes around that.
- **Detailed explanation:** Redis single-node commands are linearizable on the primary. With replicas, reads from replicas are eventually consistent. Cluster does not offer strong consistency: writes acknowledged by a primary can be lost during failover. `WAIT n timeout` blocks until `n` replicas acknowledge, reducing but not eliminating loss. Define per data class: read-your-writes, monotonic reads, bounded staleness.
- **Practical example:**

```bash
SET order:1 paid
WAIT 1 100        # returns number of replicas that acked within 100 ms
# (integer) 1
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"Does `WAIT` make Redis CP?"* **Answer:** No. It informs the client about replica acknowledgements but a failover can still promote a replica that missed the write if the acknowledged replica is not the one elected, and the cluster has no consensus log for data writes.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Redis Cluster is strongly consistent."

### Q35. [Senior] How are keys distributed in Redis Cluster?

- **Short answer:** There are 16,384 hash slots. A key's slot is `CRC16(key) mod 16384` (using only the `{hash tag}` if present). Each primary owns a subset of slots.
- **Detailed explanation:** Clients cache the slot map and follow `MOVED` (permanent) and `ASK` (during migration) redirects. Multi-key commands and transactions require all keys in one slot, otherwise `CROSSSLOT` error. Resharding moves slots between nodes online with `redis-cli --cluster reshard` or `rebalance`. Databases other than 0 are not supported.
- **Practical example:**

```bash
redis-cli CLUSTER KEYSLOT user:42          # (integer) 5474 (example)
redis-cli CLUSTER KEYSLOT "{user:42}:cart" # same slot as "{user:42}:profile"
redis-cli -c -p 7000 SET foo bar           # -c follows redirects
# -> Redirected to slot [12182] located at 127.0.0.1:7002
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"Why 16,384 slots and not more?"* **Answer:** Cluster bus gossip messages carry the slot bitmap; 16,384 slots fits in 2 KB per heartbeat, and clusters beyond about 1,000 primaries are not the design target, so more slots would add overhead without benefit.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Consistent hashing with a ring" (Redis uses fixed hash slots).

### Q36. [Senior] What are the limits of Pub/Sub?

- **Short answer:** At-most-once delivery, no persistence, no replay, no acknowledgements, and subscribers that are slow can be disconnected. Use Streams if you need durability.
- **Detailed explanation:** Messages are delivered only to currently connected subscribers. A disconnected subscriber misses everything. Slow subscribers accumulate output buffer; `client-output-buffer-limit pubsub` disconnects them. In Cluster, classic `PUBLISH` is broadcast to all nodes (cost grows with nodes); sharded Pub/Sub (7.0+, `SPUBLISH`/`SSUBSCRIBE`) keeps messages within a shard. A subscribed connection cannot run other commands (RESP2), so use a dedicated connection.
- **Practical example:**

```ts
const sub = redis.duplicate();
await sub.subscribe('orders');
sub.on('message', (ch, msg) => console.log(ch, msg));
await redis.publish('orders', JSON.stringify({ id: 1 }));
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"Use Pub/Sub for WebSocket fan-out across 6 Node instances. What breaks?"* **Answer:** Messages sent during a reconnect are lost. That is acceptable for presence/notifications, but not for chat history; persist in DB or a Stream and let clients resync from a last-seen ID.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Pub/Sub queues messages for offline subscribers."

### Q37. [Staff] How do you implement a rate limiter that is correct across multiple app instances?

- **Short answer:** Keep the counter in Redis and make check-and-increment atomic with Lua. Choose the algorithm (fixed window, sliding window log, sliding window counter, token bucket) based on accuracy and cost.
- **Detailed explanation:** Fixed window is cheapest but allows 2x bursts at window boundaries. Sliding window log (sorted set) is exact but memory-heavy. Sliding counter approximates using two windows. Token bucket permits controlled bursts. All must be atomic to avoid races; and in Cluster, the keys must be in one slot per limiter identity. Decide fail-open or fail-closed if Redis is unreachable.
- **Practical example:**

```lua
-- fixed window: KEYS[1]=counter, ARGV[1]=limit, ARGV[2]=window seconds
local c = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1])
if c == 1 then redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[2]) end
if c > tonumber(ARGV[1]) then return 0 end
return 1
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"What is the bug if `EXPIRE` is called in a separate round trip?"* **Answer:** If the client crashes between `INCR` and `EXPIRE`, the key never expires and the user is blocked permanently. Doing both in Lua (or `SET NX EX` first) avoids it.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Rate limit in memory per instance" (limit multiplies by instance count).

### Q38. [Senior] Redis is used for idempotency keys on an HTTP API. Describe the design.

- **Short answer:** On the first request with an `Idempotency-Key`, `SET key in-progress NX EX`, process, then store the response under the key. Repeated requests return the stored response, or 409 if still in progress.
- **Detailed explanation:** Store a small state machine: `processing` then `done:<response-hash>`. TTL should cover the client retry window (24 h is typical). If the process crashes in `processing`, the entry expires and the client may retry; side effects must still be protected by DB constraints. Bind the key to the request fingerprint (method, path, body hash) to reject key reuse with a different payload.
- **Practical example:**

```ts
const k = `idem:${userId}:${idemKey}`;
const claimed = await redis.set(k, JSON.stringify({ s: 'processing', fp }), 'EX', 86400, 'NX');
if (!claimed) {
  const prev = JSON.parse((await redis.get(k))!);
  if (prev.fp !== fp) throw new UnprocessableEntityException('key reuse');
  if (prev.s === 'processing') throw new ConflictException();
  return prev.response;
}
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"Redis fails over and loses the key. What is the exposure?"* **Answer:** A retried request may execute twice. For payments, add a DB unique constraint on the idempotency key in the same transaction as the side effect. Redis is the fast path, the DB is the guard.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Idempotency means caching the response forever."

### Q39. [Staff] How do you elect a leader or run a "singleton cron" across NestJS instances using Redis?

- **Short answer:** Use a lock with TTL and renewal (`SET NX PX` plus a heartbeat). Better: use BullMQ repeatable jobs or a scheduler so the queue guarantees one job per tick.
- **Detailed explanation:** A lock-based leader can be lost on failover, GC pause, or clock jumps, so the leader must check validity before each unit of work and tolerate rare dual leaders via idempotency. Letting BullMQ schedule a repeatable job moves the "only one runs" concern into the queue; the worker that picks the job runs it. Still make the job idempotent.
- **Practical example:**

```ts
await queue.upsertJobScheduler('nightly-report', { pattern: '0 3 * * *' },
  { name: 'report', data: {} });   // BullMQ v5.16+ API; verify your installed version
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"What if the cron job takes longer than the interval?"* **Answer:** Jobs overlap. Use a concurrency guard (lock or `jobId` dedupe keyed by period) and skip or queue the next run deliberately.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Run cron on every instance, it's harmless."

### Q40. [Staff] How do you keep Redis and MongoDB/PostgreSQL consistent for a write that must update both?

- **Short answer:** Write to the database first (source of truth), then invalidate or update Redis. For guaranteed propagation use the transactional outbox pattern: write the change and an outbox row in one DB transaction, and a relay publishes to Redis or a queue.
- **Detailed explanation:** There is no distributed transaction across Redis and a SQL/Mongo DB. Dual writes fail partially. The outbox pattern gives at-least-once propagation, with consumers made idempotent. Alternatives: CDC (Debezium, Mongo change streams) feeding invalidation. TTLs repair missed invalidations.
- **Practical example:**

```sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE products SET price = 19 WHERE id = 7;
INSERT INTO outbox(topic, payload) VALUES ('product.updated', '{"id":7}');
COMMIT;
-- relay: poll outbox -> redis.del('product:v2:7') -> mark sent
```

- **Senior follow-up:** *"What if the relay delivers the invalidation twice or out of order?"* **Answer:** Deleting a key is idempotent, so duplicates are safe. For update-style messages, include a version and apply only newer ones.
- **Common incorrect answers:** "Wrap both in a try/catch and roll back."
